items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505, the geopolitical landscape of early modern Europe would have been radically transformed, most notably by averting the English Reformation and establishing an independent, sovereign Kingdom of Naples. 

In 1505, Catherine was living in a state of political limbo in England following the death of her first husband, Arthur Tudor. Her betrothal to the future Henry VIII was stalled by diplomatic and financial disputes between Henry VII and her father, Ferdinand II of Aragon. Historically, Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, was the heir to the deposed Neapolitan branch of the House of Trastámara and was living as a captive of Ferdinand of Aragon. If the Aragonese king had chosen to marry his daughter to the Duke, it would have been a strategic masterstroke to pacify the rebellious Neapolitan nobility. By restoring the native Neapolitan heir to the throne alongside his own fiercely loyal daughter, Ferdinand of Aragon would have transitioned Naples from a contested territory into a secure, semi-independent client kingdom, rather than absorbing it as a direct Spanish viceroyalty.

The most profound global consequence of this union would be the alteration of English history. Without Catherine of Aragon in England, Henry VIII would have married a different European royal—likely a French princess or a Habsburg. Consequently, the specific dynastic crisis that defined Henry’s reign—his desperate pursuit of an annulment from Catherine to secure a male heir—would never have occurred. Without the "King's Great Matter," Henry’s schism with Rome would be entirely averted. England would likely have remained a staunchly Catholic nation, profoundly altering the religious demographics of Europe, preventing the eventual rise of Puritanism, and completely erasing the historical Tudor succession of Mary I and Elizabeth I.

In Italy, the establishment of an independent Naples under Catherine and the Duke of Calabria would have shifted the balance of power during the Italian Wars. Rather than being heavily taxed and administered by Spanish viceroys, a sovereign Naples would have retained its wealth, fostering a distinct Southern Italian Renaissance. Catherine, known historically for her formidable political acumen and education, would have been a highly effective queen consort or regent, helping to centralize Neapolitan power and defend the kingdom against French incursions. The Neapolitan court would have become a major diplomatic hub in the Mediterranean, serving as a buffer state between the Papal States, the expanding Ottoman Empire, and rival European powers. 

Furthermore, this marriage would have lightened the administrative burden on the future Emperor Charles V (Catherine’s nephew). Historically, Charles inherited Naples along with Spain, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Americas, leading to massive imperial overextension. With Naples ruled by a cadet branch of his family, Charles would still enjoy a reliable military ally in the Mediterranean without the financial drain of directly garrisoning the territory. Ultimately, this single marital pivot in 1505 would have preserved the religious unity of Western Europe while permanently altering the map of Italy, allowing a sovereign Southern Italian kingdom to flourish centuries before the historical unification of the peninsula.

items.question: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980
human_answers: India has only recently emerged as one of the world’s chief polluters; some two decades ago, Russia and Japan had a bigger mark, and in 1980 Canada was the bigger polluter. Depending on how decarbonized the economies of the First World are by 2000, India’s subsequent economic growth could be magnitudes cleaner than it was OTL. China you have a better point about, though first, their massive economic rise in the three decades after Mao’s death or so is pretty contingent, and second, they still only caught up to the already carbon stagnant EU in 2002. Imagine if the US was still comparable, as they were OTL until the mid 1980’s; now imagine, as China is getting ready to join the WTO in the late 90’s and early 2000’s, the west is also pushing a world climate treaty that (among other things) pushed these three major blocs (the US, Europe, and China) to curb their emissions going into the future. Even if India still sees their emissions rise, wouldn’t the fact that by far the largest producers are simultaneously cutting emissions lead to net reduction?

Well, is the point of your question, can we limit temperature rise by today , or in perpetuity? If the former, then greater adoption of nuclear energy in the West is probably a good enough answer; by the time Chinese and Indian energy use spikes, the resultant temperature spike won't come until after today. Maybe. But that seems like the wrong question, I interpret it as how to prevent such a spike from EVER occurring, rather than just occurring 10 years late. And for that, there's a big challenge. How do developing countries get off the ground? Hydrocarbons are great for that. If the big emitters of the 60s all switched to nuclear, that's fantastic--but China and India can't afford to START with nuclear, nobody can, which means a huge amount of hydrocarbons being burned when they start heavily industrializing. As a solution, perhaps their rise as industrial powers can be delayed a few decades? If they started industrializing in 2025 instead, they might use shale gas or solar, which are now the cheapest sources of power. But the production of those isn't domestic to China, which is a huge part of their use of coal--they don't have to import it. Tentatively, maybe the Soviet Union needs to have greater economic development and a softer landing when it falls? If they can be an industrial exporter while powered off domestic nuclear and natural gas, and remain so in the 1990s, then Chinese growth will be very different, and overall emissions will be lower. Cars and planes are obvious problems. I would also posit beef as a problem--methane is significantly more powerful than carbon in greenhouse effect, and is estimated as responsible for 20 to 30 percent of human-origin warming. Sixty percent of methane emissions are estimated as human-caused, with a big one being agriculture, and beef is responsible for a LOT of agriculture. So a poorer world, that eats less meat, would have lower methane emissions. So too would a world with fewer wetlands, so perhaps a little more paving of swamps would be good from the perspective of this question. Just thoughts. I'll be back for more, probably.

No, because they're already too anti-nuclear. The R&D and thus cost curves on silicon-based solar cell production, and on improved battery capacity, are both pushed pretty hard historically by electronics industry spinoffs. It's hard to see any sort of policy pushes for renewables accelerating those more than marginally, and dramatic acceleration is what you need to make them cost-viable decades ahead of schedule. On the other hand, nuclear was deliberately hobbled by US policy in the 1970s. People like to blame 1979's Three Mile Island, but (for a couple examples) the AEC to NRC switchover was passed by Congress and signed by Ford in 1974, while Carter's anti-reprocessing moratorium was in 1977. If you instead have the US adopt its own version of France's Messmer Plan in 1974 (which is tricky, because Messmer was able to simply ignore anti-nuclear sentiments due to government and economy structure in ways the US government couldn't), you get nuclear power economies of scale driven by the joint US-French demand that make it a more-attractive alternative throughout the rest of the industrialized world. Imagine Thatcher's government nuclearizing Britain in part to undercut the coal unions, for example. Then, if US electricity is something like 75% nuclear in 1990 (like France in 1990, instead of the historical 20%), with the UK fast-following? Now you have the necessary condition (it not hobbling the US) for international trade treaties and the like based on carbon emissions, after a decade of greenhouse effect publicity (since the 1979 NAS report), with the first IPCC report coming out. (Yes, sure, butterflies will scramble the details, but "coal is bad" science, if anything, will be better-funded if the US is transitioning from coal.) If Japan has (as is likely) lagged the US/France/UK in adoption of nuclear, this will be a particularly easy sell, since everybody in the West in 1990 is looking for an excuse to be protectionist against "Japan, Inc." And with that set up, you have the trick for going forward. If China (etc.) has to avoid coal power to export to Western markets, China either will figure out how to avoid coal, or it won't develop because it won't have markets to sell into.

I can give you two, PODs, One being no 3 Mile Island and the other being no John Sununu. So the real easy way to cut down on CO2 emissions is to cut down on coal use, and both PODs give easy ways to do just that. After the banning of CFCs in the late 80s, momentum existed for much harder caps on carbon than were discussed later. In particular, serious curtailment of coal as an energy source in the developed world was mooted. However, this momentum was handicapped with a lack of US Presidential support, with Bush Sr being advised against supporting these efforts by his Chief of Staff, John Sununu. Remove Sununu, and US support for carbon caps become more likely earlier. In addition with no 3MI incident, nuclear technology in the west could become less taboo, giving a viable alternative to coal fired power earlier. I could see a scenario where industry, much like CFCs, sees the financial opportunities in replacing coal with a nuclear/gas mix, and does not get in the way of any cuts to carbon emissions. A good book on the subject in your timeframe is Loosing Earth, by Nathanial Rich, which goes into detail about the drive to curtail emissions in the late 80s. would highly recommend giving it a read.
items.original_question:
AHC: Curb Global Warming after 1980

So you know how Global Surface Temperatures have increased 1.3°C over pre-industrial levels at present, and how a big part of the current Climate Movement is trying to limit further change as much as possible, 1.5°C being the best known* goal? Well, as recently as circa 1980, GST above PIL was only about 0.3°C, and had been hovering just below those levels for decades since the aftermath of WWII; in other words, a full degrees celsius of global warming only happened in the past 45 years alone. This is actually pretty astonishing when you realize how much of a turning point circa 1980 was to global carbon emissions -- both the biggest producers world-wide at the time, the US and Europe, initially saw their emissions peak, with Europe remaining controlled even as the US reversed course after a few years; Japan and Canada have a similar "false peaks" around the same time as the US; the USSR, of course, collapse circa 1990 and saw their emissions collapse thereafter, never to recover; and China was about to undergo a massive economic expansion that would see them become the world's largest emitters. So what I want to determine here is -- what is the latest PoD for avoiding this massive escalation of climate change, or of making it as small as possible? Could a PoD in the late 1970's (eg a continuation of Carter's energy policies in the US) have done the trick? If avoiding a full degrees celsius of warming wasn't seriously avertable by, say, 1975, how early do we need to go? 1960? The aftermath of WWII? In the event we can come to a consensus on the latest possible PoD and what would do the trick, we might also discuss how those changes to said countries' energy polices and to the global economy as a whole would have changed things overall. Thanks. *I'm really trying to avoid getting sidetracked in this discussion for the thread, so for anyone wanting to weigh in on whether its still feasible or how big of a deal missing that goal is, please take that to one of the Chat discussions -- much thanks!
items.model_answer:
If the world had successfully acted to curb global warming after 1980—capitalizing on the scientific consensus established by the 1979 Charney Report and the political momentum of the 1970s energy crises—the trajectory of global technology, geopolitics, and environmental health would be radically different today. 

To achieve this, governments would have had to aggressively pivot away from fossil fuels, likely sparking a massive, sustained renaissance in nuclear power while accelerating the commercial maturity of solar and wind technologies by decades. The automotive industry would have faced strict emissions regulations much earlier, pushing the widespread adoption of electric vehicles into the late 1990s or early 2000s rather than the 2020s. 

Economically and geopolitically, the early decline of the fossil fuel industry would have severely curtailed the wealth and global influence of petrostates. Nations heavily reliant on oil exports, such as the Soviet Union, Saudi Arabia, and Iran, would have faced premature economic crises, potentially altering the outcome of the Cold War and reducing the frequency of oil-driven conflicts in the Middle East. Meanwhile, early implementation of global carbon pricing—enacted before climate change became a hyper-polarized political wedge issue—would have reshaped global supply chains, favoring energy efficiency, localized manufacturing, and nations leading in green technology.

Environmentally, the Earth would have avoided the drastic temperature spikes of the 21st century. The Arctic ice cap would remain largely intact, global sea-level rise would have been minimized, and marine ecosystems would have been spared from catastrophic mass bleaching and rapid ocean acidification. Furthermore, the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, such as mega-wildfires, super-hurricanes, and deadly heatwaves, would be significantly lower, saving millions of lives and trillions of dollars in disaster recovery. 

Ultimately, climate change would be viewed today as a successfully managed 20th-century environmental triumph—much like the mitigation of acid rain or the closing of the ozone hole—rather than an existential and deeply polarizing global crisis.

items.original_question: What if No Seven Bishops' Death in 1558? Everyone knows about the death of Cardinal Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury shortly after Queen Mary in 1558. But less known- as in, not even listed when you google them- is that there were six other bishops who died around the same time (including Maurice Griffith, Bishop of Rochester). This led to the opening of several vacancies in the English Catholic Church at the start of Elizabeth I's reign. To the seven bishops who died, can be added Bishop Oglethorpe of Carlisle (who, while he crowned Elizabeth, was no fan of hers after she stormed out of his celebration of Christmas Mass in 1558 because he defied her) and Nicolas Heath, the archbishop of York, who, as the highest ranked cleric in England should've crowned Elizabeth, but declined the "honour". He lost his see in 1559. What would've happened to the Elizabethan Settlement if those seven (or nine) sees had not fallen vacant at exactly the same time (many remaining vacant until 1561). How much opposition would there be to Elizabeth TTL? And how would Elizabeth have dealt with the situation TTL? @BlueFlowwer @isabella @RedKing @HortenseMancini
items.model_answer:
If the seven Catholic bishops who died during the devastating influenza epidemic of 1558 had survived, the immediate result would have been the likely defeat of the Elizabethan Religious Settlement, fundamentally altering the course of English history. 

When Mary I died in November 1558, her Protestant half-sister Elizabeth I ascended the throne intending to sever England from Rome once again. However, any changes to the nation’s religion had to be passed by Parliament. In the House of Lords, the Marian bishops formed a unified, uncompromising Catholic bloc. Historically, the epidemic of 1558 wiped out the Archbishop of Canterbury, Reginald Pole, along with several other prominent Catholic bishops, leaving their sees vacant. Even with these vacancies, Elizabeth’s Act of Uniformity in 1559—the foundational document of the modern Church of England—passed the House of Lords by a razor-thin margin of just 21 to 18. All surviving bishops voted against it. 

Had those seven bishops lived to take their seats in the 1559 Parliament, their votes would have easily flipped the majority, defeating the Act of Uniformity by a margin of 25 to 21. This would have precipitated a massive constitutional and political crisis at the very dawn of Elizabeth’s reign. 

Faced with a House of Lords that outright rejected her Protestant settlement, Elizabeth would have been forced into a corner. She could not easily replace the bishops without them first resigning or being legally deprived of their sees, which required them to break a law that Parliament was now refusing to pass. To force her reforms through, Elizabeth would have had to resort to highly authoritarian measures. She might have been forced to artificially pack the House of Lords by creating a large number of new Protestant peers, or she might have had to manufacture treason charges to imprison the bishops—a drastic escalation of the tactic she historically used when she detained two bishops to secure her narrow victory. Either action would have alienated the moderate nobility, severely damaged her early legitimacy, and likely provoked an immediate Catholic rebellion.

Alternatively, Elizabeth might have been forced to compromise, accepting a much more conservative, quasi-Catholic religious settlement to appease the Lords. This could have resulted in a "Henrician" church model—Catholic in its rituals and theology, but independent of the Pope—delaying the true Protestantization of England for decades. 

In the long term, the survival of these bishops would have provided English Catholics with strong, institutional leadership during a highly vulnerable transition period. Without the swift and legal establishment of the Church of England in 1559, the country would have remained deeply divided and legally tied to Catholic traditions for much longer. This would have emboldened Catholic powers like Spain and France to intervene in English politics much earlier, potentially leading to a full-scale religious civil war rather than the relatively stable, gradual Protestant consolidation that historically characterized the Elizabethan era.

items.question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead?
human_answers: Alright, so here are some changes: I wash my hands of the issue with the Marian reforms. Let's move on from that. Marius helps coordinate the Dimidiatio Senatus by spreading rumors and disrupting trade and grain shipments. After the creation of the Roman Tribunal Republic, he stays in Italia, raises an army of soldiers, professionally trains them, and leads the early Tribunal Republic. Sulla comes to Rome, and while the battle is intense, Marius and Rome win a pyrrhic victory, with Marius dying later that year. During the Battle of Rome, which even enters the city itself and causes immense destruction, young Gaius Julius Caesar dies. The Tribunal Republic fights remnants of people sympathetic to Sulla, and just continues on as normal. The proscriptions never happen. The closest equivalent is that many wealthy families were killed by poorer people and their wealth confiscated during the Sullarian War. But there's not really a reign of terror, just a violent popular revolt. The way the Roman Tribunal Republic gets set up still gradually happens, and the Tribunal Senate eventually creates a regular militia force within Rome itself, so that way no general can march on Rome like Sulla did. Christianity already exists, but doesn't spread far, remaining a religion in Levant and Egypt. It's never institutionalized. Because of this, and other butterfly effects with regular peoples, Mohammed is never born, so Islam never comes to be. The Tribunal Republic is still militarized, but focuses on strategically allying Celtic and Germanic kings against their allies, trading with them using Rome's vast reach and access to trade routes, and slowly integrating them. Rome stays mostly to the coastline to enforce this and use the sea as easy travel, so the navy becomes larger. Once trade settlements eventually reach southern Morocco and find the sub-Saharan trade route and its goods, the effects from trade deals are amplified. Attila still happens, and while it shakes up Rome, they fight them off thanks to alliances and mercenaries. Cassius still exists, and he helps kickstart Roman mercantile economics after the Hunnic Invasion, beginning the gradual plutocratic trend in Roman politics with merchants. Also, slavery still exists. With wars not bringing in as many war-slaves, laws increasingly punished severe crimes with debt slavery, and also enslaved the children of slaves if both parents were enslaved at the time of birth. Chattel slavery and debt/penal slavery still firmly exists, and slaves are traded across the Mediterranean. Sources of war slaves are largely from rivals of allied Celtic, Germanic, African, or Arabic tribes, plus some hostile invading tribes, such as the Norse, the Avars, the Khazars, and various Turkic tribes, keeping Anatolia as "Anatolia" and Greek/Roman/Persian. By 1000, Rome has slowly expanded militarily, commercially, and culturally. There are Roman trade ports along the coast of the whole Mediterranean, the Red Sea, and Western Europe, including Britannia and Hibernia. There are military presences, but the trade of goods from far away was used as a carrot to keep Celts, Germans, Africans, and Arabs in line (alongside the stick of Roman military garrisons). It's less depopulation and colonialism and more commerce and trading settlement (think Islamic merchants). Zoroastrian Persia, having not collapsed from Islam in this timeline, is still around. However, the House of Karen took over after a civil war in the late 800s, so now they're the Karenian Empire, not the Sasanian Empire anymore. Instead of an emergency military command being called "Caesar," it's instead called a "Consul." However, Consuls explicitly only lead armies, while the Tribunal Senate and the Orator did their thing, with the highly-professional, well-paid Roman city garrison (named the "Custodes Romae") preventing any Consuls or generals from marching on Rome, as well as acting as the final line of defense against barbarian Invasions. The title of "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIT) is put on legion banners, and is otherwise just a term that proud Romans use to praise the Roman Tribunal Republic, or the "Res Publica Tribunorum Romanorum" (RPTR). Roman poets and generals say things like "Ave res publica inter marium!" Did I miss anything?

To a certain point, it may have been possible, given what happened in parts of Medieval Europe, but that was only possible because of Christianity, and even then, forced labour continued being an important part of the economy, but in the form of serfdom instead of chattel slavery. Also, some other things I'd like to point out: I can guess the inspiration for this, but in all likelihood it wouldn't work like that - remember that given the way Roman politics works all of those people have their own clients to call on, and who would likely be around the forum in Senate meetings - visa how quickly Scipio Nasica gathered enough support to take on the supporters of Tiberius Gracchus in 133. The senators wouldn't be sitting ducks, and what you'd probably see is a street battle between each side's mobs of supporters, more like the riots of 52 BC or 100 BC than anything else. Also, remember that the Senate wasn't continuously in session - each session had to be convened by a magistrate and each session only lasted one day, for religious reasons. May I remind you that (assuming this happens in 88 BC) Caesar is 12 years old around that time? Even Pompey was twice that age when he first gained military proeminence, and he only did so by raising and equipping a legion out of his own pocket, because he was too young to be officially appointed to any command.

Okay, let me try to tackle this. Keep in mind this is just my opinion, with the primary goal always being plausibility: As mentioned by others, Marian reforms is a historiographic myth. You'll have to find a reason for the optimates to support land reform. If your main PoD is Marius failing to outmaneuver Sulla, then that's a good starting point. A sunken grain ship won't be enough to inspire the people to want to topple the government. A year or two of very little grain coming in could do that. Remember Marius is very old and probably mentally sick by now. I doubt he lives far beyond early 87 BC. Other populares can take up that mantle, but again, they have to deal with all the rest of the First Class in the years following. Remember also in OTL how the Sullans won literally every single military engagement. In another thread I called it a curbstomp, and it really was a curbstomp. There is extreme support for the optimates in this time period in the Senate, and among soldiers too. There would be no reason to go to Anatolia to fight Sulla, since the populares control Rome. They would force Sulla to come to them as in OTL. Citizen militia can't do anything against legions. Rome has no garrison. Caesar is a teenage kid who's never led armies, he would never be given command. Unless you mean Caesar's father, who is kind of a nonentity. There are dozens of grown men who would command before he's even considered. No such thing as patrician armies. You might mean optimas/optimate armies. The vast majority of forces and leaders on both sides are plebeians. Patrician versus plebeian is by this time almost entirely a religious and social distinction, not a political one. I'll end it here, since the rest of it rests on ever deepening misunderstandings. It's not bad for a story that doesn't mind plausibility and wants to go by "Rule of Cool", so if you want to do it, go ahead. The way I'd try to do something similar, realistically: 1. Marius never breaks with Saturninus and Glaucia 2. Saturninus passes increasingly radical laws, with Marius supporting him due to thinking he can control him 3. The Senate comes into open conflict with Saturninus, passing a Senatus Consultum Ultimum against him and Glaucia 4. With the support of Marius's wealth and veterans, Saturninus and Glaucia are able to subdue the Senate; some senators are killed, others exiled 5. The Republic retains her name, or perhaps is renamed Populus Senatusque Romanus, thus putting the people first; tribunician powers are greatly expanded, to the point where consuls have little legislative power 6. Marius and allies legislate for Italian citizenship to increase their support 7. The crowd begins to realize Marius and allies can't provide the easier life and reforms they promised 8. Decreased provincial incomes due to recalcitrant governors and uncertain political situations create an economic slump Then there are several ways this could go, depending on what the author wants. Romans resistant to Italian citizenship start a much smaller Social War; hard economic times cause worse slave rebellions; a few governors gang up to march on Rome and topple this regime? There are multiple interesting paths. Things that would not happen: 1. Romans peacefully integrating barbarians into Roman government. Most you can expect is Friends and Allies, or barbarians living free but under Roman law in Roman provinces. Rome succeeded for a reason, and part of that reason was being chauvinistic. It's not a moral judgment, just something that made them very good at obtaining and maintaining control completely loyal to decisions emanating from the city of Rome. Famously Cato the Censor, a man from Tusculum (not even 15 miles from Rome), whose ancestors were all Roman and whose father and grandfather had had several horses killed under them in combat, was considered as being a barely Roman peasant by the senators of Rome. Even in OTL the first non-Julio-Claudian emperors were of old senatorial families. Then men whose ancestors had been Roman for generations 2. Anything touching the institution of slavery. Unfree labor is, to this very day, the basis of civilization. Not even in their wildest crack-smoking, mushroom-eating, smoke-puffing dreams would anybody in antiquity think of seriously ending unfree labor 3. A divorce of military from politics. That's an extremely modern concept, and even today not true of the vast majority of states. Prior to the 18th century it would be almost laughable to think the two aren't intertwined. Whoever has the force of arms makes the decisions; where there are more groups with force, they bargain to make decisions, or go to war. That's politics. It's also why barbarian emperors happened, because that's who started having military power. While ever Romans held military power, they made the decisions, they were the emperors. When they left that to barbarians, the situation quickly turned in the barbarians' favor 4. A centuries-long run of kumbaya where wars decrease in intensity and rivalries are mostly commercial. Commercial wars turn into military wars really quickly when one side can't establish complete dominance very quickly. Starting out commercial, the money comes in handy paying mercenaries to fight. Things only escalate from there. Commerce, the control of cash and goods and people, is actually one of the only reasons wars were fought historically. The only bigger one I can think of is agriculture (land) itself, that produces those goods and people Anyway, interesting idea. I would say read some more history, and understand how these processes actually evolve and shape the world. Also how the government in Rome worked. History works in grand, broad strokes and movements, so don't expect cultures and governments to turn on a dime. Even the transformation of Rome from a Republic to the Principate was gradual. People forget the civil wars actually took over five decades to get through. It was very much a process, and in the end rested very much on preserving some image and veneer of the old. For example Augustus holding imperium maius everywhere, becoming eventually pontifex maximus, retaining tribunician powers (despite being patrician by adoption), etc. were all very old, traditional things just twisted acceptably by time and political necessity (and with the force of legions backing it, of course). Changing how Rome works? Fine! Changing how Rome is called? Hmmmm, not so good! It took over three centuries, from Augustus to Diocletian, before it became acceptable to verbally acknowledge the emperor as Dominus (Master), and to prostrate before him. That's how long it took from Rome's government to transform from an Italian city-state to a Hellenistic autocracy. Anyway I've written too long anyway. Learn more and never stop thinking, you'll do fine with any timeline you write
items.original_question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead? This is a scenario I've imagined for a Rome that never becomes an empire. And also because I wanted to create a Roman Republic I could call "Intermarium" because I wanted to. This is how I see it happening as an origin lore for the story following this: In the 100s BCE, the Marian reforms happen. However, Optimates senators ensure that land reform is decided by the Senate. Eventually, when the Mithridatic War happens, Marius fails to outmanuever Sulla, and Sulla goes to fight King Mithridates VI. Resentful, Marius uses his populist rhetoric, connections with Roman tribunes, and a sunken grain ship to incite a riot in Rome. This riot, later called the "Dimidiatio Senatus," resulted in the Roman Senate being attacked and half of the senators killed, with the majority of the remainder (all Populares senators) joining the rioters, and the surviving Optimates senators fleeing Rome to the countryside. Following the Dimidiatio Senatus, Marius declares the creation of the "Tribuni Romanae Res Publicae" (TRRP), or "Roman Tribunal Republic," denouncing the old Senate as a now-dead continuation of the old hated kingdom and their sycophants. Marius establishes a Tribunal Senate of people aligned with him (later called Marians) to govern Rome, then marches to Anatolia to fight Sulla. In a battle in Greece, Sulla defeats Marius and executes him. Sulla marches his legion into Italia. At Rome, Sulla finds a large citizen militia and the Roman city garrison opposing him, and a bloody battle begins. With the help of a certain Gaius Julius Caesar, Rome defeats Sulla, albeit it's a pyrrhic victory due to larger casualties on Rome's side. Sulla is beaten to death by a furious mob. Following the Battle of Rome, Caesar asks the Marian Tribunal Senate to entrust him with command of the Roman Army in the fight against remaining Patrician armies outside of Rome that seek to crush what Marius created. The Tribunal Senate trusts Caesar, and orders him to quash the opposition (later called Sullarians). In what is later known as the Sullarian War, Caesar crushes Patrician armies and confiscates the families' wealth and grants it to a Tribunal Senatorial Treasury, which is used as the central place of wealth of Rome, and funds from it are used to pay standard wages to soldiers. Caesar is a revered war hero, praised as Marius' heir. Caesar then relieves himself of command of the Sullarian Campaign, and suggests expanding Rome into Gaul. However, before his request his accepted, he suffers a stroke and dies. In the aftermath of the Sullarian War, around the 1st Century AD, the Tribunal Senate tries to stabilize the Tribunal Republic. The previous classifications of plebeian or patrician are abolished; Romans are just "Civii," or "Citizens" (Civis for singular). Additionally, some laws are established or confirmed, such as the ban on mobilized troops within Italia, the prohibition of army officials in public offices, and a system where Roman Provinces each elect two senators to the Tribunal Senate, plus two senators elected by the city of Rome itself to the Tribunal Senate. Following the Sullarian War, there is a huge cultural shift away from militarized politics and aristocracy. Two new factions emerge: the Marians, who are reformists loyal to Marius' rhetoric and believe in helping the common people and pragmatically responding to crises, and the Caesarians, radicals who idolize Caesar that believe that all aristocracy should be destroyed and the republic only serve the common people. In the decades that followed, Rome would gradually expand, but mainly by courting Celtic and Germanic tribes and negotiating integration into the Roman Tribunal Republic. New provinces emerge, and Celtic/Germanic warriors are used as mercenaries alongside Roman armies. Trade and commerce began to prosper, and so the Roman Navy was prioritized for funding and seen as less corruptible. Also, Christianity happens. However, it does not expand as fast because of a lack of a Constantine figure, and eventually becomes a recognized, non-persecuted religion within Rome, like the Roman Pantheon, Celtic paganism, Germanic paganism, and the slowly-dying Cult of Mithras. Basically, Rome slowly turns into a mercantile, seafaring republic with integration treaties with as many Celtic and Germanic tribes they could negotiate with. Kind of like a republican Carthage, ironically. Additionally, as wars reduce in scale and more non-Romans join provincial and senatorial administration, slavery is gradually banned. Persia remains a strategic rival over competition for Arabia and Mesopotamia, yet wars reduce in intensity and the rivalry turns mostly commercial. Rome expands through trade and treaties, sticking to the coast, where ships can easily transport goods and protect cities (again, Carthage-like and kinda Venice-like). It also trades with Aksum, Nubian Kingdoms south of Sudan, and sub-Saharan nations like Mali and Ghana (since North African coastal settlements reach Morocco and the Canary Islands eventually). Eventually, the Hunnic Invasions happen. Rome managed to better deal with the invasion thanks to greater stability, Germanic cooperation/mercenary armies, and more stable politics. The Tribunal Senate appoints a general to the position of "Caesar," which becomes the title of a military commander charged with winning a campaign vital to Rome's survival. The Huns are repelled, but Rome's maritime and mercantile economy is disrupted. In the aftermath, a young merchant named Cassius Atticus Felix emerges. A shrewd merchant and tactical investor, he focuses on creating merchant fleets and creating more merchant outposts along the Mediterranean and Mare Hibericum (the Atlantic Ocean). It is because of him that coastal cities in Morocco expanded as far west as they did, and he advocated for reduced taxes and regulations on Roman merchants, calling for "Mercator Autonomia," or "Merchant Autonomy," to revitalize Rome's economy and create prosperity. Cassius was heading to personally found a trading town on the Canary Islands when a hurricane hit the area and killed him. However, Cassius becomes immortalized as a rebuilder of post-Hun Rome's economy. The merchant class, and those sympathetic to them, form a new faction based on his ideals, called the Cassians. A while after this, conservative Romans who disliked the existence of "uncivilized barbarians" in Rome and merchant "luxury and decadence" form a traditionalist faction named the Catonians, named after Cato the Elder. They believe in the superiority of Roman culture, worship the old Roman/Greek Pantheon, oppose luxury, and don't oppose the idea of re-establishing slavery. Gradually, merchant oligarchy seeps into the Roman Tribunal Republic as merchants start buying out senators and provincial representatives. The Caesarians firmly oppose it, and so grow closer with the Catonians. Inside the Caesarian faction, a schism slowly begins to brew as those who oppose Catonian traditionalism and Romano-centrism clash with those who do support it. After some more tribal integration, province establishment, commerce expansion, and minor warfare, Mohammad creates Islam, and unites the Arab tribes (slowly being integrated by the Romans and the Persians) in opposition to them. Rome and Persia temporarily create a defensive pact against the Islamic Invasions, otherwise known as the "Crisis of the 7th Century." If Gaius Marius had marched on Rome in 88 BC instead of Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the most profound consequence would be the shifting of the historical precedent of turning Roman legions against the capital. In actual history, Sulla broke this ultimate taboo, forever staining his legacy and setting the stage for the Republic's fall. In this counterfactual, Marius would bear the infamy of being the first general to march on Rome, fundamentally altering how both men are remembered. Marius would be viewed not merely as the savior of Rome from Germanic tribes, but as a tyrant who destroyed the Republic's sacred norms out of jealousy and an unquenchable thirst for the eastern command. Conversely, Sulla, having peacefully departed to fight Mithridates VI, would be remembered as the legitimate consul and loyal defender of the Senate.

Upon violently seizing Rome, Marius would likely have initiated his infamous purges of political rivals earlier than he did historically. However, given his advanced age and declining health, he would still likely die shortly after taking power, leaving the Populares faction in the hands of successors like Lucius Cornelius Cinna. Meanwhile, Sulla would prosecute the First Mithridatic War in the East with the undisputed moral high ground. Stripped of his command by an illegal military coup, Sulla would be viewed as the exiled champion of the Republic. After defeating Mithridates, Sulla’s eventual return to Italy would not be framed as a rogue general invading his homeland, but as a righteous campaign of liberation to free Rome from a hostile, unconstitutional junta. 

Following his victory in the ensuing civil war, Sulla would still likely assume the dictatorship to implement his conservative constitutional reforms and purge his enemies. Yet, without the original sin of his 88 BC march on Rome, his dictatorship would be interpreted by contemporary and future historians as a harsh but necessary restoration of law and order, rather than a hypocritical power grab. 

This role reversal would drastically alter the political paradigm for the next generation of Roman leaders, particularly the political "heirs" to Sulla and Marius. Julius Caesar, who historically leveraged his familial connection to Marius to build populist support, would struggle to rehabilitate his uncle’s image, as Marius would be universally condemned as the architect of military usurpation. When Caesar later crossed the Rubicon, it would be viewed as a direct continuation of Marian treason. On the other hand, the conservative Optimates would possess a much stronger ideological foundation, holding Sulla up as the ultimate model of republican loyalty. The precedent for using military force to seize political power would be entirely associated with the populist faction, completely reshaping the ideological battlegrounds of the late Roman Republic.

If al-Andalus had survived the Christian Reconquista and maintained a permanent Islamic state in the Iberian Peninsula, the trajectory of global history—particularly the Age of Discovery and European geopolitics—would have been fundamentally altered. 

The most immediate global consequence would be the disruption of the European colonization of the Americas. If the Iberian Peninsula remained divided between northern Christian kingdoms and a southern Islamic state, a unified Catholic Spain would not have emerged in the late 15th century. Without the victorious conclusion of the Reconquista in 1492, monarchs like Ferdinand and Isabella would not have had the political stability or financial capital to sponsor Christopher Columbus. Consequently, the "discovery" and subsequent colonization of the Americas would have been delayed or spearheaded by other emerging maritime powers, such as Portugal, England, or France. This would completely erase the Spanish Empire from history, along with the massive influx of New World silver that drove the early modern global economy.

In Europe, the geopolitical balance of power would shift dramatically. Without a unified, imperial Spain, the Habsburg dynasty would lack the vast wealth and military might it used to dominate 16th- and 17th-century European politics. This power vacuum would likely have allowed France to emerge as the undisputed continental hegemon much earlier, facing far less resistance in its territorial expansions. Meanwhile, the Iberian Peninsula itself would remain a multipolar region, defined by a complex web of alliances and conflicts between Christian kingdoms, the surviving Andalusian state, and North African powers. A surviving al-Andalus, likely wealthy from Mediterranean trade, could have developed into a formidable naval power, altering the dynamics of the Mediterranean Sea and acting as a permanent geopolitical bridge between Europe and the Islamic world.

Culturally and demographically, the survival of al-Andalus would mean that Islam would remain a major, indigenous presence in Western Europe into the modern era. The rich cultural exchange that characterized the medieval period—which heavily influenced the European Renaissance through the translation of classical, philosophical, and scientific texts—would have continued to evolve. Furthermore, the Spanish Inquisition and the Alhambra Decree of 1492 would likely never have occurred, meaning Sephardic Jews and Iberian Muslims would not have been expelled or forced to convert. This would preserve a vibrant, multi-religious society in southwestern Europe, leaving a permanent linguistic and cultural legacy where Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic romance languages would coexist and evolve alongside Castilian and Portuguese.

If Louis the Pious had successfully passed and maintained his reforms—most notably the *Ordinatio Imperii* of 817—the entire political and cultural trajectory of Western Europe would have been fundamentally altered, likely preventing the birth of the distinct nation-states of France and Germany. 

Historically, traditional Frankish custom dictated that an empire be divided equally among a ruler's surviving sons. Louis the Pious recognized that this partible inheritance would fracture the massive Carolingian Empire built by his father, Charlemagne. His *Ordinatio Imperii* was a revolutionary legal reform designed to establish a hierarchy: his eldest son, Lothair, would become the sole supreme Emperor, while his younger sons would rule as strictly subordinate kings. Historically, this reform failed because Louis later attempted to carve out a kingdom for his fourth son, Charles the Bald, sparking a series of civil wars that culminated in the 843 Treaty of Verdun, which permanently shattered the empire into West, Middle, and East Francia.

Had the *Ordinatio Imperii* succeeded and established a lasting precedent of primogeniture, the Carolingian Empire would have remained a unified, hegemonic superpower dominating Western and Central Europe. Without the fracturing of the empire into East and West Francia, the distinct geopolitical and linguistic boundaries that eventually formed modern Germany and France would not have materialized in the 9th century. Instead, Europe might have developed a singular, overarching imperial identity, akin to the dynastic cycles of imperial China or a more cohesive version of the Holy Roman Empire.

Militarily, a unified Carolingian state would have been far better equipped to handle the existential threats of the 9th and 10th centuries. Historically, the Vikings, Magyars, and Saracens exploited the internal civil wars and fragmented defenses of the divided Frankish kingdoms. A centralized imperial army under a single emperor could have coordinated massive, unified responses to these incursions. Consequently, devastating events like the Siege of Paris might have been thwarted, and the Vikings may never have been granted the territory that became the Duchy of Normandy, which later profoundly impacted the histories of England and the Mediterranean.

Religiously and culturally, Louis’s ecclesiastical reforms would have permanently centralized European Christianity. Working with Benedict of Aniane, Louis sought to standardize monastic life strictly under the Rule of Saint Benedict and bind the Church closely to the imperial crown. A successful implementation of these reforms within a unified empire would have created a deeply integrated church-state apparatus. This could have prevented the later extreme fragmentation of secular and religious authority, potentially altering or entirely averting future conflicts like the Investiture Controversy. 

Ultimately, if Louis the Pious's reforms had succeeded, Western Europe would have bypassed the highly fragmented, competitive feudal state system that characterized the Middle Ages. While this fragmentation historically drove European military and technological competition, a unified Carolingian Empire would have provided centuries of relative internal stability, drastically rewriting the map and the modernization of the Western world.

Particularly after the Sengoku period, cycles of civil war, the birth of new regimes, and expansion toward the continent were repeatedly observed. The navy would constitute the principal military force, and national defense strategy and institutional design would likewise be shaped under naval leadership. Furthermore, the direction of external expansion would be determined from the perspective of a maritime power, rather than that of a continental state. If Japan had chosen the route of a maritime power like Britain or the Venetian Republic, or if its modernization had been deliberately oriented toward a completely navy-led military structure, how would Japanese history have unfolded differently?
