Avoiding this massive, resource-draining land war would have removed the primary source of diplomatic friction between Japan and the Western powers. Without the aggressive continental expansion and the resulting atrocities in China, the United States would not have imposed the crippling scrap metal and oil embargoes in 1941, thereby removing the immediate catalyst for the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor.

Instead of military conquest on the continent, a navy-centric Japan would have likely modeled itself after the British Empire, focusing on securing sea lanes, building a formidable merchant marine, and establishing economic hegemony over Southeast Asia and the Pacific islands. By relying on naval deterrence and trade rather than military occupation, Japan could have maintained peaceful, or at least pragmatic, relations with the United States and Great Britain. The Anglo-Japanese Alliance, which lapsed in 1922, might even have been preserved or renegotiated if Japan had positioned itself as a stabilizing maritime trading power rather than a continental aggressor.

Militarily, Japan's industrial output would have been heavily concentrated on shipbuilding, naval aviation, and maritime logistics, creating an even more powerful fleet than it historically possessed. However, without the desperate need to secure oil by force to feed an army bogged down in China, this fleet would have served primarily as an instrument of deterrence, diplomacy, and economic protection. 

Ultimately, by avoiding the catastrophic overextension of the Pacific War, Japan could have survived the mid-20th century with its empire, infrastructure, and economy intact. This would have left Japan as the undisputed indigenous superpower in Asia, drastically changing the trajectory of the Cold War, the Chinese Civil War, and the decolonization of Southeast Asia.

items.question: What If Joseph Bonaparte became a US Senator in 1829?
human_answers: The Know-Nothings don't exist yet in the 1820s. That said, there is something that might alienate him from the nascent Whigs - he's a Freemason, and a pretty involved one - he was Grand Master of the Grand Orient of France during Napoleon's entire reign as emperor, founded the National Lodge of Spain, and that aspect in particular helped hurt his legitimacy among the Spanish when he was made king there. Now, the period where Joseph would enter American politics in your scenario largely coincides with the spread of the Anti-Masonic movement in New York, and their members would largely go on to integrate the Whig party later down the line. In the other hand, as time passed, the Anti-Masonic aspect was diluted so much that they ended up running a Mason as their 1832 presidential candidate, who even defended the Order in a speech before the convention that nominated him, so he might go either way.

In 1908? Highly doubtful, given Bonaparte's Catholic faith. That wouldn't have played at all in much of the South (not that it would have mattered much in terms of getting votes for the GOP there), and might have been a hindrance elsewhere. If he had somehow gotten the nomination, his running mate would certainly have been a Protestant from (likely) the midwest (Albert Beveridge?); TR would have had to do some strenuous campaigning on his behalf especially if Bryan (often referred to as "the Protestant pope") had been his opponent. The result would have been close if Bonaparte had won, and he'd have had to go to great lengths to demonstrate his independence from the Vatican. Still, the idea is intriguing: imagine the polling place schizophrenia of the Irish community in Boston, for example, given how accustomed that segment was to voting a straight Democrat ticket at the time. Also fascinating: Bonaparte was a strong advocate for civil rights for African-Americans. Had he somehow been elected, perhaps the entire cause of civil rights might have been advanced five years or so.
items.original_question: What if Joseph Bonaparte became a US Senator in 1829? Joseph Bonaparte in the early 1830s. ​ Yes, this is completely unrealistic, but it's not quite as outlandish as an actual ASB (hence why I'm posting it on here), as it was theoretically something that could have happened. Joseph Bonaparte had lived in the US since 1817, seemed to have been relatively well-liked during his time in America, and to be a senator you need to be a US citizen for at least nine years. Theoretically, had the former king of Naples and then Spain had desired it, he could have very well becoming a senator by the beginning of the Jacksonian period, when both of New Jersey's seats in the US senate were up for grabs in the 1828-29 senate elections. For this scenario, Joseph Bonaparte comes to decide he wants to integrate himself in the United States. After becoming a US citizen in 1819, Joseph manages to be elected to the US Senate representing New Jersey in the 1828-29. replacing Theodore Frelinghuysen from our own timeline. What exactly happens, domestically, and in terms of the US' relationships with foreign countries, and in any other conceivable aspect, in this timeline where a former monarch manages to become a US Senator at the beginning of the Jackson administration.
items.model_answer:
If Joseph Bonaparte, Napoleon’s older brother and the former King of Naples and Spain, had become a United States Senator in 1829, it would have triggered a severe international diplomatic crisis while introducing a bizarre aristocratic dynamic into the populist era of Jacksonian Democracy. Historically, Joseph lived in luxurious exile at his Point Breeze estate in New Jersey from 1815 to 1832. To take a Senate seat in 1829, he would have had to pursue American citizenship immediately upon his arrival to satisfy the Constitution's nine-year citizenship requirement for senators. 

The most immediate consequence of Senator Bonaparte would be an international uproar. The restored Bourbon monarchy in France, along with the conservative Holy Alliance of Russia, Prussia, and Austria, would have viewed his political elevation as a direct provocation. European powers already harbored deep suspicions of the United States as a cradle of revolution; seeing a Bonaparte wielding federal legislative power would likely have led to recalled ambassadors, severe trade embargoes, and a freezing of transatlantic relations. It would have severely tested the Monroe Doctrine, forcing newly inaugurated President Andrew Jackson to navigate a precarious line between defending American democratic sovereignty and avoiding a naval or economic conflict with European empires.

Domestically, Joseph’s entry into the Senate would have created a fascinating political paradox. The year 1829 marked the beginning of Jacksonian Democracy, defined by frontier populism and the championing of the "common man." Bonaparte, however, was a fabulously wealthy, highly cultured European exile. Despite his imperial background, Joseph’s political inclinations in the U.S. would likely have aligned him with the National Republicans (the precursor to the Whig Party) led by figures like Henry Clay and John Quincy Adams. Drawing on his administrative experience in Europe and his personal investments in American canals, Bonaparte would have been a vocal proponent of the "American System," advocating heavily for federal funding of internal improvements, infrastructure, and the national promotion of the arts and sciences. 

Culturally, his presence in the Senate chamber would have tested the American republican ethos. Political opponents would undoubtedly have used his former royal titles to smear him as an anti-democratic monarchist and a foreign infiltrator. However, his supporters would have framed his senatorial role as the ultimate triumph of American republicanism, proudly demonstrating to the world that in the United States, even former European kings were reduced to mere citizen-legislators. 

Ultimately, a Senator Bonaparte would have enriched American cultural institutions and accelerated infrastructure development, but at the high cost of dragging the young nation directly into the crosshairs of post-Napoleonic European paranoia.

items.question: What If Empress Elizabeth of Russia lives longer, long term trajectory of Germany without the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg?
human_answers: I mean, that was more or less the agreement. The Prussians, or more likely Brandenburgers, most likely considered that they would not control Prussia, would be a power on the level of Saxony or Bavaria. Prussia would be divided between Austria (Silesia + border areas), Saxony (Magdeburg/Halberstadt), Sweden (Pomerania), Russia (East Prussia), and possibly others for the Rhineland territories. The kingdom would be drastically reduced, possibly returning to approximately the size of the central Electorate of Brandenburg, destroying its status as a great power. France would likely gain the Austrian Netherlands unless Austria withdrew from the deal. However, I'm not sure if they would do that. What, Germany? The kingdom that united the German kingdoms is no longer a great power. France, which became a republic in OTL, may very well not experience total collapse, instead becoming a constitutional monarchy. Eliminating the entire process of potentially creating Germany. Honestly, the idea of Germany may very well never leave the drawing board. Austria didn't really want to unify the German kingdoms; it was quite happy with the kingdoms being linked to it but not absorbed. Perhaps some form of federation of northern Germany will occur, but that's not a certainty.

I think it depends on the exact settlement. What are the full concessions Prussia is forced to make? Does Frederick II remain in power or does he abdicate or just maybe try in die on the battlefield if it seems like all is lost? Are events in the west impacted, the Franco-British peace settlement? And how is the domestic situation in Russia impacted with Elizbeth living longer? And do changes in Russia spill over into Poland ie with the election for the successor to Augustus III? Then I think you really have to run through the events of the 1770-80s to figure out what the international scene looks like by the 1790s which in tern dictates how much room to maneuver Austria has in Germany as the subject of Imperial reform becomes a pressing issue. If we go with a healthy butterfly net and assume the war mostly ends as IOTL but with Austria regaining Silesia then yes, Austria retains preeminence in Germany and Prussia is knocked down a peg to the level of the other Electors. That certainly changes Austria's strategic outlook. I think there would be less pressure to secure Bavaria on the death of Max III. Since the claims were mostly fabricated Joseph may just let it pass to Charles Theodore without incident. The Balkans are probably where you would first see the new strategic situation begin to change things. To some extent that depends on the fate of Russia. Again, assuming a butterfly net that still places Catherine on the throne with a similar eye cast towards the south and things get interesting. Without the threat of Prussia to the north Austria is better positioned to make gains in the Balkans. IOTL the Prussians were fairly obsessed with blocking any Austrian gains to the south which would strengthen Austria and upset the relative balance of power between the two. I still think the Greek Plan is a fantasy but its entirely possible that Austria recovers something along the lines of the Passarowitz borders, perhaps incrementally over the course or the rest of the century. IOTL Austria almost took Oltenia but instead opted for Bukovina when Prussia redirected everyone towards a partition of Poland. ITTL attention Austria will be focused squarely to the south and the Danube so gains in Serbia, Bosnia and Wallachia are likely but Moldavia less so. Poland meanwhile probably does not undergo partition and remains a Russian client state in the near term. Although its also possible in a different context post ATL Seven Years War that the Polish Royal election in 1764 leads to a falling out between Russia and Austria. Then the next big question is whether the French revolution still breaks out and still proceeds as IOTL and what kind of state Austria is in internally at the end of Joseph II's reign. Presumably even if the Josephine reforms spark a backlash Austria is much better positioned to ride them out with the southern border secure and gains already made from the Ottomans and with no Prussia threat in the north. So even if the Austrian Netherlands break out in rebellion Joseph or Leopold would be able to put down the revolt more easily without it posing any kind of existential threat.

Considering that theoretically the agreement signed between Russia, Austria and Saxony, envisaged a territorial exchange between Royal Prussia and Courland ( with the recognition that the Wettins would retain the throne of the PLC ) while the Habsburgs would recover Silesia or parts of it, that said, the internal balance of the HRE, would be brought back to the previous Leopoldine period, with Vienna as the undisputed leader, and therefore there would be more room for maneuver to try to pass a new package of imperial reforms, certainly France gaining control of the Austrian Netherlands, would not let the imperial princes of the Rhineland and the Hanoverians sleep peacefully, but unfortunately the latter pay the price of having sided with Prussia or of wanting to remain neutral, regarding the possible idea of German unification, it is difficult for the Habsburgs to show a real interest, when they would prefer to maintain the Status Quo or at most consolidate their position in Swabia / Bavaria ( I could see the Bavarian crisis being easily resolved through an agreement, with Charles Theodore inheriting a good part of the duchy, while Vienna annexes small border areas ) finally I am of the opinion that in this scenario, the role of leadership of the Protestant front ( in Otl led by Berlin ) will be taken by the Hanover, who paradoxically will have to review their political priorities ( especially from the London point of view ), because with their choices they will find themselves diplomatically isolated, therefore they will necessarily have to be more active on the continent

It was already happening: Elizabeth could not force Buturlin to get out of his bases and start acting against Prussia. The only meaningful operation was capture of Kolberg and even it was to provide a secure supply line because the Austrians were refusing to do so and getting supplies from the PLC was extremely problematic. Among the Russian military (except those safely away from the front) there was not too much of an appetite for the further fighting and definitely no serious anymosity toward Fritz. Rumyantsev in OTL was quite happy when PIII made peace and Russian #2 general was Fritz’s admirer. It would take very little time for Russia, no matter who was in charge, to figure out that Prussia is more convenient ally than the Hapsburgs. Even under Elizabeth, no matter what the politicians in St.Petersburg were deciding, relations between the Russian and Austrian commanders hd been steadily deteriorating since Kolberg. The Austrians could not reconquer Silesia on their own and the Russian commanders were not willing to keep doing the Austrian job, especially after Doun failed in obligations to provide them with the food and was very cautious in risking the Austrian troops. Anyway, even in OTL, Fritz was playing a second fiddle to CII until she managed to screw up her foreign policy to a degree which gave Fritz “an opening”.
items.original_question: What if Empress Elizabeth of Russia lives longer, long term trajectory of Germany without the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg? She lives between a few months to a few years longer in this scenario. Peter III does not withdraw Russian troops from the Seven Years War, the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg does not materialize. Now, nobody was interested in total defeat of Prussia, it would remain a viable country but remains a second rate power in Europe, Silesia would go back to Austria, there would be possibly other territorial concessions as well. What happens to Germany long term in this timeline? Austria obviously becomes the natural candidate for unification of the country but the timeline will likely change.
items.model_answer:
If Empress Elizabeth of Russia had lived just a few years longer, the "Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg"—the sudden ascension of the Prussophile Tsar Peter III, who withdrew Russia from the Seven Years' War—would never have occurred. Without this miracle, the long-term trajectory of Germany would have been fundamentally altered, shifting away from Prussian militarism and Northern Protestant dominance toward an Austrian, Habsburg-centric future.

In the immediate term, a prolonged Russian presence in the Seven Years' War would have meant the total defeat and partition of Prussia. Frederick the Great’s overstretched armies were already on the brink of collapse in 1762. Under a victorious Austro-Russian alliance, Prussia would have been systematically dismantled. East Prussia would have been annexed by Russia (as Elizabeth had explicitly planned), Silesia would have been returned to Austria, and other territories would likely have been stripped away to reward Saxony and Sweden. Prussia would have been reduced back to the minor Electorate of Brandenburg, permanently aborting its rise to great power status.

The most profound long-term consequence for Germany would be the elimination of Austro-Prussian dualism. Historically, the intense rivalry between Berlin and Vienna defined Central European politics for a century. Without a powerful Prussia to challenge it, the Habsburg Monarchy would have remained the undisputed hegemon of the Holy Roman Empire and the broader German-speaking world. 

Consequently, the 19th-century unification of Germany would not have followed the historical path forged by Otto von Bismarck. The historical "Kleindeutschland" (Lesser Germany) solution—which united Germany under Prussian dominance while excluding Austria—would have been impossible. Instead, the German states would have either remained a decentralized, loose confederation acting as a buffer zone, or they would have eventually unified under a "Grossdeutschland" (Greater Germany) model led by Vienna. 

Culturally and politically, a Germany not forged by Prussian "blood and iron" would look vastly different. The defining German ethos would not be associated with Northern Protestantism, strict military discipline, and authoritarian bureaucracy. Instead, German identity would be heavily influenced by the Southern, Catholic, and cosmopolitan character of the Habsburg empire. Munich and Vienna, rather than Berlin, would be the undisputed political and cultural capitals of the German-speaking world.

Ultimately, the absence of a unified, highly industrialized, and militaristic Prussian-led German Empire in 1871 would have completely rewritten the 20th century. Without the aggressive foreign policy of a Prussianized Germany seeking its "place in the sun," the specific geopolitical friction that ignited World War I would not have materialized. While European empires would likely still clash over imperial and nationalist ambitions, the world-shattering conflicts of the 20th century—and the subsequent rise of the Third Reich—would have been entirely averted, leaving Central Europe under the complex, multi-ethnic, and comparatively conservative stewardship of the Habsburgs.

items.question: What If New Spain kept appointing a tlatoani?
human_answers: Yes, really. The social organization was hierarchical and defined by race, as many are even today, with the whites at the top. Again nothing unheard of. It's also true that the Peninsulars were usually assigned the top positions in the Viceroyalties, but even there there were exceptions. Three criollos were viceroys in New Spain and two more in Peru. Apart of that, there was no legal impediment for marriages between whites, mestizos and indios, with the children of such unions considered belonging to the upper class. "Rigid caste systems" never allow marriages outside one's caste and even less allow upwards movement. In many cases, mestizos bribed their way into the white class. Ironically, there were also cases where mestizos bribed their way down to be considered indios, because that put them outside the control from the Inquisition. Black people got it worse, certainly, but even there the social system never reached the hysteric levels of the United States. Intermarriage was complex due to slavery, but still legal. The first registered marriage between a white man and a black woman happened in 1564 in Florida. Of course, the whitest the skin of the children were, the better future they had.

It wouldn't give any advantages to the Spanish, the entire coalition hated the Mexica, keeping him around is not helping them score any points with them. In OTL, the local nobility got incorporated into the Spanish aristocracy, through marriage or by appointment as cacique (lord) of a region. By the Independence War, the most ardent loyalists were the natives, which had the most to lose, together with the Spanish, from a change in government. The enconmienda phase (1500s) was brutal, but by the 1600s, things had settled, and life was back to normal, with a Spanish/Native aristocracy above mestizo and native peasants. The worst abuses to the natives were behind, and the native nobility thrived. Unless there is no total victory, and the Spanish make the the Mexica vassals instead, then they will be in a need for someone to stay in charge. After a few decades, that might even go away if there is a Spanish-Mexica match, the children will be considered Spanish in less than two generations. Unlike the Inca, which I think could survive as a figurehead in Cuzco, the Tlatoani's case is more complicated.
items.original_question: What if New Spain kept appointing a tlatoani? When we think of the Fall of the Aztec Empire, we think of the Spanish coming in and overthrowing the existing order and building New Spain upon the ashes of the Aztec Empire. Well, the answer is a lot more complicated than that thought. One aspect from the Aztec Empire Spain kept was the position of a Tlatoani. Initially, the last sovereign of the Aztec Empire, Cuauhtémoc, was kept alive until Hernan Cortes killed him while bringing along to Honduras. However, Hernan then appointed a person named Tlacotzin (A former advisor of Cuauhtémoc) as tlatoani, (Though he was titled Cuauhtlatoani) but he died the next year before he could return to Tenochtitlan. So, Cortes then appointed a commoner named Motelchiuhtzin net, then he died fighting the Chichimeca up north. Then a man named Xochiquentzin ruled until he died of natural causes. So after that stint, the Spanish appointed Tlatoanis from the previous Aztec dynasty, who were both Tlatoani and Governor of Tenochtitlan (By this point Mexico City) under the Spanish colonial government of New Spain. It started with Panitzin and ended with Cipac. The last one got into frequent disputes over legal issues and disagreements on taxes with the colonial authorities. Afterwards, in just 1565, the Spanish ceased appointing a member of the former dynasty of Tlatoani. But they did continue to appoint a native Judge-governor until Mexican independence in 1821, who were either indigenous or mixed descent and many were descendants of Aztec nobility, though not of the royal dynasty. What if the Spanish continued to appoint continued a blood member of the previous Aztec Empire as "Tlatoani," and continues this until Mexican independence? How would a direct descendent of the Aztec emperors affect the search for a Mexican monarch? Could we see a movement similar to the "Inca Plan" where the Mexicans elect a native Nahuatl as Emperor instead of a European Prince or later Iturbide?
items.model_answer:
If New Spain had permanently maintained the appointment of a *tlatoani*—the traditional Nahua monarch—the political, cultural, and social trajectory of Mexico would have been radically altered. Historically, the Spanish initially appointed puppet *tlatoque* after the fall of Tenochtitlan to ensure tribute collection and maintain order, but they gradually phased the role out by the late 16th century in favor of Spanish-style town councils (*cabildos*) and appointed indigenous governors. Had the office been preserved, it would have institutionalized a powerful dual-governance system within the colony.

Politically, the *tlatoani* would have served as the supreme head of the *República de Indios*, acting as a high-level intermediary between the indigenous masses and the Spanish Viceroy. This would have entrenched the power and wealth of the *pipiltin* (indigenous nobility). Instead of being slowly absorbed into the lower rungs of the colonial hierarchy or assimilated entirely into the Spanish aristocracy, the indigenous elite would have maintained a distinct, formalized bloc of territorial and political power. The *tlatoani* would likely have commanded a pan-indigenous political apparatus, giving native populations a centralized legal voice to negotiate taxes, labor drafts, and land disputes with the Spanish Crown.

Culturally, the preservation of the *tlatoani* would have anchored Nahua identity and language. Nahuatl, which was already used as a lingua franca by early Spanish missionaries, would likely have become a permanent, co-official language of administration and law alongside Spanish. The royal court of the *tlatoani* in Mexico City would have fostered a highly visible, syncretic Mesoamerican-European high culture, preserving pre-Columbian traditions, art, and historical records within a Christianized framework. 

The most dramatic shift would have occurred during the Mexican War of Independence in the early 19th century. Instead of a movement primarily sparked and co-opted by *criollos* (Spaniards born in the Americas) like Miguel Hidalgo and Agustín de Iturbide, a sitting *tlatoani* would have provided a ready-made, legitimate sovereign figurehead for indigenous and mestizo liberation. This could have channeled the massive indigenous uprisings into a highly organized, unified front. Consequently, post-independence Mexico might have emerged as a restored Aztec/Mexican Empire ruled by a continuous Nahua dynasty, rather than a republic or a short-lived *criollo* monarchy. 

Even if modern Mexico ultimately transitioned into a republic, the legacy of a continuous *tlatoani* lineage would have fundamentally reshaped the nation's social fabric. Indigenous peoples would have possessed a powerful historical institution to defend their land rights and political autonomy, likely mitigating the severe marginalization and land dispossession they faced under 19th-century liberal reforms. Today, the *tlatoani* might still exist as a constitutionally recognized ceremonial monarch—similar to the Māori King in New Zealand or traditional monarchs in Africa—serving as a potent, living symbol of Mexico's unbroken indigenous heritage and wielding significant political influence.

items.question: What If Almanzor had never risen to power in al-Andalus?
human_answers: I had to read about Ghalib because my knowledge of him is quite limited. Overall, he seems to be a competent Saqaliba (slave-soldier) leader and served three caliphs. I don't see why he would try to reshape the composition of the caliphate as Al-Mansur did when trying to use Berbers against the rest of Islamic Iberia. Ghālib's rise coincides with the retirement of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III from active military command following his defeat at the Battle of Simancas in 939. So he came to serve under the first caliph and had a life of distinguished service fighting against Vikings, Moroccans, Fatimids, and Christians from northern Iberia. Gaining his freedom and patronage from the Umayyad. Perhaps it will have a greater influence from the Saqaliba in general within the caliphate. But to be honest, overall, they were good slave soldiers, and in the OTL, when the caliphate began to collapse, they were the ones who desperately fought against the Berbers to try to keep the caliphate alive and prevent the sackings of the city of Córdoba. I think one factor that made them generally better managers than the Mamluks in Egypt was that the ṣaqāliba were much less institutionalized and more integrated into local society. This was largely because Andalusian power was always balanced by military pluralism. With Arabs, Berbers, local Andalusians (the Muwallads), Ṣaqāliba, and Christian mercenaries, this balance prevented a single military group from monopolizing the state, as the Mamluks had done. So a Mameluke is freed to never cease being a Mameluke, while a ṣaqāliba is freed to cease being a ṣaqāliba. I'd guess that overall, you have a continuation of the status quo of the period, with a normal caliph (not the puppets of the period). There will be ethnic tensions that rise and fall depending on the situation, disputes over spheres of influence, campaigns in North Africa against the Fatimids (and in the future the Berber caliphates if they rise to power), and campaigns against Christians in the north (Kingdom of Leon), which may or may not succeed depending on the general, as happened in the OTL. It's difficult to say whether this prevents the reconquest of Iberia, but it certainly prevents the implosion of the caliphate of OTL. I would say that what will have the greatest impact on the survival of the Caliphate is not the Christians in the north, but rather the possible rise of the Almoravids.

I think that after ibn Abi Amir is killed, Ghalib is hailed as a hero by the Arab ruling class. As hajib, the old general, committed to the survival of the Caliphate as an institution, would free Hisham II from his irrelevance and perhaps have advisors train the boy-Caliph for rule. Once he reaches the age of maturity, Hisham takes power, albeit he mostly delegates authority to capable bureaucrats. His rule might be an extension of his father’s, a time of peace and prosperity and a golden age of the arts and sciences. The Christians are still too disorganized and weak to push into al-Andalus. Sancho III of Navarre is likely never even born as a result of butterflies. So no Jimenez dynasty either. Christian Spain remains small and disunited while Cordoba remains quietly strong and prosperous. I agree, the real threat to Cordoba wouldn’t be from the north, but from the south. So Cordoba focuses on maintaining hegemonic control over Morocco for strategic purposes. And without the constant warfare against the Christians, I think this will create a favorable situation for the Umayyads in Morocco. So no Almoravids. Fanatical tribes from the desert are repelled by strong Umayyad clients. Once Hisham passes away, he likely leaves an heir. This heir would inherit a strong and stable state, one that is durable for the century to come…
items.original_question: What if No Almanzor Ibn Abi Amir ‘al-Mansur’, better known Latinized as Almanzor, was the Hajib (chamberlain) and de facto ruler of the Caliphate of Qurtubah (Córdoba) from 978 to 1002 AD. A highly ambitious man, ibn Abi Amir would rise through the collection of various powerful offices over the course of the 960s and 970s as an administrator. Through this and his alliance with Subh, mother of the Umayyad boy-caliph Hisham II, ibn Abi Amir would become the most powerful man in al-Andalus by 980. Except, he wasn’t alone. He shared this spotlight with Ghalib ibn Abd al-Rahman ‘al-Siqlabi’ (the Slav), a widely-respected octogenarian general who had served both of Hisham’s predecessors. The two men formed an alliance with one another following the death of Caliph al-Hakam II in 976, allowing for them to rise the ranks of the Caliphate. However by 980 the two men had fallen out, and were increasingly at odds. That year, while together on campaign against the Christians, Ghalib attempted to murder ibn Abi Amir during a feast. The injured ibn Abi Amir would escape with his life and then proceed to capture Ghalib’s fortress in Madinat Salim (Medinaceli). This would lead to a brief civil war between the two, culminating in 981 with the Battle of Torrevicente. There, Ghalib’s army of Andalusi soldiers and his Christian allies would initially rout the Berber troops of ibn Abi Amir. However, Ghalib would unexpectedly die of seemingly natural causes in the middle of the battle, allowing for ibn Abi Amir to claim victory and the mantle of ‘al-Mansur’. Al-Mansur would go on to rule al-Andalus with an iron fist for the next two decades, sidelining the Umayyads, Arab nobility, and Muwalladi (native Iberian Muslims) alike while utilizing increasing numbers of Berber troops to repeatedly devastate the Christian north. While al-Mansur would lead al-Andalus to its peak of dominance over the whole of Iberia, he would also destroy its literal and cultural wealth while gutting its institutions. Upon his death in 1002 the Caliphate was a house of cards waiting to collapse, which it did after Abd al-Rahman ‘Sanchol’, better known as Sanchuelo, attempted to directly usurp the Umayyads as Caliph himself in 1009. This led to the 22-year-long Fitna (unrest) of al-Andalus, ending with Córdoba in ruins and the Caliphate shattered into 30+ petty kingdoms known as Taifas . A situation that would enable the Reconquista to gain steam, culminating in the capture of Tulaytulah (Toledo) by the Christians in 1085. Had Ghalib succeeded in the attempt on his life, ibn Abi Amir would have never become al-Mansur. The Umayyads would have maintained control over their Caliphate. Al-Andalus wouldn’t come to be dominated by a single dictatorial ruler. And the seeds of the Fitna wouldn’t be planted. The Reconquista will unfold differently, or even not at all. What are your thoughts on this scenario? I’ve come to believe that it represents the best chance the Caliphate of Córdoba had at ensuring long-term survival. Averting Almanzor and his excesses would blunt the height of Andalusi authority, but paradoxically preserve the state itself. Of course, stability following his death wouldn’t be ensured, and Ghalib wouldn’t have much longer to live anyway. However, the two had taken care of most rivals, and Ghalib was in good standing with the old guard of al-Andalus. Caliph Hisham II can actually grow up and become a proper ruler, preserving the legitimacy of the Caliphate itself. And without Almanzor, you don’t see increasing numbers of Berber tribesmen relocated to Iberia, provoking ethnic strife.
items.model_answer:
If Almanzor (Ibn Abi Amir) had never risen to power in the late tenth century, the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba would likely have avoided its catastrophic collapse in the early eleventh century, fundamentally altering the political and cultural trajectory of the Iberian Peninsula. Historically, Almanzor usurped power from the legitimate Umayyad caliph, Hisham II, establishing a military dictatorship. To secure his rule, he marginalized the traditional Arab and Andalusi aristocracy and imported massive numbers of North African Berber mercenaries. Without Almanzor’s rise, the Caliphate would have likely remained under the control of the traditional Andalusi elite, preventing the severe ethnic and factional polarization that ultimately triggered the devastating civil war known as the Fitna of al-Andalus. 

Without the Fitna, the fracturing of al-Andalus into the weak, independent Taifa kingdoms would have been significantly delayed or avoided altogether. A centralized and stable Umayyad Caliphate could have maintained its economic and diplomatic hegemony over the peninsula for decades, if not centuries, longer. Culturally, the absence of Almanzor would have preserved the intellectual golden age fostered by his predecessor, Caliph Al-Hakam II. To appease conservative religious scholars and legitimize his usurpation, Almanzor famously purged the magnificent caliphal library of Córdoba, burning countless works of philosophy, astronomy, and science. If he had never taken power, Córdoba’s status as the undisputed intellectual capital of Europe would have continued uninterrupted by this wave of censorship.

The geopolitical landscape of the Christian north would also have been drastically different. Almanzor is most famous for launching over fifty devastating military campaigns (*razzias*) against the Christian kingdoms, sacking major cities like Barcelona, Pamplona, León, and most notably, the holy site of Santiago de Compostela. Without these relentless assaults, the Christian states would have been spared immense physical and economic destruction. However, this does not necessarily mean the Christian Reconquista would have accelerated. Almanzor’s campaigns forged a deep existential dread and eventual unity among the northern kingdoms. Without him, the Christian states might have remained fractured by their own internal dynastic squabbles, while a stable, centralized Umayyad government could have comfortably managed the frontier through diplomacy, tribute systems, and limited skirmishes rather than total war. 

Ultimately, Almanzor’s historical legacy is a paradox: he brought al-Andalus to the absolute zenith of its military power, but his methods hollowed out the state's legitimate institutions and doomed it to collapse. Had he never risen to power, Muslim Iberia would have likely experienced a more peaceful, intellectually vibrant, and prolonged period of centralized Umayyad rule, fundamentally shifting the timeline of the Reconquista and the broader history of medieval Europe.

items.question: What If In 1972 have Nixon make America the definitive winners in Vietnam before his re-election
human_answers: No there was still a path to victory as late as Watergate. The ARVN with US air support and a shitload of supplies showed it didn't need US ground troops to win battles in 1972 and 1973, and sometimes won without US air support too, and still was winning battles into late 1974 before their supplies and manpower reserves gave out. The problem was Watergate meant Nixon did not have the political capital to prevent Congress from reducing supplies to the ARVN, and then Ford had the same problem, but also couldn't get airstrikes approved for Phouc Long (the lack of which explicitly accelerated the NVA's final offensive by a year). NVA planners actually considered 1976 to be their last shot at winning, as after that point the ARVN would have gotten over its teething troubles So extra US aid means the ARVN wins more of the smaller engagements and US air support smacks the first post cease fire NVA Corps level offensive. That buys another year without lots (possibly any) of American deaths and thus less resistance to having airpower smack the NVA again when they try their "do or die" offensive in late 1975-early 1976. If that gets fought off, that's probably the last chance as the Sino-Vietnamese border is heating up and the ARVN will have gotten over its teething troubles, while the Soviets had become increasingly unwilling to resupply the NVA after the ceasefire

Yes, if the US could have continued the war, then the war would have continued. That's axiomatic. But it couldn't, so it didn't. Remember your Clausewitz: if your armies in the field are still capable of fighting, but there is no political support for continuing the war, then the war is over. They couldn't muster the political capital because the US had already lost. South Vietnam hadn't been defeated yet, but the writing was on the wall in 1972. The major US operations of that year weren't about winning the war - they were about getting favourable conditions for US withdrawal. Arguably everything after Nixon took power was about getting favourable conditions for US withdrawal. You don't agree to withdraw your troops from a theatre of war while your opponent leaves 200,000 of theirs because you're winning. You don't sign a peace agreement that leaves your opponent in control of territory you were trying to defend because you're winning.

Without fundamental reforms, the South Vietnamese government could not achieve any tactical victories, let alone destroy most of the northern army. I believe OP refers to the US destroying most of the North Vietnamese army. However, I doubt the South Vietnamese government was so incompetent as to be destroyed by local warlords and rebellious peasants. And the more the Americans suppressed these local forces, the more they aligned themselves with the Northern government. Things there somehow like Afganistan. Either a fundamental reshaping of the South Vietnamese government is necessary (which I don't think could be achieved during Nixon's term) or complete military control. This could come at a significant political cost and carries the risk of war with China.

By 1972 there were only around 50,000 American soldiers in Vietnam, which means with a POD of January 1, 1972, any military victories would be by the South Vietnamese ground forces, supported by US air power. I feel that the incompetence of the South Vietnamese army is greatly overstated. They were reliant on American support, but with that support they were a fairly decent force. Edit: I mean to say that the ARVN could not achieve any tactical victories is ridiculous. Look at the actual 1972 offensive of OTL. What I’m saying is basically exactly what happened. South Vietnamese ground forces defeated a northern invasion with the help of American air power. The North Vietnamese suffered 100,000 casualties. If you scale up the size of the offensive ITTL and/or the scale of the defeat, it’s not hard to get to losses that become pretty disastrous for the north Vietnamese war fighting capabilities.

The problem is doing what it would take to win Vietnam starting after Nixon is in office and winning by Fall of 72 is NOT going to make Nixon popular. It is going to take a massive build up a huge expenditure of money an increased draft and a lot of dead young men. In effect to massively over simplify you would have to form a line across the country and start marching north while keep a secure boarder. The U.S. got fascinated by the helicopters ability to drop troops wherever. But lost track that holding a small area of land doesn’t do any good. Imagine fighting WW2 only with airborne troops. Sure they are useful to capture a key point but to trully accomplish anything you need to match on the ground to join up with them and secure an area. Doing this in the S.E.A. Jungle is going to be a mess. This mess was somewhat avoided in WW2 because when fighting in that kind of area vs Japan both sides were “foreigners” and we had more support from the locals. But yo take the local? You need to stand on and hold the land. ALL the land, if you hold any hive area but large parts are not occupied by your troops then the other guys just slip away to areas your troops aren’t at. I never understood why this wasn’t pretty obvious. I can only think it WAS obvious but being as the U.S. didn’t what to commit that kind of level of force it was ignored in favor of the new high tech way of fighting. Which in defense of it, it worked in a stand up fight against traditional armies but what cost the U.S. the war was not traditional armies. items.model_answer:
If Richard Nixon had achieved a definitive American victory in Vietnam before his 1972 re-election, securing an independent, non-communist South Vietnam and forcing the total capitulation of the North, the geopolitical and domestic landscapes of the late 20th century would have been radically transformed. 

Historically, Nixon won a massive landslide in 1972 based on the mere promise of "peace with honor," but an outright military or diplomatic triumph would have elevated him to the status of an unprecedented national hero. This immense political capital could have fundamentally altered the trajectory of his presidency. His re-election committee, feeling secure in an inevitable victory, might never have authorized the Watergate break-in. Even if the scandal still occurred, a victorious Nixon might have retained enough public and congressional loyalty to survive impeachment and finish his second term, leaving a legacy defined by Cold War triumph rather than political disgrace.

Domestically, the cultural fabric of the United States would have evolved quite differently. The profound national trauma, anti-government distrust, and military disillusionment that characterized the 1970s would have been heavily mitigated by a surge of patriotic vindication. The "Vietnam Syndrome"—the subsequent decades-long American reluctance to commit ground troops to foreign conflicts—would never have materialized. Validated in its containment strategy and military doctrine, the United States likely would have pursued a much more aggressive and interventionist foreign policy throughout the remainder of the Cold War, potentially leading to more direct military engagements in proxy conflicts across Central America, Africa, and the Middle East.

In Southeast Asia, the consequences would have been monumental. South Vietnam would have survived as a heavily militarized, pro-Western state. Much like South Korea following the Korean War, it likely would have relied on a permanent garrison of American troops to deter future invasions, eventually transitioning over the decades from an authoritarian government to a prosperous "Asian Tiger" economy. The devastating fall of Saigon in 1975, the subsequent "re-education" camps, and the exodus of millions of Vietnamese boat people would never have occurred. 

Furthermore, a decisive defeat of North Vietnam would have severely weakened communist insurgencies in neighboring countries. Without North Vietnamese backing and sanctuaries, the Pathet Lao in Laos and the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia would have been starved of resources. A victorious US and a secure South Vietnam likely would have intervened to prevent the Khmer Rouge from seizing power in 1975, thereby averting the Cambodian genocide and successfully halting the "domino effect" that American policymakers had long feared. Ultimately, the Cold War would have shifted heavily in America's favor much earlier, projecting an aura of American military invincibility into the late 20th century.

items.question: What If NACA had significantly improved the P-38 early in World War II?
human_answers: "All told, these NACA modifications solve three of the biggest issues with the early combat performance of the P-38 with the 8th Air Force: Limited Dive, Engine Cooling/Reliability, and Cockpit heating. In addition, the lack of the radiator ducts in the booms reduces drag and would likely result in a better level-flight top-speed (I would expect a gain of 10-20 mph from this) and improved/decreased fuel consumption. This leaves only two big problems to solve with later models. The first of these remaining problems was that the Fuel Mixture, Propeller RPM, and Throttle controls were independent and never had an implemented solution in OTL. For those not familiar with what those are, it means that to change from a “Cruising” condition to a “Combat” condition, the pilot needed to adjust three different levers for each engine (a total of six adjustments): Move Fuel Mixture from Auto-Lean to Auto-Rich; Increase Propeller RPMs; Increase manifold pressure (throttle). I have read some anecdotal evidence* that Lockheed had developed an “automatic manifold pressure regulator” which automated all of these adjustments into a single lever per engine but that the Air Force deemed it “unnecessary” and never authorized its implementation (Allison, the engine manufacturer, implemented this system on the post-war “G” series V-1710 engines). Supposing, with the “big three” problems solved due to the NACA redesign early in the combat life of the airplane the 8th AF decided to keep the P-38’s in primary service longer it is reasonable, I think, to assume this modification would become “necessary” and it could be implemented by late 1943/early 1944 models of the airplane (OTL P-38J, but in ATL, probably be considered second or third block P-38H). The second remaining issue was that the ailerons became heavy at high speeds and the so the airplane’s roll rate was quite slow, limiting its use as a dog-fighter. In OTL this was fixed in June 1944 with the P-38J-25-LO which introduced hydraulically boosted ailerons. These exponentially increased the force on the ailerons when turning the yoke and allowed the P-38 to flick-roll faster than most other fighters of the time. I am not certain how much more quickly these would be introduced in ATL vs. OTL as the slow-roll performance wouldn’t be altered by the NACA modifications nor was its solution delayed or prevented by AF brass. So, let’s say that this modification is introduced as it was in OTL, i.e. June 1944. Finally, with the 8th AF decision to keep the P-38 as the primary long-range escort fighter I believe it is reasonable to presume that they would have dedicated more time and resources to addressing the basic and tactical training for the pilots that was largely ignored in OTL, possibly even to the extant to sharing information with the P-38 FGs in the PTO—although that is uncertain. The result is, that when the 55th FG is transferred to the 8th AF with P-38H’s in September 1943 they have an aircraft capable of escorting bombers, at high-altitude, comfortably, reliably, and with significantly improved performance over most Axis fighters. This would reduce the demand for P-51’s and while I still expect them to come in theatre I would expect the P-38 Fighter Groups to keep the P-38’s rather than switching to P-47’s and P-51’s resulting in a near even three-way split between the fighter types by war’s end. I don’t know that this would have any significant impact on the eventual course or outcome of the war but improved long-range escort earlier in the war could have had a large positive impact on bomber-loss rates and morale. The reduction in bomber-losses in turn could mean a faster buildup of US Bomber forces and an earlier launch of major 1000+ raids perhaps even increasing the time-table for the Normandy Invasion, although other logistical problems likely lock that in no earlier than May ’44. The biggest difference would be in the reception and memory of the P-38 and its potential for a continued career post-war, similar to the P-51. The possibility of keeping them in service longer could also lead to the late-war approval for the adoption of the P-38K-1 with the F15 (Allison V-1710-75/77) engines and Hamilton-Standard Hydromatic high-activity propellers. In OTL only one of these was made using the large P-38J style chin and retaining the high-drag boom radiators. Even with all that drag it was able to achieve 432mph in level flight using Military Power and was expected to make 450mph with War Emergency Power with matching improvements in range and fuel consumption (about 10%). It also had a ceiling of 46,000 feet, a max climb of 4,800 ft/minute and could make it to 20,000 feet in only five minutes. Without the full coat of pain and with the reduced drag of the NACA design modification I can only image what its performance could be. In this case the P-38K would likely replace the F/P-82 Twin-Mustang of OTL and see continued service into the early 1950’s including limited combat in Korea as bomber-escorts and Close Air Support. So, any thoughts on this, its feasibility, and any effects I may have missed?" ----------------------- * http://www.ausairpower.net/P-38-Analysis.html (Pertinent section about 45% down in the italicized letter from Col. Harold J. Rau to “Commanding General, VIII Fighter Command, APO 637, U.S. Army”)[/QUOTE] Thank-you, I wasn't aware that this investigation into the P-38 compressibility problem had been conducted. It would have been a very productive and effective modification and I'm inclined to agree if the NACA mod had been developed earlier then it would have made it into production. After Pearl Harbor the pressure to produce what ever was available delayed OTL improvements to the P-38 like for example the high-activity propellers as you mentioned. I haven't finished reading the 1942 document yet so I have some questions for you. After the NACA mod had been developed the engineers still thought that dive recovery flaps would be required? Also with the relocation of the Prestone radiators and oil coolers to the new leading edge did the designers consider the Meredith effect when designing the new installation? Making the assumption they were aware of it at the time. The P-38's OTL canopy was one of its' poorer features. If they were redesigning the canopy contours could that also mean replacing it with a bubble type sliding canopy?

1) There is no explicit mention of the Dive Recovery Flaps in the NACA report, however the information about the airflow under the wing at different flap possitions is what ultimately led to their development so it is possible that they could have still been developed although they would have been by no means neccesary (assuming the NACA estimates are accurate). 2) I haven't read any specific refereces to it but it is possible they were aware of the Meredith effect. However, if memory serves, the radiator installations in the P-38 were not well suited or designed for it producing more drag than thrust. The NACA installation would likely also be poor canidatea for Meredith thrust so it is likely a dead end for the sake of this exploration. 3) Indeed the canopy was junk. While it never happened OTL I may explore better canopy options in the ATL. I think this is likely the direction I would go anyway. Some narrative, some ATL technical evaluation reports, maybe even some Encounter Reports when the shooting starts. Yeah, several of the British twin wing designs could be good but are beyond the scope of the PoD and this ATL. The issue with the dive flaps was that the first shipment in a C-54 was shot down by the British and they never bothered sending replacements. Then they didn't want to slow down production to integrate them into the line until all the planned blocks werw complete which meant they weren't factory installed until the P-38J-25 starting June 6, 1944...what a day! And yes, the treatment of the P-38 in the 8th AF was criminal because their disdain led directly to lost aircrew. Edit: sorry for all the typoes...I am on my phone instead computer at the moment.

As a lover of the P-38, a believer in its unrealized superior potential, a person saddened that it was not properly appreciated and thus its potential to escort early US bomber raids and save the lives of countless bomber crew members (not to mention recovering and reusing their OTL shot-down planes)--let me play a bit of Devil's Advocate here. I've seen some of the online wars between P-38 fans and their detractors, and come away more convinced by the former, especially after this most informative OP! But one simple point the naysayers have is clearly true...P-38 was a two-engine plane, while its eventual successor (if we assume the -38 were improved and permitted to do the escort mission) the P-51 was single engine. Thus Lightnings were inherently more costly than any single engine plane, good, bad or mediocre. If the choice was between an excellent two engine job and terrible to mediocre single engine, we just pay the higher price as part of the necessary cost of doing business with the best--except that in Jan 1942, the USAAF needed aircraft in numbers, and soon. If single engine alternatives existed that would be cost-effective, then clearly the Army would prefer that. I don't mean to mention this as some sort of trump card killing the -38's prospects, just as pointing out a factor that was relevant in decision making. The fact is I believe the P-38 was originally authorized under the impression it would be a superstar, just as the B-17 was hoped to be a super bomber the P-38 was to be the star fighter. But that was when war was hypothetical; once it started a panic for sheer numbers set in, and the question of whether one P-38 was worth 2 of another type--or less than 2, or more--was not transparent. One big advantage the P-38 offered, especially if it had indeed been modified to remove its worst drawbacks, and more appreciated hence ordered in more numbers, is that though it used twin engines, those engines were not Merlins! Not to say anything was wrong with Merlins, quite the contrary--though I do seem to recall some comparisons over ranges of altitude wherein the Allison engines, due to being turbosupercharged, had superior perfomance, while the Merlins had a mechanical supercharger. But the point here is, Merlins were good--but in severe demand therefore, so it was most excellent that the Lightning did not require them. I particularly like the way the twin engine layout leaves the central command nacelle to be loaded with heavy and reconfigurable arms.

TTL, it seems likely the dive-recovery spoiler (even assuming it takes OTL's duration to find the answer, which seems less probable; IMO, it'd be quicker TTL) would be on a different C-54, so not shot down. (Might be soon enough to get to production directly, in the *P-38E or -F TTL.) Other improvements? Turbos are hard, but without new materials, there's still reducing the rotating mass (drill the blades, so they look a bit like Swiss cheese), & (possibly) sizing issues (boost lag). Direct improvements to the aircraft itself? Cockpit heat is a must. Adding the wing leading-edge fuel tanks sooner would be good, but TTL, better fuel economy might butterfly them away... Flipside, tho: more P-38s means more headaches, with pilots who don't like twins & aren't trained in them correctly getting themselves in trouble. There was a myth going around England: if a P-38 lost an engine on takeoff, it'd kill you. It would--because the pilots weren't trained how to recover. Tony LeVier showed 'em: kill one engine, boot the rudder hard over against the dead one, crank on full power to the other & climb out to go around...

The 1944 Report clarifies some things I'd heard elsewhere. Thanks for that. All I have for the 1940-41 period is Dolittles commentary, but since he had worked some years as a aircraft engineer for a fuel manufactor his account has some small weight. The short version is through the 1930s commercially available gasoline fuels had a very low octane rating by post WWII standards. 65 Octane is the number I recall. Dolittle & his peers were trying to persuade the corporate suits to develop and market higher octane fuels, up into the 80 & possiblly 90 octane range. The refusal was based on the lack of market since the engine manufactors provided nothing that could use such fuels. To complete the circle the motors that could use high octane fuel were not built because the fuels were not being made. Dolittle did make clear that custom built engines were common for fuels in the 70 to 90 and higher octane ranges. Additives and custom fuel mixes were available in small batches to those who could pay. Dolittle like other knowledgeable pilots carried a witches brew of additives in his aircraft for boosting the commercial fuels of the aircraft he used. Later in 1940-41 Dolittle observed the same problem in plotting the development of the Army Air Corps engines beyond 41. At one point the head of the Quartermasters Corps informed the Air Corps that only 65 octane fuel would be provided across the board to simplify logisitcs. Fortunately the reorganization of early 1942 gave the Army Air force control of its own material supply & development went ahead.
items.original_question: What if NACA Modified P-38 What if NACA Modified P-38 fighter ------------------------------------------------------- Notice to Readers: This TL is still alive but only occasionally updated at this time (Summer 2021). Real life and the greatly expanded scope of detail required to continue advancing the TL at this point (including a fair share of original design and research) has kept me from more regular postings. But, Please, follow along and keep your eyes open for updates when they occur. I really value everyone's input and often the discussion around specific developments has been key to finalizing the next development. Cheers! E Jul. 2021 ------------------------------------------------------- (This was something I had planned to post after being on the board longer but a discussion in another thread prompted some discussion of P-38 development so I thought I would go ahead with this for the sake of discussion.) I know there have been several discussions over the years surrounding the Lockheed P-38 American Twin-Engine fighter/interceptor of WWII but one part of the equation that I have never heard discussed is the “What If…” the NACA recommended modifications to the airplane had been implemented, especially at or near the beginning of P-38 operations. OTL Background : Without re-hashing the origin and initial development history of the Lockheed Model 22 / P-38 (all of that information is readily available on numerous on-line sources) I will focus on what led to the NACA studies of the airframe, their proposed solution to the problems encountered, and why these solutions weren’t put in place. A record-breaking cross-country flight in early 1939 (which resulted in the loss of the only XP-38) garnered enough attention and excitement that the US Army Air Corp (USAAC) placed orders for pre-production (YP-38) and production (P-38) aircraft in numbers greater than Lockheed had anticipated for the entire Model 22 life. This necessitated a rushed production development and major reconfiguration to accommodate the unintended mass-production. Tests in early 1941 of the first pre-production YP-38’s quickly ran into issues when at high speed (around Mach 0.68), especially in dive, where the nose of the aircraft would drop--locking into an often un-recoverable dive accompanied by “buffeting.” The problems getting the production line up and fully operational prevented Lockheed from directing any engineering resources to these problems until November 1941, but they were unable to identify the cause or provide any solutions until Gen. Hap Arnold, head of the by then renamed Army Air Forces (USAAF), ordered the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA—predecessor of NASA) to analyze the YP-38 in their full-scale wind-tunnel in December 1941 – January 1942 which resulted in the report “ Full-Scale Wind-Tunnel Investigation of Buffeting and Diving Tendencies of the YP-38 Airplane .” [EDIT: NASA reorganized its online archives in 2020 so this link is no longer functioning. The upload size limitations on this site prevent me from dropping the file here, but you can find a copy I uploaded at another site, Here ] This report was finally able to identify that the control lock and diving difficulties were the result of a high-speed pressure wake developing over the wing and fuselage resulting is loss of lift to the central wing and buffeting of the tail as the turbulent wake passes over it, a phenomenon just recently discovered at the time which led the idea of the “sound barrier.” This is often referred to a “Compressibility” problem as it related the change of aerodynamics at high speed from a traditional non-compressible fluid to a compressible one. The specific behavior of the P-38 is now better known as “Mach Tuck.” NACA tested several solutions to the problem including wing filleting, partial flap deployment, three different inboard (between the engine booms and the center gondola) wing designs, two revised canopy designs, and an extension to the trailing edge of the gondola. They found the best performance gain (delay of up to 64 mph in the formation of the shock-wave) resulted from a simple 0.2c (20% of chord) leading edge extension to the center wing section and using their second canopy revision. They also noted that although the gondola extension did not increase the Critical Mach number, it did reduce the turbulence of the wake re-joining the airstream and smoothed out the air flow over the tail surfaces. One aspect which I find very interesting with these design modifications was that the extended leading edge moved the center of lift forward causing the plane to become unbalanced. They recommended moving the coolant radiators from the mid-boom into the extended leading edge of the wing to rebalance the aircraft with the added benefit of reducing drag and further streamlining the aircraft. I will address this again in the ATL discussion to follow. The problem is that the report wasn’t completed until March 31, 1942, by which time the US was at war and Lockheed was ramping up to start production on the combat-ready P-38F (beginning in April 1942) at war-time production rates. With the P-38 the most capable fighter then in inventory there simply was not the opportunity to re-design and re-tool for the modifications NACA recommended and the P-38 was sent into combat while still suffering numerous problems, not least of which was the issues with compressibility. The results are well known and documented: the P-38 in the ETO struggled the first 18 months of combat prompting 8th Fighter Command to pre-emptively phase them out in favor of the new P-51 as they became available at the end of 1943 and through the first half of 1944 which prevented Lockheed and the USAAF from implementing a number of fixes for the problems and delayed others until it was too late to have much impact in the reputation of the P-38 in Europe. It was not until the P-38J-25-LO and P-38L-5-LO/VN the airplane really came into its own and that was realized almost entirely in the Pacific. ATL Discussion : For this examination of a “What If…” I have decided to place the POD with the NACA study. Specifically, that Gen. Arnold did not wait for Lockheed to tackle the dive issues first and instead ordered the NACA study to take place in June-July of 1941 with the final report completed September 30, 1941 (six months earlier than OTL). This updated timeline would allow Lockheed engineers to immediately go to work implementing the NACA design changes in fall 1941 prior to US entry into the War and the corresponding production pressures which prevented it from happening in OTL. The first production P-38’s with the NACA modifications would then roll out either as late block P-38E’s in early ’42 or, more likely, as the finalized P-38F in April 1942. OTL, the P-38F/G/H continued to use the enclosed intercooler in the leading edge of the outboard wings, which provided adequate cooling for the early model engines and low-boost ratings but which, by the P-38G and even more so the P-38H, limited engine power to lower settings due to in-adequate cooling. This was a problem that was not anticipated so it wasn’t until the P-38J in August 1943 that the intercoolers were switched to the core-type, chin-mounted position—squeezed between and behind the oil radiators. However, in my ATL, with the oil radiators moved adjacent the coolant radiators in the leading edge extension the space in the chin of the nacelles is completely freed up which allows the core-type intercoolers to be installed in the space previously occupied by the oil radiators as soon as it becomes apparent it is needed without re-designing the nacelles themselves. This means that the engine power limitations of the G either never occurs (because the intercoolers have already been moved) or are quickly overcome by sending field modification kits in early 1943 with full integration on the assembly line taking place with the P-38H in the spring of 1943. Additionally, moving the intercoolers in these earlier models (G or H) would allow a matching earlier installation of the leading edge fuel tanks in the outer wings, increasing the range and combat radius in 1943 sufficient to provide full escort coverage to 8th AF Bombers even to deep penetration targets. Another advantage of moving the Prestone (engine coolant) radiators to the inboard position in the extended leading edge is that the heated coolant can be run through a heater core close to the cockpit cupola, increasing available cockpit heat as soon as it becomes apparent the existing heat is insufficient for high-altitude or cold weather operations. Again, this is something I expect would be utilized no later than early-mid 1943. One final advantage of this layout is that frees up a large amount of space in the tail booms which could be utilized in later production models. With engine weight increases in the F/G and again in the H/J models the Center of Gravity could potentially have been moved forward enough to justify installation of either additional small fuel tanks in the booms where the radiators used to be, or—perhaps a better option—small water/alcohol tanks which would permit the use the Water Injection under War Emergency Power, further increasing performances and reducing the risks of detonation under high manifold pressure (> 60 in/Hg). The estimated (conservative according to NACA documents) dive performance gains of this P-38 redesign are impressive: To put this in perspective, the P-51D had an absolute Critical Mach of around 0.80, depending on the source, but was normally limited to less than 0.73 because of extreme vibrations beyond those speeds. Even if pushing the ’51 to Mach 0.8 or beyond is considered acceptable these NACA estimates for the modified ’38 show a similar diving capability considering a margin for error of the conservative estimate, especially if using Dive Recovery Flaps in addition to the NACA modifications. In these cases the P-38 would be favorable because it can accelerate to max speed faster than the P-51 allowing to either pull-away faster or to gain faster on a diving E/A. Combine that with the faster climb of the P-38, higher peak turning rate, and—in later airplanes—faster roll, there would be nothing that the P-51 could do that the P-38 couldn’t do better. All while bringing a heavier weight of fire on target (128 oz/sec vs 111 oz/sec). Here are some roughly done drawings of how these modifications would appear (done in MS Paint): All told, these NACA modifications solve three of the biggest issues with the early combat performance of the P-38 with the 8th Air Force: Limited Dive, Engine Cooling/Reliability, and Cockpit heating. In addition, the lack of the radiator ducts in the booms reduces drag and would likely result in a better level-flight top-speed (I would expect a gain of 10-20 mph from this) and improved/decreased fuel consumption. This leaves only two big problems to solve with later models. The first of these remaining problems was that the Fuel Mixture, Propeller RPM, and Throttle controls were independent and never had an implemented solution in OTL. For those not familiar with what those are, it means that to change from a “Cruising” condition to a “Combat” condition, the pilot needed to adjust three different levers for each engine (a total of six adjustments): Move Fuel Mixture from Auto-Lean to Auto-Rich; Increase Propeller RPMs; Increase manifold pressure (throttle). I have read some anecdotal evidence* that Lockheed had developed an “automatic manifold pressure regulator” which automated all of these adjustments into a single lever per engine but that the Air Force deemed it “unnecessary” and never authorized its implementation (Allison, the engine manufacturer, implemented this system on the post-war “G” series V-1710 engines). Supposing, with the “big three” problems solved due to the NACA redesign early in the combat life of the airplane the 8th AF decided to keep the P-38’s in primary service longer it is reasonable, I think, to assume this modification would become “necessary” and it could be implemented by late 1943/early 1944 models of the airplane (OTL P-38J, but in ATL, probably be considered second or third block P-38H). The second remaining issue was that the ailerons became heavy at high speeds and the so the airplane’s roll rate was quite slow, limiting its use as a dog-fighter. In OTL this was fixed in June 1944 with the P-38J-25-LO which introduced hydraulically boosted ailerons. These exponentially increased the force on the ailerons when turning the yoke and allowed the P-38 to flick-roll faster than most other fighters of the time. I am not certain how much more quickly these would be introduced in ATL vs. OTL as the slow-roll performance wouldn’t be altered by the NACA modifications nor was its solution delayed or prevented by AF brass. So, let’s say that this modification is introduced as it was in OTL, i.e. June 1944. Finally, with the 8th AF decision to keep the P-38 as the primary long-range escort fighter I believe it is reasonable to presume that they would have dedicated more time and resources to addressing the basic and tactical training for the pilots that was largely ignored in OTL, possibly even to the extant to sharing information with the P-38 FGs in the PTO—although that is uncertain. The result is, that when the 55th FG is transferred to the 8th AF with P-38H’s in September 1943 they have an aircraft capable of escorting bombers, at high-altitude, comfortably, reliably, and with significantly improved performance over most Axis fighters. This would reduce the demand for P-51’s and while I still expect them to come in theatre I would expect the P-38 Fighter Groups to keep the P-38’s rather than switching to P-47’s and P-51’s resulting in a near even three-way split between the fighter types by war’s end. I don’t know that this would have any significant impact on the eventual course or outcome of the war but improved long-range escort earlier in the war could have had a large positive impact on bomber-loss rates and morale. The reduction in bomber-losses in turn could mean a faster buildup of US Bomber forces and an earlier launch of major 1000+ raids perhaps even increasing the time-table for the Normandy Invasion, although other logistical problems likely lock that in no earlier than May ’44. The biggest difference would be in the reception and memory of the P-38 and its potential for a continued career post-war, similar to the P-51. The possibility of keeping them in service longer could also lead to the late-war approval for the adoption of the P-38K-1 with the F15 (Allison V-1710-75/77) engines and Hamilton-Standard Hydromatic high-activity propellers. In OTL only one of these was made using the large P-38J style chin and retaining the high-drag boom radiators. Even with all that drag it was able to achieve 432mph in level flight using Military Power and was expected to make 450mph with War Emergency Power with matching improvements in range and fuel consumption (about 10%). It also had a ceiling of 46,000 feet, a max climb of 4,800 ft/minute and could make it to 20,000 feet in only five minutes. Without the full coat of pain and with the reduced drag of the NACA design modification I can only image what its performance could be. In this case the P-38K would likely replace the F/P-82 Twin-Mustang of OTL and see continued service into the early 1950’s including limited combat in Korea as bomber-escorts and Close Air Support. So, any thoughts on this, its feasibility, and any effects I may have missed? ----------------------- * http://www.ausairpower.net/P-38-Analysis.html (Pertinent section about 45% down in the italicized letter from Col. Harold J. Rau to “Commanding General, VIII Fighter Command, APO 637, U.S. Army”)

If NACA had resolved the Lockheed P-38 Lightning’s aerodynamic and mechanical flaws early in World War II, the United States Army Air Forces would have possessed a premier long-range escort fighter well before the P-51 Mustang achieved dominance. Historically, early P-38s suffered from severe compressibility issues during high-speed dives—causing the controls to lock up and the nose to tuck downward—as well as cockpit temperature extremes and Allison engine reliability problems at the high altitudes required in the European Theater. If NACA had engineered and implemented solutions like dive recovery flaps and improved engine intercooling in 1941 or 1942 instead of late 1943 and 1944, the aircraft's combat effectiveness would have been drastically transformed.

Strategically, the most significant impact would have been felt in the skies over Europe. The Eighth Air Force would have had a highly capable, high-altitude fighter escort during the disastrous deep-penetration bombing raids of 1943, such as the strikes on Schweinfurt and Regensburg. By providing continuous fighter cover to and from targets deep inside Germany, an improved P-38 would have drastically reduced heavy bomber losses, potentially accelerating the destruction of the Luftwaffe and German industrial capacity. Consequently, this early success might have reduced the USAAF's urgent reliance on developing the Merlin-powered P-51 Mustang, cementing the Lightning as the definitive American fighter of the European air war. 

In the Pacific Theater, where the P-38 was already highly prized for its twin-engine reliability over vast ocean expanses, early aerodynamic improvements would have made it even more lethal. With the ability to safely execute high-speed diving attacks without fear of compressibility lock-up, American pilots could have exploited boom-and-zoom tactics to absolute perfection, making the P-38 virtually untouchable by lighter, slower Japanese fighters much earlier in the conflict.
