In a hypothetical 1996 presidential election featuring a Democratic ticket of Senator Jay Rockefeller and HUD Secretary Henry Cisneros against a Republican ticket of former Vice President Dan Quayle and former Tennessee Governor Lamar Alexander, the race would present a stark contrast between a shifting multicultural Democratic coalition and a traditional, family-values-focused Republican establishment. This scenario assumes that Bill Clinton either did not run, lost in 1992, or did not seek reelection, and that Bob Dole failed to capture the GOP nomination. 

The Democratic ticket of Rockefeller and Cisneros would attempt to bridge traditional blue-collar union politics with the emerging demographic power of the Sun Belt. Jay Rockefeller, a patrician who dedicated his career to West Virginia, would likely focus his platform on universal healthcare, labor rights, and industrial revitalization, aiming to lock down the Rust Belt, Appalachia, and the Northeast. Henry Cisneros, the charismatic former mayor of San Antonio, would be deployed to drive unprecedented Hispanic turnout and contest traditionally Republican strongholds like Texas, Florida, and the increasingly competitive state of California. However, the ticket would face vulnerabilities; Republicans would likely paint Rockefeller as a "tax-and-spend" liberal out of touch with middle America, and Cisneros’s real-life mid-1990s personal controversies regarding payments to a former mistress would likely become a major target for Republican attack ads.

On the Republican side, Dan Quayle and Lamar Alexander would run a campaign heavily anchored in the Reagan-Bush legacy, social conservatism, and the dominance of the American South. Quayle would lean into his signature "family values" rhetoric, aiming to energize the Christian Right and suburban conservatives who felt alienated by the cultural shifts of the 1990s. Lamar Alexander, known for his moderate, folksy demeanor and focus on education reform, would provide the ticket with establishment credibility and help secure the vital Southern and border states. The primary hurdle for the Republican ticket would be Quayle’s media reputation; having been heavily caricatured as gaffe-prone during his vice presidency, Quayle would have to run a flawlessly disciplined campaign to project the gravitas necessary for the Oval Office. 

Ultimately, this 1996 clash would be decided in the suburbs of the Midwest and the rapidly changing Southwest. If Quayle and Alexander could successfully capitalize on the era's conservative momentum—similar to the 1994 Republican Revolution—and keep the South and Sun Belt firmly red, they would likely secure the presidency. Conversely, if Rockefeller’s healthcare-focused economic populism held the Midwestern "Blue Wall" and Cisneros successfully accelerated the Democratic shift among Hispanic voters in states like California and New Mexico, the Democrats could forge a victorious electoral map that foreshadowed the party's 21st-century coalition.

items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

Yes ! I didn't knew they had had found Irvine (well, his foot at last). https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sandy-irvine-body-found-everest Unbelievable. And then there is this Holly cow they were so close - less than 400 meters to 8848 ! I understand better why so many people are confident they made it to the summit. Also the missing photography of Mallory wife. Unfortunately poor Irvine was found much lower and inside a melting glacier. Hopefully they will found more remains within the next few years. And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years. The remaining question is: did the fall happened while climbing, less than 400 m from glory - or descending, having done it ? And there, is the missing photography of Mallory wife. AAAAARGH we are so close from knowing the truth.

So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?
items.model_answer:
If George Mallory and Andrew Irvine had successfully summited Mount Everest and returned alive in 1924, they would have fundamentally rewritten the timeline of mountaineering history, claiming the title of the first humans to stand on the world's highest peak 29 years before Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay. 

Their success would have provided a monumental psychological boost to a British Empire still recovering from the devastation of World War I. Both men would have returned to international superstardom, almost certainly receiving knighthoods and becoming enduring national heroes. Mallory’s famous justification for climbing the mountain, "Because it's there," would be remembered not as the haunting epitaph of a doomed romantic, but as the triumphant motto of human perseverance.

In the mountaineering world, their survival would have immediately vindicated the controversial use of supplemental oxygen. At the time, the Alpine Club heavily debated whether using "English air" was sporting or ethical. A successful summit would have ended this purist debate, accelerating the technological development and widespread adoption of oxygen apparatuses in high-altitude climbing. 

Furthermore, with Everest conquered, the international race to climb the world's highest mountains would have shifted focus much earlier. Expeditions in the 1920s and 1930s would have likely pivoted toward other formidable, unclimbed 8,000-meter peaks, such as K2, Kangchenjunga, and Nanga Parbat. This could have advanced the Himalayan "Golden Age of Alpinism" by decades, drawing global resources and elite climbers away from Everest and toward the Karakoram and other ranges. 

Consequently, the legacy of the 1953 British expedition would be drastically altered. While Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay might still have achieved fame for pioneering the southern route through Nepal—since Mallory and Irvine climbed via the North Col from Tibet—they would not hold the legendary status of being the absolute first to reach the roof of the world. Ultimately, the enduring, century-long mystery of whether Mallory and Irvine reached the top before dying would be erased, replaced instead by one of the greatest exploration and survival narratives of the 20th century.

items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). Similar sets of guidelines governed graphic novels, comic books and newspaper comic strips (the Comics Code from 1954 to 2011), the National Association of Broadcasters' Code of Practices for Television Broadcasters (the so-called Television Code from 1952 to 1983) with a similar set of guidelines for radio, and the near-censorship of video games by the North American nations' governments before the Entertainment Software Association came up with the voluntary, self-regulating Entertainment Software Rating Board to inform consumers about content. There were various religious and secular moralistic censorship groups across the United States at the time dedicating themselves to preserving morality and good taste in American culture of the time through literature, music, sports, comic strips, motion pictures and radio. Various Tinseltown scandals led up to the 1915 U.S. Supreme Court case Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio which unanimously held that free speech protections of the U.S. Constitution's 1st Amendment did not extend to motion pictures. If the Supreme Court were to decide that no local, state, or federal political body had the right to regulate or censor the production and distribution of any work of radio, film, literature, music within reason and neither did any religious or business organization within reason, then what? I would suggest that instead of restrictive production/distribution codes, film distributors would possibly make an early version of the Film Rating System which would check film patrons' identifications at the box office against a film's rating. This would give many makers and distributors of motion pictures more creative freedom to explore the kinds of topics and subject matter they want to explore as well as spur various technological developments of all sorts. For our purposes, let's explore firstly what if the MPPDA Film Rating System established in the late 1910s is the one of today. One of those ways would be to convince studios, distributors and talent agencies to unionize and have their own unions so to ensure fairer treatment and hiring of prospective workers and talents, safe business practices and work hazard safety management, and fair/equal compensation for equal work for all kinds of work. This would involve the Directors Guild, Writers Guild, American Cinema Editors, Producers Guild, American Society of Cinematographers, Screen Actors Guild, Animation Guild and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees with membership being encouraged or socially pressured to watchdog for mistreatment. With creative and editorial freedom enshrined for radio and motion pictures in the Constitution, there could also be movements to establish an alliance of the Christian churches, Jewish synagogues, Islamic mosques and other religious institutions' collective motion picture production and distribution systems as a single studio called the Holy Light Studios Alliance which would be dedicated to the production and distribution of motion pictures approved by the moral standard guidelines of various local, state, national and international Christian, Jewish and Muslim faith doctrines. items.model_answer:
If film, comics, and broadcasting had gained First Amendment and union protections much earlier in the twentieth century, the American media landscape would have been vastly more diverse, politically provocative, and economically equitable for creators. Historically, films were denied free speech protections by the Supreme Court in 1915, comics were severely censored in the 1950s, and early creators across these mediums were often exploited by monopolistic studio and publishing systems. Reversing these conditions decades earlier would have fundamentally altered the trajectory of American popular culture.

Without the looming threat of government censorship, the self-regulatory bodies that sanitized American media—most notably the Hays Code in film and the Comics Code Authority in publishing—would likely never have been established or would have lacked the teeth to enforce compliance. Consequently, American cinema in the 1930s and 1940s would have resembled the gritty, socially conscious "New Hollywood" of the 1970s or contemporary European cinema. Filmmakers would have been free to explore mature themes, including systemic corruption, complex sexuality, and racial injustice, without mandated moralistic endings. Similarly, the comic book industry would not have been forced into the sanitized superhero monopoly of the Silver Age. The vibrant horror, true crime, and socially critical comics of the late 1940s—such as those published by EC Comics—would have thrived, allowing the medium to mature alongside its audience rather than being culturally relegated to children's entertainment.

Early and robust union protections would have dismantled the exploitative labor practices that defined the early entertainment industry. In Hollywood, the draconian "studio system," which bound actors, writers, and directors to restrictive seven-year contracts with little creative control, would have collapsed decades sooner. Talent would have operated as independent contractors with profit-sharing models much earlier, shifting power from studio executives to the artists. In the comic book industry, early unionization would have destroyed the predatory "work-for-hire" model. Creators like Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster (Superman) or Jack Kirby (Marvel) would have retained their copyrights, secured royalties, and amassed immense wealth, establishing a creator-owned publishing model half a century before the founding of companies like Image Comics. 

Furthermore, the intersection of entrenched First Amendment rights and powerful labor unions would have radically altered the political landscape of the mid-century United States, particularly during the Red Scare and McCarthyism. Historically, the Hollywood and broadcasting blacklists of the late 1940s and 1950s succeeded because studios and networks capitulated to government pressure, firing suspected left-leaning artists to protect their corporate interests. If these industries had been shielded by clear First Amendment precedents and backed by militant, unified guilds, the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) would have faced insurmountable legal and labor resistance. Strikes and constitutional lawsuits would have protected the careers of countless writers, directors, and broadcasters. 

Ultimately, early constitutional and labor protections would have accelerated the maturation of American mass media. By protecting both the message and the messenger, the twentieth century would have seen a richer, more subversive, and creator-driven cultural output, free from the moral panics and corporate exploitation that historically constrained it.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates. items.model_answer:
If the Haber-Bosch process were never invented, the modern world would be fundamentally unrecognizable, primarily defined by a drastically smaller global population and a completely altered trajectory of 20th-century history. The Haber process allows for the mass synthesis of ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen, which is the foundational ingredient for both synthetic fertilizers and modern munitions. Without it, the Earth's agricultural carrying capacity would be strictly limited by natural nitrogen fixation methods, such as crop rotation, manure application, and the mining of guano and saltpeter. Consequently, global food production would have hit a hard ceiling, likely capping the human population at around 3 to 4 billion people. The rapid population explosion of the 20th century would have instead been replaced by severe, widespread famines, forcing humanity to clear massive amounts of forests and wild habitats just to sustain low-yield farming.

Historically, the absence of the Haber process would have profoundly changed the outcome of World War I. Germany heavily relied on synthetic nitrates to manufacture explosives after the British Royal Navy blockaded its access to Chilean saltpeter. Without the ability to synthesize ammonia, Germany's munitions supply would have dried up by 1915 or 1916, likely forcing an early surrender. This premature end to the war would have altered the post-war geopolitical landscape entirely, potentially preventing the specific economic and political collapse that led to the rise of Nazi Germany, the outbreak of World War II, and the subsequent Cold War. 

In this alternate timeline, geopolitics would be largely dictated by the desperate need for agricultural sustenance. Nations would fiercely compete for control over the limited guano and nitrate deposits in South America and the Pacific, potentially sparking massive resource wars over bird and bat droppings. Economically, a much larger percentage of the global workforce would remain tied to labor-intensive agriculture, slowing the pace of industrialization, urbanization, and technological advancement. Ultimately, humanity would be trapped in a Malthusian reality, living on a heavily deforested planet where geopolitical power and human survival are inextricably linked to the control of natural soil nutrients.

AHC: one people, two nation-states

There have been plenty of cases where one people with a common language and ancestry are separated into two nation-states. I'm not talking about ideological reasons like in the case of Germany and Korea, but in terms of centuries-long division of religion (Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Austrians and Protestant Germans) or geopolitics (Montenegro and Ottoman-dominated Serbia, Russia-dominated Moldova and Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia). items.model_answer:
When a single national or ethnic group is divided into two sovereign nation-states—a phenomenon historically observed in Korea, Cold War-era Germany, and Vietnam—it generates a complex dynamic of ideological competition, cultural drift, and geopolitical tension. Typically resulting from external geopolitical interventions or civil wars rather than mutual consent, the two states often adopt diametrically opposed political and economic systems. This divergence transforms the divided nation into a comparative laboratory, frequently resulting in stark economic disparities and intense rivalry, as each government often claims to be the sole legitimate representative of the unified people.

Over time, prolonged political separation inevitably leads to cultural and social drift. Despite sharing a common ancestry, foundational language, and history, the populations are subjected to different educational systems, media environments, and international alliances. Consequently, linguistic dialects diverge, and younger generations often develop distinct civic identities that gradually overshadow their historical unity. What begins as a purely political boundary eventually hardens into a tangible cultural and social divide.

Geopolitically, these divided states frequently become highly militarized flashpoints and arenas for proxy conflicts between larger global powers. The relationship between the two states is usually defined by a volatile mix of diplomatic hostility and the persistent, often constitutionally mandated, aspiration for reunification. 

However, as the economic and cultural gaps widen, the practical reality of reunification becomes increasingly daunting. The ultimate trajectory of the "one people, two states" scenario generally leads to one of two outcomes: a permanent hardening into two entirely distinct nations, or eventual reunification. Even if political integration is achieved—as seen with the reunification of Germany—the process requires massive economic subsidies and decades of social reconciliation to bridge the deep systemic inequalities and psychological barriers forged during the period of separation.

AHC: Reverse Cuba and the Philippines

Your mission is to reverse the fate of Cuba and the Philippines after the Spanish-American War. That means Cuba getting annexed and the Philippines being made a protectorate. Puerto Rico can be either.
items.model_answer:
If the historical trajectories of Cuba and the Philippines were reversed following the 1898 Spanish-American War, the geopolitical landscape of the 20th century, particularly the Cold War, would have been radically transformed. In this counterfactual scenario, the United States annexes Cuba outright as a colonial territory while granting the Philippines nominal, heavily conditioned independence as a protectorate. 

For Cuba, outright annexation by the United States would likely have placed it on a path similar to Puerto Rico or Hawaii. Given its geographic proximity—just 90 miles from Florida—and its lucrative sugar industry, Cuba would have been deeply integrated into the American economy and political system, potentially achieving US statehood or permanent commonwealth status by the mid-20th century. Because of this direct American governance and military presence, the conditions that allowed Fidel Castro’s 1959 revolution to succeed would not have materialized. Consequently, the Western Hemisphere would have remained an undisputed American sphere of influence. The Bay of Pigs invasion and the Cuban Missile Crisis would never have occurred, sparing the United States its most terrifying, close-proximity brush with nuclear war.

Conversely, the Philippines would have experienced the turbulent fate of a marginalized neo-colony. Granted early but hollow independence, the archipelago would have been dominated by US corporate interests and a corrupt local oligarchy, mirroring the historical plight of pre-revolutionary Cuba. Following the devastation of World War II, massive wealth inequality and anti-imperialist sentiment would have provided fertile ground for a communist revolution. In this timeline, the communist Hukbalahap rebellion of the 1940s and 50s likely succeeds, transforming the Philippines into a Soviet or Chinese-aligned communist state right on the edge of the Pacific.

A communist Philippines would have been a catastrophic strategic loss for the United States during the Cold War. Historically, American military installations in the Philippines, such as Subic Bay Naval Base and Clark Air Base, were vital logistical hubs for US operations in both the Korean and Vietnam Wars. Without these bases, the US military's ability to project power and contain communism in Southeast Asia would have been severely crippled, potentially leading to faster and broader communist victories in Indochina. 

Furthermore, the Soviet Union might have attempted to place nuclear weapons in the Philippines to counter US missiles in Europe. While a "Philippine Missile Crisis" would have triggered a massive geopolitical standoff, the geographic distance from the North American mainland would have made it less of an immediate, existential threat to Washington D.C. than the historical Cuban Missile Crisis. Ultimately, this reversal would have shifted the most volatile flashpoints of the Cold War entirely to the Pacific, leaving the Americas entirely secure while turning Southeast Asia into a much more formidable and unified anti-Western bloc.

Could the UK carry on alone? What aircraft could replace the Tornado and fill in this role? Could a two seat, big wing SEPECAT Jaguar work? Would an advanced Buccaneer work with a modern avionics upgrade? Regards
items.model_answer:
If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado (originally the Multi-Role Combat Aircraft, or MRCA) program at the outset in the late 1960s, the project would have almost certainly collapsed, fundamentally altering the trajectory of the European aerospace industry and Cold War air power. 

For the United Kingdom, the withdrawal of its partners would have been a devastating blow. Having already suffered the controversial cancellations of the indigenous BAC TSR-2 and the Anglo-French Variable Geometry (AFVG) aircraft, as well as abandoning the purchase of American F-111Ks, the Royal Air Force was in desperate need of a deep-strike and interdiction aircraft. Burdened by the severe economic struggles of the 1970s, the UK would not have been able to shoulder the immense research and development costs of a variable-sweep wing aircraft alone. Consequently, the UK would have been forced to buy American off-the-shelf solutions, likely adopting the F-111, expanding its fleet of F-4 Phantoms, or later investing in the F-15E Strike Eagle. This would have resulted in severe job losses and a massive loss of sovereign design capability for the British aviation industry.

West Germany and Italy, both urgently needing to replace their aging and accident-prone fleets of F-104 Starfighters, would have also pivoted toward the United States. Without the Tornado to fill the low-level strike and interception roles, West Germany would likely have expanded its use of the F-4 Phantom II and subsequently joined the European Participating Air Forces (EPAF) consortium to purchase the F-16 Fighting Falcon, aligning its procurement with neighbors like the Netherlands and Belgium. Italy would have followed a similar path, likely adopting the F-16 or F/A-18 Hornet much earlier, while perhaps accelerating domestic development of lighter strike aircraft like the AMX International. 

The most profound and lasting consequence, however, would have been the fragmentation of the European defense sector. The PANAVIA consortium was a vital pioneering effort in cross-border industrial integration, establishing the complex legal, engineering, and supply-chain frameworks necessary for multi-national European defense projects. Without the shared experience, technological transfer, and corporate relationships forged by PANAVIA, the subsequent Eurofighter Typhoon program likely would never have materialized. 

Consequently, the absence of the Tornado program would have left the British, German, and Italian aerospace industries permanently diminished. France’s Dassault Aviation, with its Mirage and later Rafale lines, might have emerged as the sole independent producer of advanced combat aircraft in Europe. Ultimately, the defense of Western Europe would have become almost entirely dependent on American aerospace dominance, permanently altering the transatlantic defense trade balance.

items.question: What If No nuclear weapons?
human_answers: As has been noted it is pretty much impossible to avoid having nuclear weapons ever being created. The science is pretty obvious. What CAN be altered, to a degree, is the "when". The U.S. threw a dramatic amount of funding at the effort, along with huge amounts of resources (Manhattan literally built the entire city of Oak Ridge TN to house the workers on the project. It was farmland, with about 3,000 people living in the area then in less than 2 years, it was a city with a population of 75,000. Government just walked in and "acquired" 59,000 acres, evicted everyone in the local farms and villages, and started building a fence (BIG ASS fence). The same thing happened in Washington with Hanford, except it was 500,000 acres and 39,000 people, Just a little less funding, or a project manager less driven than General Groves and the Bomb isn't ready.

Based on the described scenario, the USSR becomes the first country to test a nuclear weapon in the early 1950s, whereupon the US and UK governments demand an explanation for who filed the relevant reports in the wrong section back in 1940. In the case of the US, it's probably Lyman Briggs, who in OTL actually did lock away a key report in his safe without showing it to anyone else, which may have delayed the start of the Manhattan Project by several months. But even then, uranium fission was discovered in France in December 1938. The Einsten-Szilard letter warned the US government of the possibilities in August 1939. The Frisch-Peierls memorandum, the first description of a nuclear weapon, was written in March 1940 for the British government. By Frisch's own description, the work he and Peierls did was straightforward for any competent nuclear physicist. There might be a PoD wherein Frisch and Peierls are interned as enemy aliens and not allowed to work as physicists. Oliphant is focussed on the higher priority radar work, so Thomson's conclusion that it was not worth pursuing a chain reaction in uranium is accepted by the British government. There is therefore no MAUD committee, no report for Briggs to ignore, and no reason for Oliphant to kick things into gear. Instead, what is likely to happen is that eventually someone in the US does ask the questions that Frisch and Peierls asked, and they reach similar answers. Given OTL's trajectory, it's hard to see why that would happen any earlier than August 1941, given that US research was initially largely concerned with power plants rather than weapons. If we say it does, it might take the best part of a year for a US equivalent of the MAUD report to be carried out and an atomic weapons programme started. That puts a US weapons programme without the MAUD input as starting in mid-1942 - so about a six month delay. An arbitrarily longer delay is entirely plausible, but eventually - and probably sooner rather than later - someone is going to ask the right questions, and then things will start moving very quickly.

items.model_answer:
If nuclear weapons had never been developed, the geopolitical, historical, and scientific landscape of the modern world would be radically different, defined primarily by the absence of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD). 

The immediate historical impact would have materialized at the end of World War II. Without the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the Allies would have likely executed Operation Downfall, the massive amphibious invasion of the Japanese home islands. This campaign would have resulted in millions of additional Allied and Japanese casualties. Furthermore, a prolonged Pacific war would have allowed the Soviet Union to invade Japan from the north, almost certainly resulting in a divided post-war Japan, much like Germany and Korea.

The most profound change would have been the trajectory of the Cold War. Without the existential terror of nuclear annihilation to enforce a tense peace, the United States and the Soviet Union would likely have engaged in direct conventional warfare. Historical flashpoints such as the Berlin Blockade, the Korean War, or the Cuban Missile Crisis would not have been restrained by the fear of global apocalypse and would have likely escalated into World War III. Europe would have once again become a massive conventional battlefield, leading to tens of millions of deaths and repeated devastation of the continent. 

In the absence of nuclear deterrence, superpowers would have been forced to maintain colossal standing armies and continuous wartime economies. To gain strategic advantages, military powers would have heavily invested in other forms of mass destruction, likely accelerating the development and actual deployment of advanced chemical and biological weapons. Global conflicts would be resolved through direct, bloody clashes between major powers rather than the proxy wars that characterized the actual Cold War.

From a scientific and environmental perspective, if the underlying physics of nuclear fission were never harnessed, the world would also lack nuclear energy. This would have forced a heavier global reliance on coal, oil, and natural gas throughout the late 20th and early 21st centuries, significantly accelerating carbon emissions and worsening the effects of climate change. 

Ultimately, a world without nuclear weapons would be free from the psychological dread of sudden, apocalyptic annihilation. However, it would paradoxically be a far bloodier world. By removing the ultimate deterrent that forced major powers to avoid direct conflict, the 20th and 21st centuries would have likely seen continuous, devastating conventional world wars.

items.question: What If the USSR was leaked information about OB just before it happened and were thus better prepared and more competent in 1941? (No strike though)
human_answers: A couple days or weeks isn’t really enough if you’re going with the “Stalin finally makes a good decision” scenario. You need at least a couple months to have the Soviets dug in and prepared at more defensible spots further east than iotl, and considering the German initial manpower advantage (to say nothing of the purges creating widespread incompetence in the red army and said incompetence making their logistics horrible), they still probably lose pretty hard, although not quite as much as iotl. I think at least 6 or so (probably a bit more) months is needed to help close the manpower gap and create a Minsk-Kiev line that the Germans can’t penetrate if you don’t want Soviet losses to be seen as proportionally a lot bigger (though there’s a strong chance they still are in this scenario, just not enough to give the impression that all you need to do is kick in the rotten door enough and it’ll fall).

The Soviet Union possessed highly precise intelligence indicating that the German military's logistics were insufficient to sustain a protracted war and that its armaments factories had not yet shifted to a wartime footing. (This intelligence was derived from the infiltration of German industry by communist sympathizers.) Hitler also couldn't been so foolish as to believe that the mighty Soviet Union could be conquered within three months—at least, no analyst would have dared to venture such an insulting conjecture. Consequently, the less reliable intelligence from military and western country must have been false, and war is in next year. This chain of logic is remarkably robust; You cannot convince the Soviets that Germany is about to attack without introducing collateral changes—and different changes would inevitably lead to different outcomes in the war. Would they perceive their own military as weaker? Would they place their trust in Anglo-American intelligence while disregarding the Comintern’s own network? Or would they have managed to plant exceptionally reliable spies deep within the German military itself? Each of these scenarios would necessitate a distinct defensive strategy, thereby altering the very trajectory of the conflict. One thing, however, remains certain: if the Soviet Union were to lose the war while the United States remained an active belligerent, the Americans would undoubtedly drop the nuclear bomb.

Again, as usual these scenarios entirely depend on one or both sides failing to react to changing circumstances. Firstly, USSR had information about possibility of German attack and was reacting. items.model_answer:
If the USSR had received and acted upon leaked information about Operation Barbarossa just before June 1941, the initial phase of the Eastern Front would have unfolded drastically differently. Without launching a preemptive strike, a competent and prepared Red Army would have immediately dispersed its aircraft from forward airfields, preventing the Luftwaffe from obliterating the Soviet Air Force on the ground in the opening hours of the invasion. Soviet leadership would have abandoned their vulnerable forward-leaning posture, pulling troops back from the immediate border to establish a defense-in-depth. By fully mobilizing, issuing live ammunition, and manning fortified defensive lines, the Red Army would have denied the Wehrmacht the element of surprise that was absolutely crucial to the success of Blitzkrieg.

Consequently, the massive and disastrous Soviet encirclements that historically occurred at Minsk, Smolensk, and Kiev would have been largely avoided. Instead of rapidly bypassing disorganized and paralyzed Soviet units, German armored spearheads would have faced a grueling, organized fighting retreat. This would have inflicted significantly higher casualties on the Axis forces from day one and severely strained their logistical lines much earlier in the campaign. The German offensive would likely have culminated hundreds of miles further west, never posing a direct threat to Moscow or subjecting Leningrad to its devastating multi-year siege. 

With its pre-war military strength largely preserved and its western industrial base either defended or evacuated with greater efficiency, the USSR would have been positioned to launch massive counter-offensives much earlier than historically possible. This would have significantly shortened the duration of the war in Europe. Geopolitically, an earlier collapse of Nazi Germany at the hands of a stronger Red Army would likely have resulted in Soviet forces advancing much further west before meeting the Western Allies. This could have easily brought the entirety of Germany and potentially other Western European nations under Soviet influence, drastically shifting the borders of the Cold War Iron Curtain further west.

I probably know the words to 75% of the songs sung by Elvis and the Beatles but I don’t know who wrote most of Elvises songs nor who produced any songs for either of them. But I either know or have books that tell me who the major officers where at pretty much any major battle in the Civil War. And I know or can find out enough about most of them to have a good guess how swapping them will effect a given battle. But who can say what guy would have walked through the door and gotten the opportunity to perform if Elvis was gone. Frankly there are thousands of better singers in the world than Elvis that never got the chance. But the combination of his abilities and the opritunities he got made him a superstar. But it is impossible to know who would have gooten that chance if he was not there. But there are only a handful of people that may have been promoted if Montgomery got ran over by a tank.

I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. And with that you still have white singers becoming popular for their heavily sanitized covers of black R&B songs ( looks at Pat Boone ). You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

No Beatles or Elvis? Hmmm the amateur musicologist in me (that's what happens when you're a musician, who has also played in rock bands) says that rock 'n roll would still exist. The chances are also good that you would still have its superstar in the 50s - I read years ago that there were plans to push Carl Perkins (he of "Blue Suede Shoes" fame) towards superstardom by Sun Records. He might have actually become one if he hadn't suffered a major injury (he was in a car crash that kept him out of commission for a long time). Sam Phillips and even Elvis stated that Carl was doing rockabilly before Elvis, and unlike Elvis, Carl was also a songwriter. Most musicians will tell you that having that skill gives you much more staying power - you're not just a performer, you can make money off or songwriting royalties. By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?
items.model_answer:
If modern music had evolved without Elvis Presley and The Beatles, the trajectory of 20th-century popular culture would be fundamentally altered, changing the sound, business models, and cultural impact of the music industry. While the foundational genres of blues, R&B, and country would still exist, the explosive mainstream crossover of rock and roll—and its subsequent evolution into a globally dominant art form—would have been severely delayed or entirely reshaped.

Without Elvis Presley in the 1950s, rock and roll might have struggled to achieve its massive, immediate crossover into mainstream white America. Elvis did not invent rock and roll, but he served as the cultural lightning rod that brought the sounds of Black pioneers like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, and Fats Domino to a segregated, conservative audience. In his absence, rock and roll might have remained a regional or racially compartmentalized genre for much longer. The mainstream charts would likely have been dominated by traditional pop crooners, sanitized covers of R&B hits, and conservative country music well into the 1960s. Furthermore, the archetype of the rebellious, visually dynamic solo rock star would not have been established in the same way. If someone like Buddy Holly or Eddie Cochran had become the face of the genre instead, early rock might have taken on a tamer, more cerebral, or heavily country-leaning identity.

The absence of The Beatles in the 1960s would have an even more profound structural impact on modern music. Prior to The Beatles, the music industry relied heavily on the Brill Building model, where songwriters, session musicians, and singers were entirely separate entities. The Beatles popularized the concept of the self-contained rock band that wrote its own material and played its own instruments. Without them, the "band" format might not have become the default vehicle for popular music, and the industry might have remained heavily focused on solo vocalists backed by studio orchestras. 

Furthermore, The Beatles were the primary catalysts for the "British Invasion," which globalized pop music and proved that international artists could dominate the American market. Without them, British rock and pop might have remained a localized phenomenon, and bands like The Rolling Stones or The Who might never have found a global foothold. The evolution of the recording studio would also have been drastically altered. While visionaries like Brian Wilson of The Beach Boys were already pushing the boundaries of studio production, Wilson’s masterpiece, *Pet Sounds*, was a direct competitive response to The Beatles' *Rubber Soul*. Without this transatlantic rivalry driving the push toward the "concept album," the transition of pop music from disposable teenage entertainment to a respected, avant-garde art form would have been stunted. 

Consequently, the landscape of modern music today would look drastically different. Without the colossal footprint of classic rock and the British Invasion, the direct lineage of R&B, soul, and jazz would likely have faced less competition in the mainstream. Motown, Stax Records, and innovators like James Brown would still have revolutionized rhythm and groove, meaning that funk, disco, and hip-hop might have emerged on a similar timeline and potentially dominated mainstream culture much earlier. Meanwhile, the folk revival led by Bob Dylan would still have introduced deep lyrical complexity to music, but without The Beatles bridging the gap between folk-rock and pop, the singer-songwriter movement might have remained acoustic rather than electrifying. Ultimately, modern music without Elvis and The Beatles would likely be far less rock-centric, with a mainstream pop landscape built almost entirely on the direct evolution of R&B, traditional vocal pop, and electronic dance music.

human_answers: Far too big Even with folding wings I don't think they would fit on the elevators and would take up too much room in the hanger even of they fit which again I suspect not Its landing on performance of he Beaufighter is about the same as an avenger (60 knots?) but its much heavier than the TBF so I am not sure the arrestor cables of the day could handle such a plane. Its a nice idea but its too much of a plane for the carriers of the day - might work on an Audacious class but not the carriers built in the late 30s. The Whispering Death is already doing sterling work as a land based anti shipping aircraft during the war and it has great range - not quite 'Rikko' (G3m and G4m Japanese bombers) range, but close too it, but still a scourge where ever it operated.

In the last thread on the subject I mentioned, given any wing-break would have to be somewhat outboard the engines*, that you could probably take one up and down on Implacable's forward lift but the hangar height would preclude you rolling it off. You could store one in Illustrious's hangar, if you made it from a kit of parts, as the lift is too narrow. So deck parks only. You could use some form of depressing oleos to lower the Beaufighter's resting angle. You might just scrape it into Implacable's hangar but clearances would be marginal. Any kind of seaway would make deck handling tricky to impossible. You could also only load a torpedo on the flight deck with the aircraft back up to full height.
