At t=0, the people within 50 meters of the train—all 2,500 of them—pull the triggers, unleashing 100,000 BBs per second. As the train plows ahead, people in front magically fly sideways off the tracks. This is unrealistic, but we can’t let them slow down the train with their bodies—that would be cheating. As those people stop firing, people further down the tracks come into range and start shooting. The train is moving so quickly that any one person only gets off a few dozen rounds before the target moves past (or through) them. [Image: image] At any given time, there are 45,000 BBs in the air. But there’s a problem: When the steel balls bounce off the front of the train, they don’t disappear. They fly back at the shooters (who’ll probably shoot their eyes out) and into the line of fire. At its peak, this cloud of ricochets deflects nearly 1% of incoming shots via BB-BB collisions. This is a neat effect, but it doesn’t substantially interfere with our operation. Unfortunately, even this hail of steel takes several excruciating minutes—and almost two kilometers of track—to stop the train. That means we’d need over 100,000 shooters lined up along the track, and arming them would cost in the neighborhood of $50 million. We can do better, but we’ll have to relax the BB gun requirement. The AK-47 has a muzzle velocity of 715 meters per second and fires a bullet which outweighs a steel BB by a factor of 25. The bullets go so fast that they penetrate into the body of the train (which means they’re a little less efficient at transferring momentum, but it doesn’t really matter). Calculations show a crowd of 2,500 people firing two AK-47s each would be able to stop our runaway locomotive within the space of 30 meters—in only a second and a half. Mission accomplished. [Image: image] ... well. The greatly reduced drag coefficient of machine gun ammo compared to steel ball bearings means we can shoot from a much greater distance. Let’s make the crowd 200 meters deep instead of 50. At t=0, 40,000 people open fire. The AK-47 typically has a 30-round magazine and fires 10 shots per second. Within a third of a second, a quarter of a million bullets are in the air. Stray shots no doubt cause a lot of fatalities in the front of the crowd, but with a trained and disciplined group of shooters, the bulk of the shots could actually manage to hit the target. At t=15 ms, the locomotive has inched forward by half a meter and encounters the leading edge of the bullet cloud. By t=30 ms, the locomotive is being hit by a half dozen new bullets every millisecond. At t=150 ms, the locomotive has crawled forward about six meters, but it’s absorbing several hundred bullets each millisecond. This has begun to slow its forward momentum (and tear it apart—let’s assume it’s loaded full of some kind of lightweight material that distributes the shock of the bullet evenly). At around t=300ms, the full quarter of a million bullets are in the air. Most people have gotten off a total of six shots between their two guns. Interestingly, the bullets from the front rows of shooters occasionally catch up with—and collide with—slower bullets from the shooters behind them. This doesn’t happen a lot, but it does happen. The locomotive creeps forward to seven meters, seven and a half, seven and three quarters … and then seven and a half again. Success. But the shooters have only fired about a dozen rounds so far. Their magazines are still mostly full. At t=1s, almost a million shots have been fired. The locomotive is sliding backward at about 100 m/s (220 mph). At t=2s, the locomotive’s backward acceleration slows down quite a bit. This is partly because it’s starting to get out of range of the shooters. But it’s also because the locomotive is traveling at nearly the speed of sound, and the bullets are having a harder and harder time catching up. When they do, they have so little relative velocity that they can’t accelerate it much more. By this point, drag from the atmosphere is the dominant force on the locomotive’s motion. The rear end lifts from the tracks, the locomotive starts to tumble, and finally disintegrates into a cloud of shrapnel and spent bullets. Now bring on that asteroid. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 在《世界末日》中，美国宇航局的一名人员评论说，向小行星发射激光的计划就像“向货运列车发射BB枪”。仅使用 b.b. 怎样才能阻止失控的货运列车？枪？
items.model_answer:
To stop a runaway freight train with a BB gun, you would have to abandon any attempt at using direct kinetic force and instead exploit the train's mechanical and pneumatic engineering. From a physics standpoint, stopping the train by shooting at it to counter its momentum is impossible. A typical freight train weighs upwards of 10,000 tons, while a standard steel BB weighs roughly a third of a gram. The kinetic energy of the train is so massive that it would take trillions of perfectly timed BB impacts to even measurably reduce its speed. 

Therefore, the only scientifically plausible method is to use the BB gun as a precise, remote tool to trigger the train's built-in fail-safe mechanisms. Freight trains rely on a continuous pneumatic air brake system. This system requires constant air pressure to keep the brake shoes held away from the wheels; if that air pressure drops, the brakes automatically deploy across the entire train. 

To stop the train from the outside, your best target would be the "angle cock," which is the heavy valve handle located on the pressurized air hoses connecting each train car. If you could shoot the handle with enough precision and force to knock it into the open position, the pressurized air would violently vent into the atmosphere. This sudden drop in brake pipe pressure would instantly trigger an emergency brake application, bringing the massive train to a screeching halt. While a standard BB gun might lack the joules to move a stiff, heavy iron handle, hitting it perfectly on the very edge of the lever could theoretically provide enough torque to crack it open. 

Alternatively, if you were inside the locomotive cab, you could use the BB gun to shoot the emergency brake valve, the dead-man switch, or the emergency fuel cutoff button. If you were positioned miles ahead of the train on the ground, you could aim for a trackside signal relay or switch indicator. If the train is equipped with Positive Train Control (PTC)—a computerized system that monitors signals—shattering a critical trackside sensor or signal light could trigger a fault in the network. The PTC system would detect the anomaly and automatically broadcast a signal to the locomotive's onboard computers to cut the throttle and apply the brakes. 

In every viable scenario, the BB gun cannot stop the train through its own stopping power. It can only succeed if utilized as a precise instrument to initiate a chain reaction, forcing the train's own immense pneumatic and mechanical systems to do the heavy lifting.

items.question: What If It Were Actually a Tie?
human_answers: In most states, a popular vote tie is broken by a coin toss or drawing names from a hat. The odds of a many-state tie are slimmer than the odds of the hat being hit by a bale of cocaine dumped from a drug-smuggling airplane. Nate Silver flippantly posted his 'tie' question on Twitter during the tallying of the extremely close 2012 Republican Iowa Caucus results. In that case, an exact tie was averted—Santorum ended up winning by 34 votes out of 121,503. And since it was a non-binding nominating vote, the Iowa Republican Party could handle a tie any way they wanted. But since it’s Election Day, let’s apply his question to the current contest. What will happen if there's a tie? I don't mean an electoral college tie. There’s probably about a 1 in 500 chance of one of those this year, and the consequences are thoroughly explored (http://blog.constitutioncenter.org/2012/11/an-electoral-college-tie-explained/). Instead, the question concerns both candidates getting the same number of votes in a state. Several researchers—including Silver himself (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/probdecisive2.pdf)—have calculated the odds of a state winner being decided by a single vote, which is effectively the same as the probability of a tie vote. For typical close states, the linked article calculates the probabilities to be in the neighborhood of 1 in 100,000—which makes intuitive sense, since 100,000 is the sort of vote margin by which swing state elections are typically decided. So what if there's a tie in a close state this year? [Image: image] For that matter, what if there’s a tie in every battleground state? [Image: image] Well, for starters, recounts happen. But since recounts happen in close elections in general, these are just as likely to create ties as to break them. They don’t change the underlying probability. So let’s assume that after all recounts, there’s a tie. What then? The short answer is that it’s up to the state’s laws. I went through the general laws of nine competitive states to see how they handle popular vote ties. In most of them, the tie is broken by “drawing lots”—that is, randomly. (If you’re curious, here are links to some tie vote laws in each state: Virginia (http://leg1.state.va.us/cgi-bin/legp504.exe?000+cod+24.2-674), North Carolina (http://law.onecle.com/north-carolina/163-elections-and-election-laws/163-182.8.html), Florida (http://election.dos.state.fl.us/publications/pdf/2012/2012_Election_Laws.pdf), Ohio (http://codes.ohio.gov/orc/3505.33), New Hampshire (http://www.gencourt.state.nh.us/rsa/html/lxiii/667/667-17.htm), Wisconsin (http://docs.legis.wi.gov/statutes/statutes/5/I/01), Colorado (http://www.state.co.us/gov_dir/leg_dir/olls/sl1999/sl_154.htm), Iowa (http://search.legis.state.ia.us/nxt/gateway.dll/ic/1/13/2174/2175/2582/2629?f=templates$fn=document-frameset.htm$q=[field%2050.44]$x=Advanced), Nevada (http://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-293.html#NRS293Sec400)). [Image: image] “Drawing lots” can mean a coin toss, drawing straws, or picking a name from a hat. Most states leave the details up to the Secretary of State or an electoral board, although Iowa Code 50.44 specifies that the names be written on pieces of paper and placed in a “receptacle”. In North Carolina, however, a tie vote (when more than 5,000 votes are cast) results in a new election. (Which could potentially itself result in a tie ...) But let’s imagine that there’s not just one state that’s tied—instead, the nine most competitive states are tied (and the rest go as expected). If North Carolina held a runoff to break the tie, and the other eight states flipped coins (or picked from Iowa’s receptacle), Obama would be reelected in 431 out of 512 cases (http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2012/11/02/us/politics/paths-to-the-white-house.html)—about 84% of the time. But how likely is a nine-state tie? If we ballpark the odds of a tie vote in each close state at 1 in 100,000, then the odds of a tie vote in all nine states is in the neighborhood of one in a quattuordecillion—1 followed by 45 zeroes. (This ignores vote correlation between states, but it’s good enough for a first-order estimate). Florida is hit by an average of 66 tornadoes per year (http://www1.ncdc.noaa.gov/pub/data/cmb/images/tornado/clim/ann-avg-torn1991-2010.gif). If each tornado is 50 yards wide and has a path 1.5 miles long (which is typical (http://www.crh.noaa.gov/lmk/soo/docu/tornado_faq.php), if not necessarily the mean), we can calculate that a typical location in Florida experiences an average 1.4 picotornados per second: \[66\tfrac{\text{tornadoes}}{\text{year}}\times\frac{1.5\text{ miles}\times50\text{ yards}}{\text{Area of Florida}}\approx1.4\times10^{-12}\tfrac{\text{tornadoes}}{\text{second}}\] Astronomer Alan Harris calculates that a person’s lifetime odds of death from a comet or meteorite impact are about 1 in 700,000. If a typical person in the calculation lives 70 years, this suggests a Florida resident suffers an average of 0.64 femtodeaths per second from meteorite impacts: \[\frac{\tfrac{1}{700,000}\text{deaths}}{70\text{ years}}\approx6.4\times10^{-16}\tfrac{\text{deaths}}{\text{second}}\] In 1994, drug smugglers fleeing the authorities dropped an estimated 20 bales of cocaine from an airplane over Florida—one of which crashed through the roof of a Crime Watch meeting and narrowly missed the Homestead Chief of Police (http://www.deseretnews.com/article/392575/ONLY-IN-FLORIDA-DOES-COCAINE-DROP-FROM-SKY.html?pg=all). If Florida has been hit by 20 bales of cocaine over the last 20 years, then the average person in Florida is struck by an average of 29 zeptobales of cocaine per second: \[\frac{20\text{ bales}}{20\text{ years}}\times\frac{\left (\tfrac{75\text{ kg}}{\text{Density of cocaine}} \right )^\tfrac{2}{3}}{\text{Area of Florida}}\approx2.9\times10^{-21}\tfrac{\text{bales}}{\text{second}}\] (By the way—this means that given a street price of $20,000 per kilogram, a typical acre of Florida land produces an average revenue of three cents per year in falling cocaine bales). Putting all this together: The probability that every battleground state is exactly tied is roughly equal to the probability that, when one of the Florida electors reaches into the hat to draw a name, he or she is struck by a falling cocaine bale, the hat is hurled away within the next few seconds by a tornado, and the elector is obliterated minutes later by a meteorite impact. [Image: image] If you’re in the US, don’t forget to vote—your vote could make or break a tie. And if you’re voting in Florida, keep an eye on the sky.
items.original_question: 如果真的打成平手怎么办？
items.model_answer:
Because the concept of a "tie" can refer to several different phenomena across science and engineering, the outcome of this counterfactual depends entirely on which STEM domain is being considered. Here is what would happen in the most notable scientific scenarios if they resulted in an actual "tie":

*   **An Absolute Tie in Time (Physics and Relativity):** 
    In our universe, absolute simultaneity does not exist. According to Einstein’s theory of special relativity, if two spatially separated events happen at the exact same time (a "tie") for one observer, they will happen at different times for an observer moving at a different speed. If a cosmic race or pair of events were *actually* an absolute tie—meaning every possible observer in the universe agreed they happened at the exact same instant—it would break special relativity. It would imply the existence of an absolute, universal clock or a preferred reference frame (like the disproven "luminiferous aether"), which would completely upend modern physics.

*   **A Tie Between Cosmic Expansion and Gravity (Cosmology):** 
    For decades, astrophysicists wondered if the universe would expand forever (the Big Freeze) or if gravity would eventually pull everything back together (the Big Crunch). If the outward kinetic energy of the Big Bang and the inward pull of all the universe's gravity were an exact tie, the universe would have a density parameter of exactly 1 ($\Omega = 1$). In this "flat universe" scenario, the universe would expand forever, but the rate of expansion would gradually slow down, asymptoting toward zero but never quite stopping. (We now know dark energy is causing the expansion to accelerate, meaning expansion is currently "winning").

*   **A Real "TIE" Spacecraft (Aerospace Engineering):** 
    If we interpret the question as referring to the famous Star Wars TIE Fighter—which stands for Twin Ion Engine—a real-world version would behave nothing like it does in the movies. Real ion thrusters exist and are incredibly fuel-efficient, but they produce a minuscule amount of thrust (roughly equivalent to the weight of a piece of paper resting on your hand). A real spacecraft powered by a twin ion engine could not dogfight, hover, or fly in an atmosphere; instead, it would slowly and silently accelerate over months in the vacuum of space to eventually reach incredible speeds.

*   **A Physical Tie Between Celestial Bodies (Materials Science):**

items.question: What If a 100-Foot Diamond Meteor Hit Earth at Light Speed?
human_answers: Nothing made of matter can go at the speed of light. But that’s ok—we can get close enough! No matter how fast you push something, it will never quite get up to light speed. This seems like it can’t be right, but it is. Our universe has some weird rules. But the closer something gets to the speed of light, the more energy and momentum it has—and this energy and momentum go up without limit. We’ll start slow and work our way up. 1 kilometer per second: If we drop the meteor from the edge of space, 100 kilometers up, it’ll punch through the atmosphere without slowing down too much and hit the ground moving about Mach 3—over a kilometer a second. As it falls, it compresses the air in front of it. When the air is compressed, it heats it up. (This is the same thing that heats up spacecraft and meteors—actual air friction has little to do with that.) By the time it reaches the ground, the lower surface will have heated to over 500℃, which is enough to glow visibly. When it hits the ground, two minutes after it was released, it makes a crater 300 meters across—the size of a school, shattering into fragments in the process. [Image: image] 11 kilometers per second: If we set the diamond in space a little ways away from the Earth, and let it fall toward us, it will hit at about 11 kilometers per second. This is Earth’s escape velocity, and anything that hits the Earth from space will—thanks to gravity—be going at least that fast. At 11 kilometers per second, the brief descent would be visible as a fireball. The energy of the impact would be comparable to a small atomic bomb, and the crater it would create would be a kilometer across—a little smaller than Meteor Crater in Arizona. [Image: image] 72 kilometers per second: This is just about the fastest that anything can hit the Earth if it’s orbiting the Sun. The Leonid meteor shower hits at this speed. Oddly, the speed that something is going doesn’t really affect how deeply it digs into the ground. Isaac Newton came up with a very clever idea (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_depth) for estimating how deeply projectiles will go in their targets before stopping. It turns out that no matter how fast a projectile is going, if it hits something that’s about the same density, it will only go about one body-length in. [Image: image] However, it will make quite a splash. The 72-kilometer-per-second diamond sphere blasts out a crater over two kilometers across, with an energy release comparable to that of the biggest fusion bombs. Here’s where things get weird. 3,000 kilometers per second = 0.01c: This would be pretty bad. The thing that makes this a little unpredictable is the fact that at speeds in the range of hundreds of kilometers per second, the air begins to undergo nuclear fusion (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0032063389900305) (Google that paper title to find the full text). This, combined with plain old plasma heating, may manage to eat apart the diamond sphere completely before it reaches the ground. But it doesn’t do the ground much good. The sphere doesn’t spread out enough to make a difference, and it still hits the ground in roughly one spot. The blast releases a thousand times more energy than the largest nuclear weapon, devastating whatever region it came down over. It gouges out a massive crater—though not the biggest one Earth has ever seen. [Image: image] 0.99c: This is where relativity kicks in. At these speeds, the bonds holding the sphere together are completely irrelevant. It’s just a collection of carbon atoms moving so fast that Lorentz contraction flattens the whole thing into a pancake (although we wouldn’t be able to see that visually (http://www.math.ubc.ca/~cass/courses/m309-01a/cook/terrell1.html)). The SRIM (http://www.srim.org/) particle physics simulation tool can help answer some questions about what happens when it hits. The carbon atoms in the ball carry about 70 GeV of energy each. They’re actually moving too fast to fuse directly with the air—they just pass through it completely. The air molecules punch three meters into the face of the ball before coming to a rest inside it, and it arrives at the ground with a bunch more matter in it than it started with. It’s also expanding rapidly. When it hits the surface, it disintegrates completely, digging downward and outward, carving a cone-shaped path down through the bedrock. The impact depth equation no longer applies, since the atoms are literally passing through each other. The energy cracks a hole in the crust and blows open a crater so big you can see the molten mantle. This delivers the energy of 50 dinosaur-killing Chicxulub impacts—enough to cause a mass extinction, if not end life completely. [Image: image] I’ve always thought that one of the the great things about physics is that you can add more digits to any number and see what happens and nobody can stop you. 0.9999999c: At this speed, every carbon molecule carries 25 TeV of energy, comparable to particles in the beam of the Large Hadron Collider. A little faster, and we might spot Higgs bosons in the impact debris. As it stands, the whole thing hits the planet with about the kinetic energy of the orbiting Moon. It’s enough to punch a gaping hole in the mantle and shake up the surface across the whole planet, turning it molten. This probably ends all life on and around Earth. Oops, cat stepped on my keyboard again and I added a bunch more 9s. 0.9999999999999999999999951c The fastest object (with mass) in recorded history might be the Oh-My-God particle (no relation to the God particle), a proton from space that plowed into the atmosphere over Utah in 1991. It was moving at 99.99999999999999999999951% of the speed of light, which meant it packed the kinetic energy of a baseball—in a single proton. The cascade of particles it blasted apart dwarfed anything the LHC could produce. Nobody knows how it got to be moving so fast. Particles moving that fast hit the Earth a handful of times a year. They seem to come from the general direction of exploding galaxies, but what happened to to make them leave in such a hurry—and why they haven’t slowed down more before they got here—is something of a mystery. Let’s give Aidan’s diamond meteor the speed of the Oh My God particle. These speeds are so high that my copy of SRIM flatly refuses to simulate them. However, we can get some idea from looking at how cosmic rays cascade through rock. The diamond sweeps out a column of atmosphere without seeming to notice and disappears into the crust. A cloud of expanding plasma and radiation grows around the entry point as the energy ripples outward through the body of the planet. Forty milliseconds later the entire far side expands outward in an incandescent cloud. The diamond meteor, and the cascade of particles it created as it collided with the crust, is spread out throughout the body of our planet. The superheated planet glows brighter than the sun. The momentum would be enough to knock the Earth into a different orbit—but the Earth is no more. The energy deposited is ten thousand times greater than the planet’s gravitational binding energy, and the planet is blown into an expanding cloud of plasma, with a particularly energetic streamer extending away from the far side of the impact site, out into space. The Sun hiccups and flares as it absorbs waves of dust. The surfaces of Mars and Venus are scoured clean by the waves of incredibly high-energy plasma. [Image: image] And in the distant future, an alien astronomer on a world hundreds of light-years from Earth frowns at a beeping detector, and wonders what violent event would make a particle move so fast.
items.original_question: “如果一颗直径为 100 英尺的钻石流星以光速撞击地球，会发生什么？”
items.model_answer:
According to the laws of physics, an object with mass—such as a 100-foot meteor—cannot travel at exactly the speed of light. Accelerating mass to light speed requires an infinite amount of energy. Therefore, if we assume the meteor magically hit Earth at exactly the speed of light, it would carry infinite kinetic energy. The impact would not just destroy Earth; it would release an infinitely expanding sphere of energy that would obliterate the entire universe. 

However, if we adjust the scenario to be physically possible by assuming the meteor is traveling at a highly relativistic speed—say, 99.9% the speed of light—the outcome is still apocalyptic, though finite. 

First, the fact that the meteor is made of diamond is entirely irrelevant. At relativistic speeds, the chemical bonds holding the carbon atoms together in a diamond lattice are negligible. The meteor would not act like a solid rock, but rather like a tightly packed cluster of individual carbon atoms. 

As this mass of carbon enters Earth's atmosphere, it would not burn up like a normal shooting star. It would be moving so fast that the air molecules in front of it wouldn't have time to move out of the way. The meteor would slam into the atmosphere so violently that the carbon atoms and atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen would undergo spontaneous nuclear fusion. This would create a blinding, world-incinerating flash of gamma radiation and a massive shower of subatomic particles that would instantly vaporize the surface of the Earth before the meteor even touched the ground.

A fraction of a millisecond later, the meteor would strike the crust. A 100-foot diamond meteor has a mass of roughly 50,000 metric tons. If traveling at 99.9% the speed of light, its kinetic energy would be roughly 300 times greater than the energy released by the Chicxulub asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. The impact would instantly vaporize the meteor, tear open the Earth's crust, trigger global magnitude 10+ earthquakes, and blanket the entire planet in superheated ejecta, completely sterilizing the Earth and turning its surface into a molten wasteland. 

If the meteor were traveling even closer to the speed of light—for example, 99.999999999% the speed of light, akin to the fastest cosmic rays ever detected—its kinetic energy would vastly exceed the gravitational binding energy of our planet. In this scenario, the impact would instantly shatter the Earth entirely, vaporizing the planet into a rapidly expanding cloud of plasma and subatomic debris.

items.model_answer:
If modern China had fully replaced Chinese characters (Hanzi) with a phonetic script—a reform seriously championed by early 20th-century intellectuals like Lu Xun and initially considered by the Chinese Communist Party—the decision would have fundamentally altered the nation's linguistic evolution, cultural continuity, and political unity. 

In the short term, the most immediate benefit would have been a rapid acceleration of mass literacy and early technological integration. A phonetic alphabet would have easily integrated with 20th-century typewriters, telegraphs, and early computing systems. China would have entirely bypassed the severe technological bottleneck it faced for decades before the invention of modern predictive character-input software (IME), making global communication and administrative modernization much smoother in the mid-to-late 20th century.

However, the linguistic mechanics of the Chinese language would have been forced into a drastic evolution. Spoken Mandarin is heavily reliant on tones and contains an extraordinary number of homophones. Because Chinese characters convey meaning visually, they easily differentiate words that sound identical. Without characters, written Chinese would suffer from severe ambiguity. To compensate, the language would have had to rapidly evolve away from its traditional conciseness, requiring much longer, multi-syllabic compound words and rigid grammatical markers just to provide the context that characters previously supplied at a glance. 

Politically and socially, abandoning characters would have posed a massive threat to Chinese national unity. For millennia, characters have served as a universal written medium, allowing speakers of mutually unintelligible regional languages—such as Cantonese, Shanghainese, and Hokkien—to read the exact same texts. If a new phonetic script were based strictly on standard Mandarin, it would have alienated hundreds of millions of non-Mandarin speakers, requiring a much harsher and more disruptive linguistic assimilation by the centralized state. Conversely, if regions were allowed to write phonetically based on their local dialects, China’s unified written language would have fractured, likely fueling regional nationalism and weakening the cohesion of the state.

Culturally, the shift would have created a hard, impenetrable barrier between the modern population and millennia of continuous historical records, poetry, and philosophy. Classical Chinese, which relies entirely on the visual distinction of single-syllable characters, would be completely incomprehensible in a phonetic script. Reading anything written before the 20th century would require specialized academic translation, similar to how modern Turks were severed from Ottoman literature following Atatürk’s alphabet reforms. Furthermore, Chinese calligraphy—one of the most revered and foundational pillars of Chinese art—would have been relegated to a dead, historical curiosity, permanently changing the aesthetic and cultural identity of the civilization.

items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the strategic landscape of the Second World War would have been drastically altered, though the ultimate outcome—American entry into the war and eventual Allied victory—would remain the same. 

The most immediate consequence of a successful strike on the canal’s locks or the Culebra Cut would be the severing of the vital maritime artery connecting the United States' Atlantic and Pacific fleets. Any naval reinforcements, troops, or merchant shipping needing to cross between the two oceans would be forced to navigate around South America’s Cape Horn, adding weeks to transit times and exposing ships to German U-boats in the Atlantic. This would have created a severe logistical bottleneck, temporarily isolating the Pacific Fleet from East Coast naval yards and complicating the global Allied supply chain.

However, because Pearl Harbor would have been spared, the US Pacific Fleet—including its formidable lineup of battleships—would have remained completely intact at the outbreak of the war. This intact fleet would have profoundly changed the opening moves of the Pacific theater. Rather than being forced by necessity to rely on aircraft carriers and submarines, the US Navy likely would have attempted to execute "War Plan Orange," steaming westward across the Pacific to relieve the besieged Philippines and engage the Imperial Japanese Navy in a decisive battle. 

Ironically, sparing Pearl Harbor could have been disastrous for the United States. In late 1941, the Japanese navy possessed superior torpedoes, better night-fighting tactics, and the most experienced carrier strike force in the world. If the US Pacific Fleet had sailed into deep water to fight the Japanese, it might have been annihilated at sea. Unlike at Pearl Harbor, where sunk battleships settled in shallow water and were easily salvaged, repaired, and returned to service, ships lost in the deep ocean would have been gone forever, along with all their crews. 

Furthermore, executing an attack on Panama would have been a logistical nightmare for Japan in 1941. The distance from Japan to Panama is vastly greater than to Hawaii, making it nearly impossible for a massive carrier fleet to cross the Pacific undetected and adequately fueled. While Japan did later develop the I-400 class submarine aircraft carriers specifically to strike the canal, a conventional 1941 carrier strike would have stretched the Imperial Japanese Navy to its breaking point, leaving their fleet highly vulnerable to counterattack.

Ultimately, an attack on the sovereign US territory of the Canal Zone would have sparked the exact same outrage and immediate declaration of war from the American public as Pearl Harbor did. While a ruined canal would have delayed the arrival of new Essex-class carriers and warships built on the East Coast, America's overwhelming industrial capacity and two-ocean shipbuilding program would still have overpowered Japan. The Pacific War would have featured an entirely different, potentially more tragic opening naval clash, but the long-term trajectory of Japanese defeat would have remained unchanged.

items.model_answer:
If eighteenth-century European armies had abandoned the flintlock musket and returned to the crossbow, it would have triggered a catastrophic military regression, forcing a complete overhaul of battlefield tactics, logistics, and global geopolitics. 

The most immediate consequence would be the loss of the socket bayonet. An eighteenth-century musket acted as both a projectile weapon and a spear, allowing every infantryman to defend against cavalry charges. Because a crossbow cannot effectively mount a bayonet or be used in melee combat, armies would be forced to reintroduce pikemen to protect their missile troops. This would reverse a century of tactical evolution, forcing armies to abandon the highly efficient, thin linear formations of the 1700s and revert to the dense, cumbersome pike-and-shot (or in this case, pike-and-bow) squares of the sixteenth century. 

This tactical reversion would be suicidal in the face of eighteenth-century field artillery. While the prompt assumes the infantry returns to crossbows, cannons would still dominate the battlefield. Dense formations of pikemen and crossbowmen would be sitting ducks for the advanced, highly mobile artillery of the era. Cannons firing solid roundshot would tear through deep ranks with ease, and close-range grapeshot or canister shot would slaughter tightly packed infantry, making offensive maneuvers nearly impossible.

In terms of infantry firefights, the crossbow would be severely outclassed by the musket it replaced. A trained eighteenth-century infantryman with a flintlock musket could fire three to four rounds per minute. A heavy military crossbow, requiring a mechanical windlass or cranequin to draw the string, could manage only one or two shots per minute. Furthermore, while a crossbow bolt could easily pierce the unarmored cloth uniforms of the era, it caused clean puncture wounds. It lacked the massive kinetic stopping power and bone-shattering trauma of a heavy .75 caliber lead musket ball, making it much harder to instantly stop a charging cavalry horse or a determined enemy advance. 

Logistically, this shift would create a nightmare. Supplying an eighteenth-century army with ammunition meant transporting barrels of gunpowder and easily moldable lead, which could be melted and cast into musket balls by the soldiers themselves while on campaign. Crossbow bolts, however, require specialized manufacturing: straight wooden shafts, precise fletching, and forged metal heads. Transporting millions of bulky, fragile arrows across Europe would require vastly larger baggage trains, slowing armies down and making supply lines highly vulnerable. 

Globally, a return to the crossbow would have severely undermined European colonial power. Without the logistical efficiency, stopping power, and psychological shock of massed firearms, European expeditionary forces would have lost their primary technological advantage. They would have been easily outmaneuvered and outgunned by indigenous forces who either utilized faster-firing traditional bows or who successfully acquired and retained gunpowder weapons. 

Ultimately, any eighteenth-century nation that adopted the crossbow would render its army logistically crippled, tactically obsolete, and highly vulnerable to artillery. If only one nation made this switch, it would be swiftly conquered by its musket-wielding neighbors; if all of Europe made the switch, the continent would become highly vulnerable to external powers that maintained gunpowder infantry.

items.model_answer:
If the Black Death had devastated Poland in the mid-14th century, it would have abruptly derailed the country’s historical "Golden Age" under King Casimir III the Great. Historically, Poland largely escaped the worst of the plague, allowing its population, economy, and geopolitical influence to surge while the rest of Europe collapsed. Had the plague killed a third to half of Poland's population, the immediate economic shock and severe labor shortages would have halted Casimir’s ambitious infrastructure and modernization projects, which are famously remembered for transforming Poland from a country built of "wood to stone."

Crucially, a plague-ravaged Poland would have drastically altered the demographic and cultural history of Eastern Europe, particularly regarding the Jewish diaspora. In reality, Casimir offered a safe haven to Jews fleeing violent plague-related scapegoating and pogroms in Western Europe, laying the foundation for Poland to become the demographic center of the Ashkenazi world for centuries. If Poland had suffered the same catastrophic mortality rates, it is highly likely that local panic would have sparked similar anti-Semitic pogroms, closing off this vital sanctuary and fundamentally changing Jewish history.

Geopolitically, a devastated and depopulated Poland would have been highly vulnerable to its aggressive neighbors. The Teutonic Knights to the north and the Kingdom of Bohemia to the west could have easily exploited Poland's weakness, potentially seizing contested territories like Pomerelia or Silesia permanently. Furthermore, Poland’s eastward expansion into Red Ruthenia would likely have failed. This weakness would have significantly altered the eventual Polish-Lithuanian union later in the century; rather than entering as an equal or dominant partner, a weakened Poland might have been absorbed as a subordinate territory to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, or both might have eventually fallen to the Teutonic Order. 

Finally, the social structure of Eastern Europe might have evolved differently. The massive labor shortages caused by the plague in Western Europe eventually helped dismantle serfdom by increasing the bargaining power of peasants. In Eastern Europe, the historical lack of such a demographic shock contributed to the eventual entrenchment of the oppressive "Second Serfdom." A devastated Polish population might have forced the nobility to offer better terms and wages to surviving peasants, potentially aligning Poland's socio-economic development more closely with Western Europe and altering its long-term political trajectory.

items.original_question: 为什么中国能够统一而欧洲却不能？如果你看一下中国历代地图，你通常会发现（大约从汉朝开始）代表中国的巨大物体。另一方面，如果你看一下欧洲地图，你通常会看到大量的国家。为什么中国能够统一，而欧洲却不能？
items.model_answer:
If Europe had unified early and maintained a centralized imperial structure similar to China's dynastic cycles—perhaps through a surviving Roman Empire or a permanently consolidated Carolingian state—the trajectory of global history would be fundamentally altered. Politically and culturally, a unified Europe would likely have developed a standardized administrative language, presumably based on Latin, functioning much like Classical Chinese to bridge diverse regional dialects. The continent would be governed by a massive, centralized bureaucracy focused on internal stability, agricultural management, and defending its frontiers against incursions from the Eurasian steppe. While this would have spared Europe centuries of devastating interstate warfare, it would have fundamentally changed the continent's relationship with the rest of the world.

Most notably, early unification would likely have prevented the "European Miracle" and the subsequent Great Divergence. In our timeline, Europe’s intense political fragmentation fostered fierce competition among rival states, which drove rapid military innovation, capitalist development, and the Scientific Revolution. A single European hegemon, lacking existential threats from peer rivals, would likely have become technologically conservative and inward-looking over time. Much like Ming or Qing China, a unified Europe might have possessed the capability for global maritime exploration but lacked the competitive incentive to sustain it. The Age of Discovery, which was driven by rival monarchs seeking alternative trade routes to bypass monopolies, would not have occurred in the same aggressive manner. Consequently, the massive waves of European colonialism in the Americas, Africa, and Asia would have been severely delayed or entirely averted.

Without the wealth extracted from the New World, the establishment of global trade networks, and the competitive pressure to mechanize production, the Industrial Revolution might never have originated in Europe. Instead, global technological and economic development would have proceeded at a much slower, more balanced pace. The world would likely have remained multipolar for centuries longer, with a unified European Empire coexisting alongside a unified China, powerful Islamic empires in the Middle East, and uninterrupted indigenous empires in the Americas, fundamentally erasing the era of Western global hegemony.

human_answers: We have to delve into two spheres to address this question, the political and the military. Militarily, the Japanese fought a series of border skirmishes with the Soviet Union at Khalkhin Gol (located along the Manchurian - Mongolian border, Mongolia then b...

Japan was interested in extending its influence in Asia and for that it had to confront either USSR or USA. While I don't think that the exact reason for choosing USA is known, Japan was at a clear disadvantage when battling USSR: while the Soviet Union had...

In August 1939, while Japan and the USSR were skirmishing, Germany and the USSR signed a Non-Aggression Pact that allowed Stalin to put some more focus on Japan (among other things). By early 1941, Japan decided it was time to focus on securing its oil supp...
items.original_question: 第二次世界大战期间日本帝国为何不进攻苏联？日本和苏联在满洲有共同边界，德国对苏联的入侵极大地削弱了苏联。鉴于日本击败苏联的优势（更不用说西伯利亚的资源了），而且日本驻有大量关东军基本上无所事事，为什么日本不进攻呢？
items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Soviet Far East during World War II—pursuing the "Northern Expansion Doctrine" (*Hokushin-ron*) instead of striking south at Pearl Harbor and Southeast Asia—the entire trajectory of the war would have been radically altered. 

The most immediate and profound impact would have been on the European theater. Historically, Soviet spy Richard Sorge assured Joseph Stalin that Japan would not attack the USSR, allowing the Red Army to transfer highly trained, winter-equipped Siberian divisions to the western front just in time to halt the German advance on Moscow in late 1941. If Japan had invaded in coordination with Operation Barbarossa, Stalin would have faced a devastating two-front war, forcing him to keep those vital reserves in the east. Without them, Moscow likely would have fallen to Nazi Germany, potentially leading to the collapse of the Soviet command structure or forcing the government to retreat past the Ural Mountains. This could have secured an Axis victory, or at least a highly favorable stalemate, in Europe.

Meanwhile, the Pacific War as history remembers it would have been delayed or entirely avoided. Without the attack on Pearl Harbor, President Franklin D. Roosevelt would have struggled to overcome strong domestic isolationist sentiment to formally bring the United States into the conflict, though American material support for Britain would have continued. 

For Japan, however, invading Siberia would have been a strategic trap. Unlike Southeast Asia, the Soviet Far East lacked the critical resources—specifically oil and rubber—that the Japanese war machine desperately needed to survive the ongoing American embargo. The Imperial Japanese Army would have found itself bogged down in a brutal, resource-draining land war across a vast, frozen, and logistically unforgiving landscape, facing the same armored disadvantages that led to their defeat by the Soviets at Khalkhin Gol in 1939. Ultimately, while a Japanese attack on the Soviet Union might have handed Nazi Germany the victory in Europe, it would have left Japan overextended, starved of oil, and locked in a grueling war of attrition in Siberia.

items.question: What If Gunpowder-Era Fortresses Were Built as Circles or Squares Instead of Stars?
human_answers: Star forts or bastion forts are designed to enable enfilade (or flanking) fire: shooting on the line of attackers from the side, significantly increasing firing efficiency of the defender. Flanking fire allows guns placed in the side wall of the bastion (pr...

Imagine that you are defending a fort with old-fashioned round bastions in the Middle Ages. Your walls are high, but once the enemy comes close and starts scaling the walls, very few of your defenders can engage them.

These outcroppings are called Bastions and they became common when muskets and cannons became common in European warfare. The problem with a square or circle forts is that when the enemy has reached the wall, they are in your dead zone.
items.original_question: 为什么古老的防御工事形状像星星而不是圆形？哥本哈根、腓特烈西亚和阿卡的防御工事呈星形。 （哥本哈根防御工事如下图所示。）为什么不把防御工事或防御工事做成纯粹的正方形或圆形呢？
items.model_answer:
If gunpowder-era fortresses had been built as simple circles or squares instead of star forts (the *trace italienne*), they would have suffered from fatal tactical flaws that would have fundamentally altered the nature of warfare and geopolitics. 

The primary architectural failure of circular and square forts in the age of cannons is the creation of massive "dead zones" or blind spots. Star forts were explicitly designed with angled bastions to provide interlocking fields of flanking fire, allowing defenders to shoot horizontally along the faces of their own walls. Without these jutting points, defenders in a circular or square fort would be forced to lean over the parapets to fire at infantry massing at the base of the wall, dangerously exposing themselves to enemy snipers. Furthermore, the flat masonry walls of a square fortress would take the full, perpendicular kinetic impact of heavy cannonballs, leading to rapid shattering and breaching. While a circular fort's curved walls would be better at deflecting artillery fire, they would still entirely lack the ability to provide enfilading fire to protect their own perimeter.

As a result, the balance of military power would have shifted decisively in favor of the attacker. Historically, star forts caused sieges to drag on for months or even years, draining national treasuries and turning wars into grinding wars of attrition. If fortresses were square or circular, besieging armies could quickly blast through the flat walls or safely march infantry into the dead zones at the base of the fortifications to plant explosives or scale the ramparts. Sieges would become remarkably brief and heavily favor the offensive force. 

This offensive supremacy would have profoundly altered global history. Because static defenses would be so easily overcome, nations would likely abandon heavy investments in fortifications, shifting their wealth entirely into mobile field artillery and massive standing armies. Geopolitically, the survival of small, independent city-states and principalities—such as those in Renaissance Italy or the Dutch Republic, which relied heavily on complex star forts to hold off larger empires—would have been nearly impossible. Power would have consolidated much faster into the hands of massive, centralized empires capable of dominating the open field, accelerating the formation of modern nation-states through rapid, aggressive conquest.

items.original_question: 二战时德国为何不封锁直布罗陀海峡？直布罗陀海峡最窄处宽约14公里。二战时德国为何不封锁？在我看来，只有少数潜艇和驱逐舰可以完成这项工作。难道德国海军（Kriegsmarine）没有能力封锁它吗？海底狼群至少在那个咽喉要道捕猎过吗？封锁将适用于美国/英国/苏联船只，但当然允许西班牙和其他中立国家。想必这对西班牙来说不会是一个政治问题。注意：我不是在谈论英国控制下的直布罗陀要塞。那是另一回事了。
items.model_answer:
If Germany had successfully blockaded the Strait of Gibraltar during World War II—most likely by executing "Operation Felix" to capture the British fortress with Spanish cooperation—the strategic landscape of the conflict would have shifted dramatically in favor of the Axis powers. The immediate consequence would have been the sealing off of the Mediterranean Sea from the Atlantic, severing Britain’s most vital maritime artery to its empire in the East. 

Without western access to the Mediterranean, the British Royal Navy would have been unable to run heavily escorted supply convoys to its regional strongholds. The island of Malta, a crucial British outpost that historically disrupted Axis shipping, would have quickly fallen to starvation and relentless aerial bombardment. Consequently, Axis supply lines across the Mediterranean to North Africa would have operated with near impunity. This logistical dominance would have provided Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps with the fuel, armor, and reinforcements needed to overwhelm British forces in Egypt. The likely fall of Alexandria and the Suez Canal would have subsequently opened the door for the Axis to seize the vital oil fields of the Middle East, dealing a crippling blow to the British war economy.

The broader ripple effects would have drastically altered the trajectory of the entire war. All Allied shipping to India, Asia, and the Middle East would have been forced to take the arduous, time-consuming route around the Cape of Good Hope, severely straining an already overextended Allied merchant fleet. Furthermore, the Allied invasion of North Africa (Operation Torch) and the subsequent campaigns in Sicily and Italy would have been rendered nearly impossible, effectively protecting the Axis's "soft underbelly" from Allied incursions. Finally, with the Middle East secured, Germany could have potentially opened a southern front against the Soviet Union through the Caucasus, threatening Soviet oil supplies in Baku, significantly complicating the Eastern Front, and potentially prolonging the war by years.

items.question: What If You Opened a 10-Meter Drain to Space at the Bottom of Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果在挑战者深渊底部创建一个半径 10 米通向太空的圆形入口，海洋的排空速度有多快？
items.model_answer:
If you opened a 10-meter circular drain to the vacuum of space at the bottom of Challenger Deep, the results would be a fascinating mix of extreme fluid dynamics, thermodynamics, and planetary scale. 

At a depth of nearly 11,000 meters, the water pressure is roughly 1,100 times greater than at sea level. Because the other side of the drain is a vacuum, this immense pressure differential would force water through the opening at extreme speeds. According to Bernoulli’s principle, the water would shoot into space at roughly 460 meters per second (over 1,000 mph). Given the 10-meter diameter of the drain, this translates to a flow rate of about 36,000 cubic meters of water per second. 

Despite this violent suction at the ocean floor, you would not see a massive, cinematic whirlpool at the surface. The ocean is simply too deep and vast. The suction would create dangerous, high-speed localized currents at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, instantly pulverizing and sucking in any deep-sea marine life or submersibles that strayed too close, but the surface of the Pacific Ocean 11 kilometers above would remain completely undisturbed.

On a global scale, the drain would barely make a dent in the Earth's oceans. A flow rate of 36,000 cubic meters per second sounds massive, but when spread across the 361 million square kilometers of the global ocean surface, it equates to a sea-level drop of only about 3.1 millimeters per year. Coincidentally, this is almost exactly the current rate of global sea-level rise caused by climate change. Therefore, in the short term, this drain would simply act as an equalizer, keeping global sea levels perfectly static. 

On the other side of the portal in space, the exiting water would put on a spectacular thermodynamic show. Because there is zero atmospheric pressure in space, the liquid water would instantly flash-boil into vapor. This rapid boiling process requires a massive amount of energy, which it would steal as heat from the surrounding water. Consequently, the remaining water would instantly flash-freeze. The result would be a continuous, high-speed, comet-like geyser of water vapor and fine ice crystals shooting into the void. 

If left open permanently, it would take hundreds of thousands of years to noticeably drain the oceans. Furthermore, as the water level eventually dropped, the pressure at the bottom of the trench would decrease, slowing the flow rate down and extending the draining process into the millions of years.

items.question: What If Earth Expanded by 1 Centimeter per Second?
human_answers: The Earth is not, currently, expanding.[1]Yes, I have a citation for this. "In conclusion, no statistically significant present expansion rate is detected by our study within the current measurement uncertainty of 0.2 mm yr−1." People have long suggested that it might be. Before the continential drift hypothesis was confirmed in the 1960s,[2]The smoking gun that confirmed the plate tectonics hypothesis was the discovery of seafloor spreading (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafloor_spreading). The way seafloor spreading and magnetic pole reversal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geomagnetic_reversal) neatly confirmed each other is one of my favorite examples of scientific discovery at work. people had noticed that the continents fit together. Various ideas were put forward to explain this, including the idea that the ocean basins were rifts that opened in the surface of a previously-smooth Earth as it expanded. This theory was never very widespread,[3]It turns out it's kind of dumb. although it still periodically makes the rounds on YouTube. To avoid the problem of rifts in the ground, let's imagine all the matter in the Earth, from the crust to the core, starts expanding uniformly. To avoid another Drain the Oceans (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/) scenario, we'll assume the ocean expands, too.[4]As it turns out, the ocean is expanding, since it's getting warmer. This is (currently) the main way global warming is raising the sea level. All human structures will stay. t = 1 second: [Image: image] As the Earth started expanding, you'd feel a slight jolt, and might even lose your balance for a moment. This would be very brief. Since you're moving steadily upward at 1 cm/s, you woudn't feel any kind of ongoing acceleration. For the rest of the day, you wouldn't notice much of anything. t = 1 day: After the first day, the Earth would have expanded by 864 meters. [Image: image] Gravity would take a long time to increase. If you weighed 70 kilograms when the expansion started, you'd weigh 70.01 at the end of the day. What about our roads and bridges? Eventually, they would have to break up, right? Not as quickly as you might think. Here's a puzzle I once heard: Imagine you tied a rope tightly around the Earth, so it was hugging the surface all the way around. [Image: image] Now imagine you wanted to raise the rope one meter off the ground. [Image: image] How much extra length will you need to add to the rope? Though it may seem like you'd need miles of rope, the answer is 6.28 meters. Circumference is proportional to radius, so if you increase radius by 1 unit, you increase circumference by 2π units. Stretching a 40,000-kilometer line an extra 6.28 meters is pretty negligible. Even after a day, the extra 5.4 kilometers would be handled easily by virtually all structures. Concrete expands and contracts by more than that every day.[5]Lawrence Grybosky, Thermal Expansion and Contraction (http://www.engr.psu.edu/ce/courses/ce584/concrete/library/cracking/thermalexpansioncontraction/thermalexpcontr.htm) After the initial jolt, one of the first effects you'd notice would be that your GPS would stop working. The satellites would stay in roughly the same orbits, but the delicate timing that the GPS system is based on would be completely ruined within hours. GPS timing is incredibly precise; of all the problems in engineering, it's one of the only ones in which engineers have been forced to include both special and general relativity in their calculations. Most other clocks would keep working fine. However, if you have a very precise pendulum clock, you might notice something odd—by the end of the day, it would be three seconds ahead of where it should be. t = 1 month: After a month, the Earth would have expanded by 26 kilometers—an increase of 0.4%—and its mass would have increased by 1.2%. Surface gravity would only have gone up by 0.4%, rather than 1.2%, since surface gravity is proportional to radius.[6]Mass is proportional to radius cubed, and gravity is proportional to mass times inverse square of radius, so radius3 / radius2 = radius. You might notice the difference in weight on a scale, but it's not a big deal. Gravity varies by this much between different cities already. This is a good thing to keep in mind if you buy a digital scale. If your scale has a precision of more than two decimal places, you need to calibrate it with a test weight—the force of gravity at the scale factory isn't necessarily the same as the force of gravity at your house. While you might not notice the increased gravity just yet, you'd notice the expansion. After a month, you'd see a lot of cracks opening up in long concrete structures and the failure of elevated roads and old bridges. Most buildings would probably be ok, although those anchored firmly into bedrock might start to behave unpredictably.[7]Just what you want in a skyscraper. At this point, astronauts on the ISS would start getting worried. Not only would the ground (and atmosphere) be rising toward them, but the increased gravity would also cause their orbit to slowly shrink. They'd need to evacuate quickly; they'd have at most a few months before the station reentered the atmosphere and deorbited. t = 1 year: After a year, gravity would be 5% stronger. You'd probably notice the weight gain, and you'd definitely notice the failure of roads, bridges, power lines, satellites, and undersea cables. Your pendulum clock would now be ahead by five days. What about the atmosphere? If the atmosphere isn't growing like the land and water are, air pressure would start dropping. This is due to a combination of factors. As gravity increases, then air gets heavier. But since that air is spread out over a larger area, the overall effect would be decreasing air pressure. On the other hand, if the atmosphere is also expanding, surface air pressure would rise. After years had passed, the top of Mt. Everest would no longer be in the "death zone".[8]See What-If #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/). On the other hand, since you'd be heavier—and the mountain would be taller—climbing would be more work. t = 5 years: After five years, gravity would be 25% stronger. If you weighed 70 kg when the expansion started, you'd weigh 88 kg now. Most of our infrastructure would have collapsed. The cause of the collapse would be the expanding ground below them, not the increased gravity. Surprisingly, most skyscrapers would hold up fine under much higher gravity.[9]Although I wouldn't trust the elevators. For most of them, the limiting factor isn't weight, but wind. t = 10 years: After 10 years, gravity would be 50% stronger. In the scenario where the atmosphere isn't expanding, the air would become thin enough to be difficult to breathe even at sea level. In the other scenario, we'd be ok for a little while longer. t = 40 years: After 40 years, Earth's surface gravity would have tripled.[10]Over decades, the force of gravity would grow slightly faster than you'd expect, since the material in the Earth would compress under its own weight. The pressure inside planets is roughly proportional to the square of their surface area (http://cseligman.com/text/planets/internalpressure.htm), so the Earth's core would be squeezed tightly. At this point, even the strongest humans would only be able to walk with great difficulty. Breathing would be difficult. Trees would collapse. Crops wouldn't stand up under their own weight. Virtually every mountainside would see massive landslides as material sought out a shallower angle of repose (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_of_repose). Geologic activity would also accelerate. Most of the Earth's heat is provided by radioactive decay of minerals in the crust and mantle,[12]Although some radioactive elements, like uranium, are heavy, they get squeezed out of the lower layers because their atoms don't mesh well with the rock lattices at those depths. For more, see this chapter (http://igppweb.ucsd.edu/~guy/sio103/chap3.pdf) and this article (http://world-nuclear.org/info/Nuclear-Fuel-Cycle/Uranium-Resources/The-Cosmic-Origins-of-Uranium/#.UlxuGmRDJf4). and more Earth means more heat. Since the volume expands faster than the surface area, the overall heat flowing out per square meter will increase. It's not actually enough to substantially warm the planet—Earth's surface temperature is dominated by the atmosphere and the Sun—but it would lead to more volcanoes, more earthquakes, and faster tectonic movement. This would be similar to the situation on Earth billions of years ago, when we had more radioactive material and thus a hotter mantle. More active plate tectonics might be good for life. Plate tectonics play a key role in stabilizing the Earth's climate, and planets smaller than Earth (like Mars) don't have enough internal heat to sustain long-term geologic activity. A larger planet would allow for more geologic activity, which is why some scientists think that exoplanets slightly larger than Earth ("super-Earths") could be more friendly to life than Earth-sized ones.[11]Sasselov, Dimitar D.. The life of super-Earths: how the hunt for alien worlds and artificial cells will revolutionize life on our planet. New York: Basic Books, 2012. t = 100 years: After 100 years, we'd be experiencing over six gees of gravity. Not only would we be unable to move around to find food, but our hearts would be unable to pump blood to our brains. Only small insects (and sea animals) would be physically able to move around. Perhaps humans could survive in specially-built controlled-pressure domes, moving around by keeping most of our bodies submerged in water. [Image: image] Breathing in this situation would be difficult. It's hard to suck in air against the weight of the water, which is why snorkels can only work when your lungs are near the surface. Outside of low-pressure domes, the air would become unbreathable for a different reason. At somewhere around 6 atmospheres, even ordinary air becomes toxic.[13]R.M. Franz and P.C. Schutte, Barometric hazards within the context of deep-level mining (http://www.saimm.co.za/Journal/v105n06p387.pdf), The Journal of The South African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy Even if we'd managed to survive all the other problems, by 100 years, we'd be dead from oxygen toxicity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_toxicity). Toxicity aside, breathing dense air is difficult simply because it's heavy. Black hole? When would the Earth eventually become a black hole? It's hard to answer that, because the premise of the question is that the radius is steadily expanding while the density stays the same—whereas a black hole, the density increases. The dynamics of really huge rocky planets aren't often analyzed, since there's no obvious way that they could form; anything that large will have enough gravity to gather hydrogen and helium during planet formation and become a gas giant. At some point, our growing Earth would reach the point where adding more mass causes it to contract, rather than expand. After this point, it would collapse into something like a sputtering white dwarf or neutron star, and then—if its mass kept increasing—eventually become a black hole. But before it gets that far ... t = 300 years: It's a shame humans wouldn't live this long, because at this point, something really neat would happen. As the Earth grows, the Moon would, like all our satellites, gradually spiral inward.[14]Plummer, H. C., Note on the motion about an attracting centre of slowly increasing mass (http://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1906MNRAS..66...83P), Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, Vol. 66, p.83 After several centuries, it would be close enough to the swollen Earth that the tidal forces between Earth and the Moon would be stronger than the gravitational forces holding the Moon together. When the Moon passed this boundary—called the Roche limit (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roche_limit)—it would gradually break apart ... [Image: image] ... and Earth would, for a short time, have rings.
items.original_question: 如果世界平均半径每秒扩大 1 厘米，人们需要多长时间才能注意到自己的体重增加？
items.model_answer:
If the Earth were to expand at a rate of 1 centimeter per second, the planet would undergo immediate and total catastrophic destruction. At this rate, the Earth’s radius would increase by 864 meters every day. Consequently, the planet’s circumference would grow by about 5.4 kilometers daily. Because the Earth’s rigid lithosphere (the crust and upper mantle) cannot stretch to accommodate this rapid expansion, it would violently fracture. The entire surface would be ripped apart by continuous, massive earthquakes, and global tectonic fault lines would tear open. Magma from the mantle would constantly erupt through these expanding fissures, covering the surface in fresh lava and volcanic ash. All human infrastructure would be obliterated within the first few days.

As the crust splits open, the oceans would drain into the newly formed, miles-deep chasms. When trillions of gallons of seawater inevitably make contact with the exposed mantle and rising magma, the water would flash-boil. This would blast unimaginable quantities of steam and volcanic gases into the sky, creating a hyper-dense, superheated atmosphere. The resulting runaway greenhouse effect would bake the planet, quickly sterilizing the Earth of any surviving surface life. 

The expansion would also radically alter the planet's physics, specifically its rotation and gravity. Due to the conservation of angular momentum—much like a spinning ice skater extending their arms—the increasing radius would cause the Earth’s rotation to rapidly slow down, making days progressively longer. 

The ultimate fate of the planet's gravity depends on whether its mass increases along with its size. If the Earth's mass remains constant while its volume expands, the planet's density and surface gravity would plummet. Over time, gravity would become so weak that the Earth could no longer hold onto its atmosphere, allowing it to bleed away into space. Conversely, if the Earth magically generated new matter to maintain its current density, surface gravity would steadily increase. This rising gravity would eventually crush any remaining terrestrial structures and severely disrupt the Moon's orbit, either pulling it into a devastating collision course or violently altering the Earth-Moon tidal dynamics.

items.question: What If the Romans Had Built a Working Steam Engine?
human_answers: If a civilization finds an example of advanced technology, can they learn to duplicate the technology? You have two variables: The current technological state of the civilization. Call this "A." The technological difference between the civilization and the example. Call this "B." Therefore... The earlier "A" is, the more likely the answer is "No." The greater "B" is, the more likely the answer is "No." (This is a necessary axiom of Clarkian Magic .) As "A" advances, "B" can grow wider and the answer can still be a "Yes." What is our year point of reference? The Romans were technological marvels, but most of their advancement was in structural engineering. Had your example technology been anything involving electricity my instant answer would have been "absolutely not." However, the Roman empire encompassed a large amount of time and a large amount of technological innovation. Just as my grandmother during her lifetime saw the horse-and-buggy and steam ships as the pinnacle of transportation technology give way to walking on the moon and air flight so common people don't dress up for it any more, the Romans shifted from their early years ("absolutely not") to 300ish AD when the answer becomes "possibly, maybe even probably." An important date is 1 AD. That's when Hero of Alexandria created the Aeolipile . The Aeolipile was, basically, the first steam turbine. At this point they may not have had the other technological know-how to build a fully functioning 1800s steam engine... but they would have played with it for a while and, maybe, would have concluded, "you know, that looks an awful lot like a really complicated Aeolipile." So far, I'm convinced that Romans from at least, say, 50 A.D. would have understood what they were looking at (after enough examination & experimentation) just as we have the ability to understand string theory without having the slightest idea how to prove it. That leaves the question, could they duplicate it? The components of a steam engine are improved with milling, but do not require milling. They can all be cast. The Romans knew how to do this, so they could build the shape of everything they need. That leaves metallurgical strength. And that's where the last point I can make comes into play. The Romans knew how to think The ancient Romans knew how to figure things out. It would take time, because they're basically stuck with empirical research, but they could do it. Now the answer is "Yes, given enough time." How much time do you need between when they found the engine and when you need them to duplicate the engine? The following are all gut instinct and open to vociferous argument, but... If the answer is found in 50 A.D., needed by 300 A.D., I'm willing to go out on a limb and say "Yes." If the answer is found in 50 A.D., needed by 100 A.D., it's "very unlikely." If the answer is found in 50 B.C., needed by anything less than 200 A.D., it's "probably no." If the answer is found before 50 B.C., the answer is "impossible." There's not enough technological understanding in the Roman Empire to be capable of comprehending what they're looking at and by the time the Aeliopile came into being the example would be deteriorated or lost. Some of the comments are wondering why the Romans would care to pursue steam engine technology. The OP hasn't told us the context of the future technology appearing in the past. If all that appeared was the engine, then it might be a hard sell unless someone was bright enough to think, "what if we hook this sucker up to a cart?" On the other hand, if what appeared was a working car... the Romans would be all over this technology considering the difficulties of their wide-spread empire. The real question is, what if it was a train engine? Something that needed tracks to be valuable? That's a whomping maybe because suddenly the infrastructure investment (laying rail) is enormous. However, none of that is relevant as the OP didn't ask about it. It's the OP's problem to solve. If he hasn't, it's another question and not a valid answer to this one. A number of commenters have expressed disbelief that reverse engineering can bring substantial value to the technological innovation process. Their premise is that the technologies didn't develop for a millennia or more on their own, which assumes they couldn't have developed in 200-300 years with a working example to experiment with or to motivate them. Such commenters have no experience with reverse engineering. I do. Knowing that something is possible and you only need to duplicate it is much, much, much more powerful than not knowing something is possible and waiting around for the combination of imagination and scientific development to merge. The simple truth is if the Romans were shown with irrefutable proof the value of a working steam engine, they wouldn't have one or two guys out there tinkering around with a vague idea (which is why it took millennia naturally). They'd have thousands and more people dedicated to realizing the military advantage. (Unless as previously indicated you want to choose that they don't see the value, in which case this is all a moot conversation. You won't invent what you don't care about.) Some people like to think that innovation is somehow a fixed process, that it can't happen any faster than it did, but our own recent history in computer development has proven that wrong time and time again. You need not understand why something works to duplicate it. To conclude with an example, I wonder if some believe the specifications of an antique steam engine are as difficult to achieve as a 2017 combustion engine. Obviously, the metals and precision needed for a 2017 engine could not be duplicated by the romans during their time. But that isn't what was asked for. When I once read The Grapes of Wrath I noted a moment in the story when the family had to repair their engine. They'd lost compression, so they wrapped copper wire around the piston, shoved it back into the chamber, and off they went. I wondered about that and so asked my grandmother, who said things like that did, indeed, happen. That's an awful lot of imprecision to still have a working and useful engine. If you still want to believe the Romans couldn't reverse engineer something as simple as a steam engine (with operating documents!) under the conditions I've specified, by all means, downvote my answer. I won't feel bad.

What's a "steam engine"? A steam engine is an external combustion engine which uses steam as the working fluid. So we have: Newcomen's original atmospheric engine ? The Romans (or rather the Greek engineers on which the empire depended) could have copied it, most likely; using it is another question -- it's a very very inefficient engine, which was useful only to pump water out of coal mines, eating lots of locally extracted coal in the process. The Romans did not have coal mines... An early separate-condenser Watt engine ? Copying it would have been either impossible or very very difficult; using it may have been possible. This type of engine is much more efficient than Newcomen's contraption, but it uses axles and bearings which may or may not be possible to make with late Greco-Roman technology. Anyway, this is the only type of engine which is both useful and not light-years beyond late Greco-Roman technology.
