The viscosity is similar to water, but the sheer mass of the fluid means pulling the oars would require immense physical strength. However, because you are pushing against such a dense mass, every successful stroke would generate massive forward momentum. 
*   **Bromine:** Bromine is a liquid at room temperature and is about three times denser than water. Your boat would sit high, and rowing would feel heavy and sluggish. However, the physical rowing experience would quickly become irrelevant; bromine constantly emits a thick, red-brown gas that is highly toxic and corrosive. Without a heavy-duty hazmat suit and oxygen supply, you would quickly die from inhaling the fumes.
*   **Gallium:** Gallium melts at 85.6°F (29.8°C), so on a hot summer day, it forms a silvery lake about six times denser than water. Rowing would be a heavy, exhausting workout, though easier than mercury. Crucially, you must not use an aluminum boat. Liquid gallium rapidly infiltrates the grain boundaries of aluminum, making it as brittle as wet paper. Your hull would crumble, dropping you into the heavy metal.
*   **Tungsten:** Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, turning to liquid at a staggering 6,192°F (3,422°C). Long before you reached the lake, the intense radiant heat would instantly incinerate you, your oars, and your boat. If you magically possessed an indestructible, perfectly insulated boat, the liquid tungsten (which is even denser than mercury) would make rowing virtually impossible for a human due to the extreme weight of the fluid.
*   **Liquid Nitrogen:** At -320°F (-196°C), liquid nitrogen is about 80% as dense as water, so your boat would sit a bit lower. The main physical hurdle is the Leidenfrost effect. Because your oars are vastly hotter than the liquid, the nitrogen would instantly boil upon contact, creating a frictionless jacket of nitrogen gas around the blades. Your oars would slip uselessly through the fluid, providing almost no thrust. Furthermore, the extreme cold would likely turn a standard boat hull brittle, causing it to crack.
*   **Liquid Helium:** At near absolute zero (-452°F / -269°C), liquid helium is only about one-eighth as dense as water. A standard boat would immediately sink because it couldn't displace enough fluid weight to stay afloat. If you had a highly buoyant, insulated boat and the helium was cooled below 2.17 Kelvin, it would become a *superfluid* with zero viscosity. Your oars would slip through the liquid with absolutely no drag, meaning you could not generate any propulsion. Worse, the superfluid would defy gravity via the Rollin film effect, creeping up the outside of your boat, over the gunwales, and filling the inside until you sank.

items.question: What If You Dropped 3,000 Super Balls onto a Pedestrian from a Seven-Story Parking Garage?
human_answers: After falling from seven stories, the mass of bouncy balls would be moving at about 20 meters per second. 20 meters per second is about how fast an average person with a good arm could throw a bouncy ball. Therefore, to determine the result of an impact, we can make use of what Einstein called a gedankenexperiment, or "thought experiment": [Image: image] In science, it's important that results be repeatable, so let's try that again: [Image: image] The tricky thing about this scenario is that 3,000 one-inch bouncy balls is not as many as you probably think—it'd be enough to fill a large bucket. This bucket would weigh about as much as a small child, which leads us to another gedankenexperiment: [Image: image] Of course, in reality, the average person can't throw a small child as fast as they can throw a bouncy ball.[citation needed (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetacean)] Furthermore, they won't all fall in one clump. If you poured the balls from a container, they would bounce around and spread out as they fell, and most of them would probably miss the target. This effect was demonstrated in an experiment by Utah State University students, who poured 20,000 bouncy balls from a helicopter (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fd7D1LWzWmo) as part of their Geek Week. The balls fell as a cloud, rather than a single mass. If you wanted to be sure of killing someone, you'd need a lot more balls. 3,000,000 of them—enough to fill a large room—would be be enough to guarantee that the target would either be crushed to death by the impact or buried too deep to dig themselves out. To your last question, if someone just happened to walk underneath when you dropped the bouncy balls, and they were killed by the impact, you'd most likely be guilty of some form of manslaughter. However, by asking this question, you've shown your intent to cause harm to the victim, demonstrating clear malice aforethought. By writing in to this blog, you've probably upgraded your charge to murder. All in all, you should probably stick to gedankenexperiments. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果将 3,000 个弹力球从七层停车场扔到下面人行道上行走的人身上会怎样？如果这个人活下来，需要多少个弹力球才能杀死他？会发生什么伤害以及相关的犯罪是什么？
items.model_answer:
Dropping 3,000 Super Balls from a seven-story parking garage—a height of roughly 70 feet—would result in a chaotic, highly painful, and dangerous event for the pedestrian below. 

As the balls are released, they would spread out into a wide cloud rather than falling in a single dense mass. By the time they reach the ground, they would be traveling at approximately 45 miles per hour. Because a standard Super Ball weighs only about 15 grams, an individual ball carries just a few joules of kinetic energy. A single strike would feel like a sharp sting, somewhat less forceful than a paintball hit, and would not be lethal or cause major trauma on its own. 

However, the sheer volume of the drop changes the dynamics entirely. The pedestrian would be pelted by dozens or hundreds of these hard rubber projectiles in a fraction of a second. This rapid, collective impact would cause severe bruising, welts, and immense pain. The surprise and physical force of the barrage would almost certainly disorient the pedestrian and knock them to the ground. If the person were to look up during the drop, they would be at a high risk for serious facial trauma or permanent eye damage. 

The immediate aftermath would be just as chaotic as the impact. Because Super Balls are made of highly elastic synthetic rubber (like Zectron) with an extreme coefficient of restitution, they conserve most of their kinetic energy upon impact. The balls that hit the concrete would ricochet violently, bouncing back up as high as five or six stories. The pedestrian would be caught in a blinding storm of thousands of high-speed, ricocheting projectiles bouncing in every conceivable direction. As the bouncing subsides, the ground would be entirely blanketed in rolling rubber balls, creating a severe slipping hazard that would make it incredibly difficult for the battered pedestrian to stand up or escape the area.

items.question: What If You Drained the Oceans through a 10-Meter Hole at Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果在海洋最深点“挑战者深渊”的底部建造一个半径 10 米通向太空的圆形入口，海洋的排水速度有多快？当水被排干时，地球会发生什么变化？
items.model_answer:
If you were to open a 10-meter portal at the bottom of the Challenger Deep—nearly 11 kilometers below the surface—the immense pressure of the ocean above would force water through the hole at incredible speeds. Driven by over 1,000 times standard atmospheric pressure, the water would blast through the opening at roughly 460 meters per second (over 1,000 mph). This would result in a massive flow rate, draining tens of thousands of cubic meters of water every second.

However, because the Earth’s oceans are unimaginably vast, holding about 1.335 billion cubic kilometers of water, this dramatic leak would be surprisingly imperceptible on a human timescale. At that initial flow rate, the global sea level would drop by only a few millimeters per year. You could live your entire life on the coast and never notice that the ocean was draining. 

As the centuries passed and the sea level did eventually begin to fall, the weight of the water above the hole would decrease. This drop in pressure means the flow rate would continuously slow down as the oceans got shallower. Because of this deceleration, it would take well over a million years to actually drain the oceans. 

Long before the oceans emptied, the Earth would undergo radical transformations. As the seas receded, massive expanses of new land would be exposed, connecting continents and drastically altering the global climate. The disruption of ocean currents and the water cycle would likely plunge the Earth into extreme weather patterns, eventually turning most of the planet into an arid wasteland. Furthermore, because a million years is a significant amount of time on a geological scale, tectonic plate movement would drastically reshape the ocean floor—meaning continental drift would likely crush and seal the hole shut long before the oceans ever finished draining.

items.question: What If You Dumped Earth's Oceans onto Mars?
human_answers: In the previous What If (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/), we opened a portal at the bottom of the Mariana Trench and let the oceans drain out. We didn't worry too much about where the oceans were draining to. I picked Mars; the Curiosity rover is working so hard to find evidence of water, so I figured we could make things easier for it. [Image: image] Curiosity is sitting in Gale Crater, a round depression in the Martian surface with a peak, nicknamed Mt. Sharp, in the center. There's a lot of water on Mars.[1]Donald Rapp, Accessible Water on Mars (http://spaceclimate.net/Mars.Water.7.06R.pdf), JPL D-31343-Rev.7 The problem is, it's frozen. Liquid water doesn't last long there, because it's too cold and there's too little air. If you set out a cup of warm water on Mars, it'll try to boil, freeze, and sublimate, practically all at once.[2]D. L. Santiago et. al., Mars climate and outflow events (http://spacescience.arc.nasa.gov/mars-climate-workshop-2012/documents/extendedabstracts/Santiago_DL_ExAbst.pdf) Water on Mars seems to want to be in any state except liquid. However, we're dumping a lot of water very fast (all of it at a few degrees above 0°C), and it won't have much time to freeze, boil, or sublimate. If our portal is big enough, the water will start to turn Gale Crater into a lake, just like it would on Earth. We can use the excellent USGS Mars Topographic Map (http://pubs.usgs.gov/imap/i2782/) to chart the water's progress. Here's Gale Crater at the start of our experiment: [Image: image] As the flow continues, the lake fills in, burying Curiosity under hundreds of meters of water: [Image: image] Eventually, Mt. Sharp becomes an island. However, before the peak can disappear completely, the water spills over the north rim of the crater and starts flowing out across the sand. [Image: image] When this kind of thing happens on Mars in real life, the trickle of water quickly dries up before it can get very far.[3]D. L. Santiago et. al., Cloud formation and water transport on mars after major outflow events (http://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2012/pdf/2438.pdf), 43rd Planetary Science Conference (2012) However, we've got a lot of ocean at our disposal. [Image: image] The water pools in the North Polar Basin: [Image: image] Gradually, it will fill the basin: [Image: image] However, if we look at a map of the more equatorial regions of Mars, where the volcanoes are, we'll see that there's still a lot of land far from the water: [Image: image] Frankly, I think this map is kind of boring; there's not a lot going on. It's just a big empty swath of land with some ocean at the top. [Image: image] We haven't come close to running out of ocean yet. Although there was a lot of blue on the map of the Earth at the end of our last article, the seas that remained were shallow; most of the volume of the oceans was gone. And Mars is much smaller than Earth, so the same volume of water will make a deeper sea. At this point, the water fills in the Valles Marineris (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valles_Marineris), creating some unusual coastlines. The map is less boring, but the terrain around the great canyons makes for some odd shapes. [Image: image] The water now reaches and swallows up Spirit and Opportunity. Eventually, it breaks into the Hellas Impact Crater, the basin containing the lowest point on Mars. In my opinion, the rest of the map is starting to look pretty good. [Image: image] As the water spreads across the surface in earnest, the map splits into several large islands (and innumerable smaller ones). [Image: image] The water quickly finishes covering most of the high plateaus, leaving only a few islands left. [Image: image] And then, at last, the flow stops; the oceans back on Earth are drained. Let's take a closer look at the main islands: [Image: image] Olympus Mons, and a few other volcanoes, remain above water. Surprisingly, they aren't even close to being covered. Olympus Mons still rises well over 10 kilometers above the new sea level. Mars has some huge mountains. Those crazy islands are the result of water filling in 'Noctis Labyrinthus' ('the Labyrinth of the Night'), a bizarre set of canyons whose origin is still a mystery. The oceans on Mars wouldn't last. There might be some transient greenhouse warming, but in the end, Mars is just too cold. Eventually, the oceans will freeze over, become covered with dust, and gradually migrate to the permafrost at the poles.[4]Maggie Fox, Mars May Not Have Been Warm Or Wet (http://rense.com/general32/marsmaynothave.htm) However, it would take a long time, and until it did, Mars would be a much more interesting place. When you consider that there's a ready-made portal system to allow transit between the two planets, the consequences are inevitable: [Image: image]
items.original_question: 假设你做了“排干海洋”，并将水倒在好奇号火星车顶部，随着水的积累，火星会发生什么变化？
items.model_answer:
If you dumped Earth’s oceans—approximately 1.3 billion cubic kilometers of water—onto Mars, it would radically transform the Red Planet's geography, climate, and atmosphere, though the changes would not be permanent. 

Because Mars has only about 28% of Earth’s surface area, this massive volume of water would cover a much larger percentage of the planet. Gravity would immediately pull the water into Mars's lowest elevations, primarily the vast northern lowlands. This would create a colossal Northern Ocean (often theorized by scientists as the ancient *Oceanus Borealis*) that would cover most of the northern hemisphere. The southern hemisphere, which consists of heavily cratered highlands, would become a massive, continuous supercontinent. Deep impact craters like the Hellas Basin and the massive canyon system Valles Marineris would fill to the brim, becoming deep inland seas or massive fjords connecting to the northern ocean. Olympus Mons and the Tharsis volcanoes would remain towering high above the water level.

The immediate reaction of the water to the Martian environment would be violent. Mars has an average surface temperature of -60°C (-76°F) and an atmospheric pressure less than 1% of Earth's, which is close to the triple point of water. As a result, the dumped oceans would simultaneously boil and freeze. In warmer equatorial regions, the low pressure would cause the water to rapidly evaporate and boil, while in the colder regions, the surface of the ocean would quickly flash-freeze into a thick crust of ice.

This rapid evaporation would trigger a dramatic, temporary climate shift. Water vapor is a highly effective greenhouse gas. As massive quantities of water vapor flooded the thin Martian atmosphere, it would trap incoming solar radiation, significantly warming the planet and increasing the atmospheric pressure. This runaway greenhouse effect could temporarily stabilize the climate, allowing liquid water to exist on the surface without boiling away. Mars would suddenly experience complex weather systems, thick cloud cover, massive storms, and heavy rainfall, which would aggressively erode the dry, ancient Martian landscape.

However, this newly aquatic Mars would be doomed on a geological timescale. Mars lacks two critical features needed to keep its oceans: a strong global magnetic field and sufficient gravity. Without a magnetic shield, the planet is constantly battered by the solar wind. Solar radiation would strike the water vapor in the upper atmosphere, breaking the $H_2O$ molecules apart through photodissociation. The lighter hydrogen atoms would easily reach escape velocity and be swept away into deep space, while the heavier oxygen would react with surface rocks to create more rust. Over tens of millions of years, the atmosphere would thin out again, the greenhouse effect would collapse, and the remaining oceans would freeze solid. Ultimately, Mars would be left as a frozen, icy wasteland, with its once-great oceans locked away in massive glaciers and subterranean ice, slowly sublimating into the void.

items.question: What If You Tried to Hold an Airplane to the Ground with a Rope?
human_answers: Ah, the Just Cause 2 scenario (http://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=just+cause+2+plane+grapple). At takeoff, a 747's four engines can each generate 281.57 kN of thrust. I have no real sense for what that number means, so let's put it in different terms: [Image: image] A 747 with all engines at full could roughly balance the weight of a dangling blue whale. With all that weight, how thick would the cable need to be? Surprisingly, not all that thick! A cable a little over an inch in diameter would do it.[1]Bethlehem Wire Rope General Purpose Catalog (http://www.wwwrope.com/product_pdfs/GP_CAT.pdf) Let's suppose you don't have a cable lying around. What else could you use? If you're into fishing, you might have some fishing line. A typical line for saltwater fishing might have a 50-100 lb strength,[2]West Marine: Selecting Fishing Line (http://www.wwwrope.com/product_pdfs/GP_CAT.pdf) so it would take a brigade of several thousand people armed with fishing rods to restrain the plane. [Image: image] If you don't have fishing line, there's one thing you probably do have: Hair. While hair isn't as strong as steel, it's just about the strongest material in your body,[3]Examples of the Tensile Strength of Materials (http://web2.clarkson.edu/class/me380/materials_tenstrength.pdf) with a tensile strength rivaling or exceeding that of bone.[4]Properties of Textile Fibers (http://www.academia.edu/2179355/Properties_of_Textile_Fibers) This tensile strength is why performers are able to hang by their hair at the circus. In fact, from a materials standpoint, it's actually more impressive that performers are able to hang by their arms. Based on these hair strength figures, a piece of hair three inches in diameter would be strong enough to restrain a 747.[5]If you wanted to measure the strength of a strand of hair, you could use the device described by US Patent #4628742A (http://www.google.com/patents/US4628742), "Tensile strength tester for hair" Hairs that big around are hard to come by.[6]... I hope. Since most of us have many small hairs, instead of one big hair ... [Image: image] ... we'd need to get a lot of hairs and bundle them together. Given that individual hairs can support about 50 grams of weight, we'd need roughly 20 heads of hair to restrain the aircraft. [Image: image] Conclusion: Restraining a plane with a cable would be pretty easy. Further conclusion: Blue whales are not typically covered in hair,[8]Although they are mammals, most whales do not have coats of hair like land mammals typically do (http://bioweb.uwlax.edu/bio203/s2012/olson_rile/adaptation.htm) but if we transplanted the hair from at least 20 human heads onto a blue whale ... [Image: image] ... it would have enough hair to perform acrobatics at a circus.
items.original_question: 如果你想将一架飞机固定在地面上，使其无法起飞，那么绳子必须用什么材料制成？
items.model_answer:
If you tried to hold an airplane to the ground with a rope, the exact outcome would depend on the tensile strength of the rope, the structural integrity of the airplane, and whether the rope is already taut when the engines throttle up. 

If the rope is unbreakable, securely anchored, and already pulled tight before the pilot throttles up, the airplane will simply sit on the runway and strain against the tether. Airplanes do not fly by pushing off the ground; they fly because forward motion forces air over the wings, generating lift. Without forward movement, the wings generate zero lift. The engines will run at maximum thrust, burning fuel and creating a massive windstorm behind the aircraft, but the plane will remain completely grounded. 

If the rope is left slack, allowing the airplane to accelerate down the runway before reaching the end of the tether, the result would be catastrophic. A commercial airliner generates immense kinetic energy during its takeoff roll. When the rope suddenly goes taut, that energy must be instantly dissipated. If the rope and ground anchor are strong enough to hold, the sudden deceleration will rip the airplane apart. The immense force will tear off the landing gear, the tail section, or wherever the rope is attached, causing the airframe to collapse and likely resulting in a fiery crash. 

However, if you use a standard rope—even a very thick nylon marine rope—on a large commercial jet, the airplane will win. The thrust of a modern jetliner can exceed 100,000 pounds of force, which easily surpasses the breaking strength of most conventional ropes. In this scenario, the engines will spool up, the rope will snap almost instantly, and the airplane will take off normally with nothing more than a slight jolt. 

Ultimately, you will either snap the rope, destroy the airplane, or create a very loud, stationary wind machine, but in no scenario does the airplane successfully take flight while tethered.

items.question: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?
human_answers: The one-inch gap would take about 70 milliseconds to close. Don't stick your hand in. [Image: image] The impact could trigger an earthquake. Denali (also known as Mount McKinley) is a mountain in Alaska that sits just to the south of a major fault line.[1]Roger A. Hansen, Earthquake and Seismic Monitoring in Denali National Park (http://www.nps.gov/akso/nature/science/ak_park_science/PDF/2006Vol5-1/Earthquake-Monitoring.pdf), National Park Service This fault is active,[2]Alaska Earthquake Information Center, M 7.9 Denali Fault earthquake of November 3, 2002 (http://www.aeic.alaska.edu/Denali_Fault_2002/) and we know that drilling can trigger earthquakes.[3]Van der elst NJ, Savage HM, Keranen KM, Abers GA. Enhanced remote earthquake triggering at fluid-injection sites in the midwestern United States (http://www.sciencemag.org/content/341/6142/164.abstract). Science. 2013;341(6142):164-7. Earthquakes can happen at any time, so there's always a chance that dropping a mountain any distance could trigger one. So could kicking a tree. The only way to find out for sure would be to try it.[4]This article has an awful lot of citations. Assuming it didn't trigger an earthquake, the impact wouldn't be all that dramatic. If you were standing on the mountain when it happened, you'd definitely feel a jolt, but it probably wouldn't even be enough to knock you down. [Image: image] When the mountain hit the ground, the rock under it would be damaged, but only a little. The granite base is strong enough to hold up under the tremendous resting weight of a mountain;[5]Citation: The rock was holding up a mountain when you got there. the shockwave from dropping it an inch doesn't add too much pressure on top of that, and the rock would survive with a little minor cracking. People nearby would definitely feel the impact, and probably hear it; the sound would likely resemble the crack of a lightning strike (if you were standing near the mountain) fading into a long, deep rumble.[6]Citation: A dream I had once. The vibration would be equivalent to that of a 3.5-magnitude earthquake[7]For more on the specific seismic details, see Stein, Seth, and Michael Wysession. "Earthquakes." An Introduction to Seismology, Earthquakes, and Earth Structure. Malden, MA: Blackwell Pub., 2003. 241 (http://books.google.com/books?id=-z80yrwFsqoC&lpg=PA241&ots=nrVTZ77_mJ&pg=PA241#v=onepage&q&f=false). Print.; at worst, it would knock a few pictures off the wall if you happened to be living next to the mountain. Frankly, I'd be more worried about debris flying out of the gap.[8]If your magical mountain-cutter put air in the space where the rock used to be, you should avoid standing near the crack when it falls. The air will come jetting out from the closing crack, spraying rocks and dust at speeds approaching, or even—thanks to some fun heat-related effects—exceeding, Mach 1. [Image: image] Oh. You again. Ok. Dropping from a height of one foot wouldn't be all that different. [Image: image] The mountain would hit the ground at 2.5 m/s, or roughly walking speed. The shockwave from that impact would be in the range of 50 megapascals of pressure,[9]You can calculate the peak pressure of the compressive strain wave in the rock using the Joukowsky equation, which says that the peak pressure of the compressive wave in a material is (material's density)x(speed at impact)x(the speed of sound in the material). items.original_question: 如果一座巨大的山峰（比如麦金利山）的底部一英寸消失了怎么办？山体下降1英寸的影响会发生什么？ 1英尺呢？如果山脚升高到山顶现在的高度，然后让整个山落到地上怎么办？
items.model_answer:
If the bottom inch of a massive mountain suddenly vanished, the entire mountain would instantly fall into the newly empty space, resulting in a catastrophic release of energy, a massive earthquake, and structural collapse. 

While a one-inch drop sounds negligible to a human, a massive mountain weighs anywhere from billions to trillions of tons. When gravity pulls this colossal mass downward, it converts a tremendous amount of potential energy into kinetic energy. As the mountain free-falls for a fraction of a second and violently slams into the bedrock below, all of that kinetic energy must be dissipated instantly. 

For a mountain the size of Mount Everest or Mount Fuji, dropping just one inch and suddenly decelerating would release energy equivalent to hundreds of kilotons of TNT—comparable to a large thermonuclear detonation or a magnitude 6 to 7 earthquake. Because this energy is released precisely at the surface boundary, it would generate a severe, incredibly shallow seismic shockwave that would ripple destructively through the surrounding Earth's crust.

Furthermore, mountains are not solid, unbreakable blocks of stone; they are highly fractured masses of rock held together by gravity and friction. Rock is highly brittle and terrible at handling sudden shear stress. The violent jolt of stopping after a one-inch drop would shatter the mountain's internal structural integrity. 

The immediate surface aftermath would be apocalyptic for the local environment. The shockwave would instantly destabilize the slopes, triggering colossal landslides, massive rockfalls, and avalanches in every direction. Millions of tons of pulverized rock and debris would cascade into the surrounding valleys at highway speeds. Ultimately, the mountain would not simply sit an inch lower and remain intact; the violent impact would cause it to slump, fracture, and shed a massive portion of its exterior, permanently altering the geography of the region.

items.question: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?
human_answers: The answers to these questions all hinge on the same idea. It's an idea I've touched on in other articles, but today I want to focus on it specifically: The reason it's hard to get to orbit isn't that space is high up. It's hard to get to orbit because you have to go so fast. Space isn't like this: [Image: image] Space is like this: [Image: image] Space is about 100 kilometers away. That's far away—I wouldn't want to climb a ladder to get there—but it isn't that far away. If you're in Sacramento, Seattle, Canberra, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Phnom Penh, Cairo, Beijing, central Japan, central Sri Lanka, or Portland, space is closer than the sea. Getting to space[1]Specifically, low Earth orbit, which is where the International Space Station is and where the shuttles could go. is easy. It's not, like, something you could do in your car, but it's not a huge challenge. You could get a person to space with a small sounding rocket the size of a telephone pole. The X-15 aircraft reached space[2]The X-15 reached 100 km on two occasions, both when flown by Joe Walker. just by going fast and then steering up.[3]Make sure to remember to steer up and not down, or you will have a bad time. [Image: image] But getting to space is easy. The problem is staying there. Gravity in low Earth orbit is almost as strong as gravity on the surface. The Space Station hasn't escaped Earth's gravity at all; it's experiencing about 90% the pull that we feel on the surface. To avoid falling back into the atmosphere, you have to go sideways really, really fast. The speed you need to stay in orbit is about 8 kilometers per second.[4]It's a little less if you're in the higher region of low Earth orbit. Only a fraction of a rocket's energy is used to lift up out of the atmosphere; the vast majority of it is used to gain orbital (sideways) speed. This leads us to the central problem of getting into orbit: Reaching orbital speed takes much more fuel than reaching orbital height. Getting a ship up to 8 km/s takes a lot of booster rockets. Reaching orbital speed is hard enough; reaching to orbital speed while carrying enough fuel to slow back down would be completely impractical.[5]This exponential increase is the central problem of rocketry: The fuel required to increase your speed by one km/s multiplies your weight by about 1.4. To get into orbit, you need to increase your speed to 8 km/s, which means you'll need a lot of fuel: $ 1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\approx 15$ times the original weight of your ship. Using a rocket to slow down carries the same problem: Every 1 km/s decrease in speed multiplies your starting mass by that same factor of 1.4. If you want to slow all the way down to zero—and drop gently into the atmosphere—the fuel requirements multiply your weight by 15 again. These outrageous fuel requirements are why every spacecraft entering an atmosphere has braked using a heat shield instead of rockets—slamming into the air is the most practical way to slow down. (And to answer Brian's question, the Curiosity rover was no exception to this; although it used small rockets to hover when it was near the surface, it first used air-braking to shed the majority of its speed.) How fast is 8 km/s, anyway? I think the reason for a lot of confusion about these issues is that when astronauts are in orbit, it doesn't seem like they're moving that fast; they look like they're drifting slowly over a blue marble. But 8 km/s is blisteringly fast. When you look at the sky near sunset, you can sometimes see the ISS go past ... and then, 90 minutes later, see it go past again.[6]There are some good apps and online tools to help you spot the station, along with other neat satellites. My favorite is ISS Detector (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.runar.issdetector), but if you Google you can find lots of others. In those 90 minutes, it's circled the entire world. The ISS moves so quickly that if you fired a rifle bullet from one end of a football field,[7]Either kind. the International Space Station could cross the length of the field before the bullet traveled 10 yards.[8]This type of play is legal in Australian rules football. Let's imagine what it would look like if you were speed-walking across the Earth's surface at 8 km/s. To get a better sense of the pace at which you're traveling, let's use the beat of a song to mark the passage of time.[9]Using song beats to help measure the passage of time is a technique also used in CPR training, where the song "Stayin' Alive" is used to . suppose you started playing the 1988 song by The Proclaimers, I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles). That song is about 131.9 beats per minute, so imagine that with every beat of the song, you move forward more than two miles. In the time it took to sing the first line of the chorus, you could walk from the Statue of Liberty all the way to the Bronx: [Image: image] It would take you about two lines of the chorus (16 beats of the song) to cross the English Channel between London and France. The song's length leads to an odd coincidence. The interval between the start and the end of I'm Gonna Be is 3 minutes and 30 seconds,[10]Based on timing from the official Youtube video (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tbNlMtqrYS0) and the ISS is moving at 7.66 km/s. This means that if an astronaut on the ISS listens to I'm Gonna Be, in the time between the first beat of the song and the final lines ... [Image: image] ... they will have traveled just about exactly 1,000 miles.
items.original_question: 如果航天器使用火星天空起重机等火箭助推器在重返大气层时减速至每小时几英里会怎么样？它会消除对隔热罩的需要吗？
items.model_answer:
If a spacecraft used rockets to slow from orbital speeds (about 17,500 mph) to a few miles per hour before reentering the Earth's atmosphere, it would avoid the extreme heat and plasma of a standard fiery reentry, but the mission would be practically impossible due to the sheer amount of fuel required. 

To cancel its orbital velocity entirely, the spacecraft would need to execute a retrograde burn requiring roughly the same amount of energy and delta-v (change in velocity) that it took to achieve orbit in the first place. Because of the "tyranny of the rocket equation," every pound of fuel needed to stop the spacecraft in space must be launched from Earth. To carry enough braking propellant to a low Earth orbit, the initial launch vehicle would have to be exponentially larger and heavier—likely requiring a rocket vastly larger than the Saturn V just to return a tiny, Apollo-sized capsule.

Furthermore, if the spacecraft successfully scrubbed all its forward velocity and stopped in space, it would lose the outward centrifugal force keeping it in orbit and immediately begin falling straight down. As it fell, Earth's gravity would quickly accelerate it back up to a high terminal velocity. To actually maintain a speed of just a few miles per hour all the way down to the surface, the spacecraft would have to continuously fire its engines against gravity for the entire descent, demanding an even more absurd amount of fuel. 

Because of this extreme weight penalty, aerospace engineers use the Earth's atmosphere as a "free" brake. It is vastly lighter and cheaper to equip a spacecraft with a heat shield to dissipate its immense kinetic energy through aerodynamic drag than it is to carry the millions of pounds of rocket fuel required to slow down mechanically.

items.question: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?
human_answers: This many: [Image: image] That's surprisingly few printers! But before you try to create a live-updating paper Wikipedia, let's look at what those printers would be doing ... and how much they'd cost. Printing Wikipedia People have considered printing out Wikipedia before. A few years ago, student Rob Matthews printed every Wikipedia featured article (http://www.brandnew.uk.com/wikipedia-as-a-printed-book/), creating a book several feet thick. Of course, that's just a small slice of the best of Wikipedia; the entire encyclopedia would be a lot bigger. Wikipedia user Tompw (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User:Tompw) has set up a page (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Size_in_volumes) for calculating the size of the whole English Wikipedia in printed volumes. It would currently fill a lot of bookshelves. Keeping up with the edits would be harder. Keeping up The English Wikipedia currently receives about 125,000 to 150,000 edits each day, or 90-100 per minute.[1]ToolServer: Edit rate (http://toolserver.org/~emijrp/wmcharts/wmchart0001.php) We could try to define a way to measure the "word count" of the average edit, but that's hard bordering on impossible. Fortunately, we don't need to—we can just estimate that each change is going to require us to reprint a page somewhere. Many edits will actually change multiple pages—but many other edits are reverts, which would let us put back pages we've already printed.[2]The filing system for this would be staggering (http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IBM_card_storage.NARA.jpg). One page per edit seems like a reasonable middle ground. For a mix of photos, tables, and text typical of Wikipedia, a good inkjet printer might put out 15 pages per minute. That means you'd only need about six printers running at any given time to keep pace with the edits. The paper would stack up quickly. Using Rob Matthews' book as a starting point, I did my own back-of-the-envelope estimate for the size of the current English Wikipedia. Based on the average length of featured articles vs. all articles, I came up with an estimate of 300 cubic meters for a printout of the whole thing.[3]That's a little larger than Tompw's estimate, but I'm assuming they're printed straight from the browser, which is less compact and includes images. By comparison, if you were trying to keep up with the edits, you'd print out 300 cubic meters every month. $500,000 per month Six printers isn't that many, but they'd be running all the time. And that gets expensive. The electricity to run them would be cheap—a few dollars a day. The paper would be about one cent per sheet, which means you'll be spending about a thousand dollars a day. You'd want to hire people to manage the printers 24/7, but that would actually cost less than the paper. Even the printers themselves wouldn't be too expensive, despite the terrifying replacement cycle. But the ink cartridges would be a nightmare. Ink A study by QualityLogic[4]QualityLogic: Cost of Ink Per Page Analysis (http://www.qualitylogic.com/tuneup/uploads/docfiles/QualityLogic-Cost-of-Ink-Per-Page-Analysis_US_1-Jun-2012.pdf), June 2012 found that for a typical inkjet printer, the real-life cost of ink ran from 5 cents per page for black-and-white to around 30 cents per page for photos. That means you'd be spending four to five figures per day on ink cartridges. You definitely want to invest in a laser printer. Otherwise, in just a month or two, this project could end up costing you half a million dollars: [Image: image] But that's not even the worst part. If, someday, Wikipedia decides to go dark (http://sys01-public.msnbc.msn.com/technology/wikipedia-goes-dark-piracy-bill-protest-day-117714) again, and you want to join the protest ... [Image: image] You'll have to get a crate of markers and color every page solid black yourself. I would definitely stick to digital.
items.original_question: 如果您有整个（例如英文）维基百科的印刷版本，您需要多少台打印机才能跟上对实时版本所做的更改？
items.model_answer:
If you tried to print the entire English Wikipedia in real time, you would immediately face an insurmountable logistical and physical nightmare driven by the sheer volume of existing text and the relentless speed of continuous edits. 

First, to print the existing backlog of over 6.8 million articles, you would generate the equivalent of a massive physical library. In 2015, artist Michael Mandiberg wrote software to parse the English Wikipedia and calculated that printing just the text at that time would fill 7,473 volumes of 700 pages each. Today, that number would easily exceed 10,000 volumes. Printing this baseline alone would take a standard commercial printer months of continuous operation, consuming thousands of gallons of ink, hundreds of trees, and filling a large warehouse.

However, the "real-time" aspect is where the experiment completely breaks down. The English Wikipedia is a living document that experiences an average of 1.5 to 2 edits every single second. If your goal is to maintain an accurate printed copy by reprinting a page every time it is altered, a standard home printer—which typically maxes out at 15 to 30 pages per minute—would instantly fall behind the roughly 90 to 120 edits occurring per minute. You would need a continuous feed from a high-speed industrial printing press or a parallel array of multiple commercial printers just to output the changing pages. 

Even if you possessed the hardware to print the updates at a rate of two pages per second, the physical management of the archive would be impossible for a single person. You would need a dedicated team of workers constantly running through your warehouse to locate the outdated pages in the tens of thousands of bound volumes, remove them, and insert the newly printed revisions. Because heavily trafficked articles (like current events or pop culture pages) are sometimes edited dozens of times in a single minute, your team would be replacing the same pages over and over again.

Ultimately, attempting to print Wikipedia in real time would result in an ever-growing mountain of wasted paper, an astronomical financial drain for ink and electricity, and a physical archive that is perpetually out of date the exact moment the ink hits the page.

items.question: What If You Jumped from a Plane with Helium Tanks and a Giant Balloon?
human_answers: As ridiculous as it sounds, this is—sort of—possible. Falling from great heights is dangerous.[citation needed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Republic_Presidential_Unit_Citation)] A balloon could actually help save you, although a regular helium one from a party obviously won't do the trick. [Image: image] If the balloon is large enough, you don't even need the helium. A balloon will act as a parachute, slowing your fall to non-fatal speeds. Avoiding a high-speed landing is, unsurprisingly, the key to survival. As one medical paper[1]De Haven H. Mechanical analysis of survival in falls from heights of fifty to one hundred and fifty feet (http://injuryprevention.bmj.com/content/6/1/62.3.long). Injury Prevention. 6(1):62-b-68. put it, It is, of course, obvious that speed, or height of fall, is not in itself injurious ... but a high rate of change of velocity, such as occurs after a 10 story fall onto concrete, is another matter. ... which is just a wordy version of the old saying, "It's not the fall that kills you, it's the sudden stop at the end." To act as a parachute, a balloon filled with air, rather than helium, would have to be 10 to 20 meters across—far too big to be inflated with portable tanks. A powerful fan could be used to fill it with ambient air, but at that point, you may as well just use a parachute. Helium The helium makes things easier. It doesn't take too many helium balloons to lift a person. In 1982, Larry Walters (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Walters) flew across Los Angeles in a lawn chair lifted by weather balloons, eventually reaching several miles in altitude. After passing through LAX airspace, he descended by shooting some of the balloons with a pellet gun. On landing, Walters was arrested, although the authorities had some trouble figuring out what to charge him with. At the time, an FAA safety inspector told the New York Times, "We know he broke some part of the Federal Aviation Act, and as soon as we decide which part it is, some type of charge will be filed."[2]ARMCHAIR AIRMAN SAYS FLIGHT FULFILLED HIS LIFELONG DREAM (http://www.nytimes.com/1982/07/04/us/armchair-airman-says-flight-fulfilled-his-lifelong-dream.html?pagewanted=all), New York Times, July 4, 1982 A relatively small helium balloon—certainly smaller than a parachute—will suffice slow your fall, but it still has to be huge by party balloon standards. The biggest consumer rental helium tanks are about 250 cubic feet, and you'd need to empty at least 10 of them to put enough air in the balloon to support your weight. You'd have to do it quickly. The compressed helium cylinders are smooth and often quite heavy, which means they have a high terminal velocity. You'll only have a few minutes to use up all the cylinders. (As soon as you emptied one, you could drop it.) You can't get around this problem by moving your starting point higher. Since the upper atmosphere is pretty thin, anything dropped from the stratosphere up will accelerate to very high speeds until it hits the lower atmosphere, then fall slowly the rest of the way. This is true of everything from small meteors[3]By the time meteors hit the Earth, they have slowed down (http://www.geology.wisc.edu/~museum/meteorite.html) to a few hundred miles per hour. to Felix Baumgartner.[4]Jason Martinez, Falling Faster than the Speed of Sound (http://blog.wolfram.com/2012/10/24/falling-faster-than-the-speed-of-sound/), Wolfram Blog, October 24, 2012 [Image: image] But if you inflated the balloons quickly, possibly by connecting many canisters to it at once, you'd be able to slow your fall. Just don't use too much helium, or you'll end up floating at 16,000 feet like Larry Walters.http://xkcd.com/1110 [Image: image] While researching this article,[5]Additionally, while researching impact speeds for this article, I came across a discussion (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=361878) on the Straight Dope Message Boards about survivable fall heights. One poster compared a fall from height to being hit by a bus. Another user, a medical examiner, replied (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showpost.php?p=7180162&postcount=40) that this was a bad comparison: "When hit by a car, the vast majority of people are not run over; they are run under. The lower legs break, sending them into the air. They usually strike the hood of the car, often with the back of the head impacting the windshield, "starring" the windshield, possibly leaving a few hairs in the glass. They then go over the top of the car. They are still alive, although with broken legs, and maybe with head pain from the nonfatal windshield impact. They die when they hit the ground. They die from head injury." The lesson: Don't mess with medical examiners. They're apparently pretty hardcore. I managed to lock up my copy of Mathematica several times on balloon-related differential equations, and subsequently got my IP address banned from Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=how+many+days+have+i+been+alive) for making too many requests. The ban-appeal form asked me to explain what task I was performing that necessitated so many queries, so this is what I put: [Image: image] I hope they understand.
items.original_question: 如果我带着几罐氦气和一个巨大的未充气的气球从飞机上跳下来怎么办？然后，在下降时，我释放氦气并填充气球。我需要下落多长时间才能让气球减慢我的速度以便我能够安全着陆？
items.model_answer:
If you jumped from a plane with helium tanks and a giant balloon, you would plummet to the ground and not survive, as the setup would completely fail to slow your fall due to several fundamental laws of physics. 

First, there is the insurmountable problem of weight. To hold enough helium to lift a human, the gas must be highly pressurized inside heavy metal or composite cylinders. The lifting force of helium is roughly 1 kilogram per cubic meter. A standard steel high-pressure tank might weigh 130 pounds (60 kg) but only hold enough expanded helium to lift about 22 pounds (10 kg). Therefore, the tanks weigh significantly more than the maximum lift their contents can provide. Instead of making you buoyant, the tanks would act as massive dead weights, pulling you down and increasing your kinetic energy.

Second, the aerodynamics of freefall would destroy your equipment. As you fall at terminal velocity (over 120 mph or 190 km/h), the uninflated balloon fabric would trail behind you in the slipstream. The violent whipping of the extreme wind shear would almost certainly shred the balloon material to pieces before you could even attempt to inflate it. 

Third, there is the issue of time and gas flow rates. A typical skydive from 10,000 feet gives you roughly 60 seconds of freefall before impact. It is physically impossible to vent the massive volume of high-pressure gas required to fill a giant balloon through standard tank valves in under a minute. 

Even if the balloon miraculously survived the wind shear and you possessed magical valves that inflated it instantly, the math still does not work in your favor. The combined weight of your body, the rigging, and the heavy tanks would far exceed the buoyant force of the helium. You would hit the ground at a lethal speed, with the added danger of heavy, highly pressurized metal cylinders strapped to your body.

items.question: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?
human_answers: [Image: image] Google almost certainly has more data storage capacity than any other organization on Earth. Google is very secretive about its operations, so it's hard to say for sure. There are only a handful of organizations who might plausibly have more storage capacity or a larger server infrastructure. Here's my short list of the top contenders: NSA (http://www.nsa.gov/) NRO (http://www.nro.gov/) NGIP (https://www1.nga.mil/Pages/default.aspx) CIA (https://www.cia.gov/index.html) Schlumberger (http://www.slb.com/) Tencent (http://www.tencent.com/en-us/index.shtml) Chevron (http://www.chevron.com/) Honorable mentions: Amazon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River) (They're huge, but probably not as big as Google.) Facebook (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_book) (They're on the right scale and growing fast, but still playing catch-up.) Microsoft (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Bob) (They have a million servers,[1]Data Center Knowledge: [Ballmer: Microsoft has 1 Million Servers although no one seems sure why.) Let's take a closer look at Google's computing platform. Follow the money We'll start by following the money. Google's aggregate capital expenditures–spending on building stuff[2]I'm excluding the cost of an extremely expensive building they bought in New York.—adds up to somewhere over $12 billion dollars.[3]Data Center Knowledge: Google’s Data Center Building Boom Continues: $1.6 Billion Investment in 3 Months (http://www.datacenterknowledge.com/archives/2013/07/19/google-data-center-spending-continues-to-soar-1-6-billion-in-3-months/) Their biggest data centers cost half a billion to a billion dollars, so they can't have more than 20 or so of those. On their website,[4]Data center locations (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/inside/locations/index.html) Google acknowledges that they have datacenters in the following locations: Berkeley County, South Carolina Council Bluffs, Iowa Atlanta, Georgia Mayes County, Oklahoma Lenoir, North Carolina The Dalles, Oregon Hong Kong Singapore Taiwan Hamina, Finland St Ghislain, Belgium Dublin, Ireland Quilicura, Chile In addition, they appear to operate a number of other large datacenters (sometimes through subsidiary corporations), including: Eemshaven, Netherlands Groningen, Netherlands Budapest, Hungary Wrocław, Poland Reston, Virginia Additional sites near Atlanta, Georgia They also operate equipment at dozens to hundreds of smaller locations around the world. Follow the power To figure out how many servers Google is running, we can look at their electricity consumption. Unfortunately, we can't just sneak up to a datacenter and read the meter.[5]Actually, wait, can we? Somebody should try that. Instead, we have to do some digging. The company disclosed that in 2010 they consumed an average of 258 megawatts of power.[6]Google used 2,259,998 MWh of electricity in 2010 (http://www.environmentalleader.com/2011/09/09/google-reveals-electricity-use-breaking-its-silence/), which translates to an average of 258 megawatts. How many computers can they run with that? We know that their datacenters are quite efficient, only spending 10-20% of their power on cooling and other overhead.[7]Google: Efficiency: How we do it (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/efficiency/internal/) To get an idea of how much power each server uses, we can look at their "container data center" concept from 2005. It's not clear whether they actually use these containers in practice—it may just have been a now-outdated experiment—but it gives an idea of what they consider(ed) reasonable power consumption. The answer: 215 watts per server. Judging from that number, in 2010, they were operating around a million servers. They've grown a lot since then. By the end of 2013, the total amount of money they've pumped into their datacenters will be three or four times what it was as of 2010. They've contracted to buy over three hundred megawatts of power at just three sites,[8]Google: Purchasing clean energy (http://www.google.com/green/energy/use/#purchasing) which is more than they used for all their operations in 2010. Based on datacenter power usage and spending estimates, my guess would be that Google is currently running—or will soon be running—between 1.8 and 2.4 million servers. But what do these "servers" actually represent? Google could be experimenting in all kinds of wild ways, running boards with 100 cores or 100 attached disks. If we assume that each server has a couple[9]Anywhere from 2 to 5 (http://xkcd.com/1070/) of 2 TB disks attached, we come up with close to 10 exabytes[10]As a refresher, the order is: kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta, exa, zetta, yotta. An exabyte is a million terabytes. of active storage attached to running clusters. 10 Exabytes The commercial hard disk industry ships about 8 exabytes worth of drives annually.[12]IDC: Worldwide External Disk Storage Systems Factory Revenue Declines for the Second Consecutive Quarter (http://www.idc.com/getdoc.jsp?containerId=prUS24302513) Those numbers don't necessarily include companies like Google, but in any case, it seems likely that Google is a large piece of the global hard drive market. To make things worse, given the huge number of drives they manage, Google has a hard drive die every few minutes.[11]Eduardo Pinheiro, Wolf-Dietrich Weber and Luiz Andre Barroso, [Failure Trends in a Large Disk Drive Population This isn't actually all that expensive a problem, in the grand scheme of things—they just get good at replacing drives—but it's weird to think that when a Googler runs a piece of code, they know that by the time it finishes executing, one of the machines it was running on will probably have suffered a drive failure. Google tape storage Of course, that only covers storage attached to running servers. What about "cold" storage? Who knows how much data Google—or anyone else—has stored in basement archives? In a 2011 phone interview with Paul Mah of SMB Tech, Simon Anderson of Tandberg Data let slip[13]SMB Tech: Is Tape Still Relevant for SMBs? (http://www.itbusinessedge.com/cm/blogs/mah/is-tape-still-relevant-for-smbs/?cs=45557) that Google is the world's biggest single consumer of magnetic tape cartridges, purchasing 200,000 per year. Assuming they've stepped up their purchasing since then as they've expanded, this could add up to another few exabytes of tape archives. Putting it all together Let's assume Google has a storage capacity of 15 exabytes, or 15,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes. A punch card can hold about 80 characters, and a box of cards holds 2000 cards: [Image: image] 15 exabytes of punch cards would be enough to cover my home region, New England, to a depth of about 4.5 kilometers. That's three times deeper than the ice sheets that covered the region during the last advance of the glaciers: [Image: image] That seems like a lot. However, it's nothing compared to the ridiculous claims by some news reports about the NSA datacenter in Utah. NSA datacenter The NSA is building a datacenter in Utah. Media reports claimed that it could hold up to a yottabyte of data,[14]CNET: NSA to store yottabytes in Utah data centre (http://crave.cnet.co.uk/gadgets/nsa-to-store-yottabytes-in-utah-data-centre-49304118/) which is patently absurd. Later reports changed their minds, suggesting that the facility could only hold on the order of 3-12 exabytes.[15]Forbes: Blueprints Of NSA's Ridiculously Expensive Data Center In Utah Suggest It Holds Less Info Than Thought (http://www.forbes.com/sites/kashmirhill/2013/07/24/blueprints-of-nsa-data-center-in-utah-suggest-its-storage-capacity-is-less-impressive-than-thought/) We also know the facility uses about 65 megawatts of power,[16]Salt-Lake City Tribune: NSA Bluffdale Center won’t gobble up Utah’s power supply (http://www.sltrib.com/sltrib/news/56493868-78/power-center-electricity-utah.html.csp) which is about what a large Google datacenter consumes. A few headlines, rather than going with one estimate or the other, announced that the facility could hold "between an exabyte and a yottabyte" of data[17]Dailykos: Utah Data Center stores data between 1 exabyte and 1 yottabyte (http://www.dailykos.com/story/2013/08/05/1228923/-Utah-Data-Center-stores-data-between-1-exabyte-and-1-yottabyte) ... which is a little like saying "eyewitnesses report that the snake was between 1 millimeter and 1 kilometer long." Uncovering further Google secrets There are a lot of tricks for digging up information about Google's operations. Ironically, many of them involve using Google itself—from Googling for job postings in strange cities to using image search to find leaked cell camera photos of datacenter visits. However, the best trick for locating secret Google facilities might be the one revealed by ex-Googler talentlessclown (http://www.reddit.com/user/talentlessclown) on reddit:[18]reddit: Can r/Australia help find Google's Sydney data center? Seems like a bit of a mystery... (http://www.reddit.com/r/australia/comments/1hctj4/can_raustralia_help_find_googles_sydney_data/catef4f) The easiest way to find manned Google data centres is to ask taxi drivers and pizza delivery people. There's something pleasing about that. Google has created what might be the most sophisticated information-gathering apparatus in the history of the Earth ... and the only people with information about them are the pizza delivery drivers. Who watches the watchers? [Image: image] Apparently, Domino's.
items.original_question: 如果所有数字数据都存储在打孔卡上，谷歌的数据仓库有多大？
items.model_answer:
If all of humanity's current digital data were stored on standard IBM punch cards, the physical, ecological, and logistical consequences would be catastrophic, fundamentally collapsing modern civilization. 

To understand the scale, we have to look at the math. A standard punch card holds exactly 80 characters, or 80 bytes of data. The global datasphere is currently estimated to be around 120 zettabytes (120 sextillion bytes). To store this much information, it would require approximately 1.5 sextillion punch cards. A single punch card is roughly 0.17 millimeters thick; if you were to stack these cards into a single pile, the tower would stretch for over 28 light-years into space. If you instead opted to spread them out, the total volume of these cards would exceed 4 million cubic kilometers. This means that if you scattered the punch cards evenly across the entire surface of the Earth, including the oceans, they would blanket the globe in a layer of paper roughly 8 meters (26 feet) deep. 

The ecological impact of manufacturing this medium would be impossible to sustain. A standard punch card weighs about 2.5 grams, bringing the total mass of our data to nearly 3.75 trillion metric tons. Producing this much cardstock would require harvesting roughly 5,000 times more trees than currently exist on the entire planet. The endeavor would completely strip Earth of its forests, devastate the global biosphere, and require more fresh water and energy than humanity produces, just for the paper milling process.

Even if the physical resources magically existed, technology and society as we know it would grind to a halt. Mechanical card readers, even at their absolute peak, can only process a few thousand cards per minute. At that speed, it would take centuries to load the data equivalent of a single modern terabyte hard drive. The internet, real-time communication, streaming media, and global financial markets would instantly cease to exist. Data retrieval would transform from an instantaneous electronic process into a massive logistical undertaking requiring trains, cargo ships, and continent-sized warehouses just to move and store basic information. Ultimately, the speed of computing would be limited by the physical transportation of paper, reverting society to a hyper-bureaucratic, pre-electronic age where only the most vital data could realistically be preserved.

items.question: What If You Began Rising Upward at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: Did you bring a coat? A foot per second isn't that fast—it's substantially slower than a typical elevator.[1]Otis: About Elevators (http://www.otisworldwide.com/pdf/AboutElevators.pdf) It would take you 5-7 seconds to rise out of arms' reach, depending how tall your friends are. [Image: image] After 30 seconds, you'd be 30 feet—9 meters—off the ground. Judging from What-If #44 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/44/), this is getting close to your last chance for a friend to throw you a sandwich or water bottle or something.[2]Not that it will help, ultimately. [Image: image] After a minute or two you would be above the trees. You'd still be about as comfortable as you were on the ground. If it's a breezy day, it will probably get chillier thanks to the steadier wind above the treeline.[3]For this article, I'm going to assume a typical atmosphere temperature profile. It can, of course, vary quite a bit. After 10 minutes you would be above all but the tallest skyscrapers, and after 25 minutes you'd pass the spire of the Empire State Building. [Image: image] The air at these heights is about 3% thinner than it is at the surface. Fortunately, your body handles air pressure changes like that all the time. Your ears may pop, but you wouldn't really notice anything else. Air pressure changes quickly with height. Surprisingly, when you're standing on the ground, air pressure is even measurably lower at your head than at your feet. If your phone has a barometer in it, as a lot of new Android phones do, you can download an app and actually see the pressure difference between your head and your feet. A foot per second is pretty close to a kilometer per hour, so after an hour, you'll be about a kilometer off the ground. At this point, you definitely start to get chilly. If you have a coat, you'll still be ok, though you might also notice the wind picking up. At about two hours and two kilometers, the temperature would drop below freezing. The wind would also, most likely, be picking up. If you have any exposed skin, this is where frostbite starts to become a concern.[4]National Weather Service: Wind Chill Temperature Index (http://www.nws.noaa.gov/om/windchill/images/wind-chill-brochure.pdf) Starting at this point, the air pressure would drop below what you'd experience in an airliner cabin,[5]... which are typically kept pressurized at about 70%-80% of sea level pressure, judging from the barometer in my phone. and the effects would start to become more significant, but unless you had a warm coat, the temperature would be a bigger problem. Over the next two hours, the air would drop to below-zero[6]Either unit.​[7]Not Kelvin, though. temperatures. Assuming for a moment that you survived the oxygen deprivation, at some point you'd freeze to death. But when? The scholarly authorities on freezing to death seem to be, unsurprisingly, Canadians. The most widely-used model for human survival in cold air was developed by Peter Tikuisis and John Frim for the Defence and Civil Institute of Environmental Medicine in Ontario.[8]Prediction of Survival Time in Cold Air (http://cradpdf.drdc-rddc.gc.ca/PDFS/zba6/p144967.pdf)—see page 24 for the relevant tables. According to their model, the main factor in the cause of death would be your clothes. If you were nude, you'd probably succumb to hypothermia somewhere around the five hour mark, before your oxygen ran out.[9]And frankly, this really raises more questions than it answers. If you were bundled up, you may be frostbitten, but you would probably survive ... ... long enough to reach the Death Zone. [Image: image] Above 8,000 meters—above the tops of all but the highest mountains—the oxygen content in the air is too low to support human life. Near this zone, you would experience a range of symptoms, possibly including confusion, dizziness, clumsiness, impaired vision, and nausea. As you approach the Death Zone, your blood oxygen content would plummet. Your veins are supposed to bring low-oxygen blood back to your lungs to be refilled with oxygen. But in the Death Zone, there's so little oxygen in the air that your veins lose oxygen to the air instead of gaining it.[10]Linda D. Pendleton, When Humans Fly High: What Pilots Should Know About High-Altitude Physiology, Hypoxia, and Rapid Decompression (http://www.avweb.com/news/aeromed/181893-1.html) The result would be a rapid loss of consciousness and death. This would happen around the seven hour mark; the chances are very slim that you would make it to eight. [Image: image] And two million years later, your frozen body, still moving along steadily at a foot per second, would pass through the heliopause into interstellar space—the same boundary that Voyager just crossed.[11]Again. Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto, died in 1997. A portion of his remains were placed on New Horizons spacecraft, which will fly past Pluto and then continue out of the Solar System. It's true that your hypothetical foot-per-second trip would be cold, unpleasant, and rapidly fatal. But when the Sun becomes a red giant in four billion years and consumes the Earth, you and Clyde would be the only ones to escape. So there's that. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果你突然开始以每秒一英尺的速度稳定上升，你到底会怎么死？你会先被冻住还是窒息？或者其他什么？
items.model_answer:
If you began rising vertically at a constant rate of one foot per second, your immediate fate would depend heavily on whether you were indoors or outdoors. 

If you were indoors, you would gently bump into the ceiling within a few seconds. Assuming the mysterious force lifting you is unstoppable and maintains your velocity regardless of resistance, you would be slowly and agonizingly crushed against the ceiling, or you would eventually break through the roof's structural supports.

If you were outdoors, your ascent would begin as a peaceful, scenic elevator ride, taking you up at a rate of 60 feet per minute. After just one minute, you would be higher than a five-story building. After an hour, you would reach an altitude of 3,600 feet—higher than the Burj Khalifa, the tallest building in the world. At this point, the temperature would be noticeably colder, as the air temperature drops by roughly 3.5 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit for every 1,000 feet of elevation.

Around the two-hour mark (7,200 feet), you would likely begin to feel the mild effects of altitude sickness. By five hours, you would pass 18,000 feet. Here, atmospheric pressure is half of what it is at sea level. You would experience severe hypoxia, leading to confusion, dizziness, and eventually unconsciousness. 

By the eight-hour mark, you would be nearly 29,000 feet in the air, matching the height of Mount Everest and the cruising altitude of commercial airliners. The ambient temperature would plummet to around -40 degrees Fahrenheit. If you had not already suffocated from the lack of oxygen, you would freeze to death shortly after reaching this zone. 

Your frozen body would continue its slow, unstoppable ascent. After roughly 3.8 days (91 hours), you would reach an altitude of 62 miles (328,000 feet) and cross the Kármán line, officially entering outer space. Because you are only moving vertically at one foot per second and completely lack the roughly 17,500 mph horizontal velocity required to achieve Earth orbit, you would not become a satellite. Instead, you would just keep moving in a straight line. As the Earth rotates and orbits the Sun away from your trajectory, your frozen remains would eventually drift out into the vacuum of the solar system.

items.question: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?
human_answers: Absolutely! [Image: image] Some things don't work like they do in the movies. Getting shot doesn't really make someone fly backward. The vacuum of space doesn't make your skin explode. But high wind can definitely pick up a person. In fact, if you were standing in the parking lot, the wind wouldn't just pick you up—it would also peel the pavement from the ground! [Image: image] It wouldn't be strong enough to peel your skin off. Humans can survive blasts of 500 mph wind, which is important because pilots sometimes need to eject from airplanes at those speeds. In the 1940s, the US government put pilots in wind tunnels to learn how they reacted to high winds. Have you ever been curious what happens to a person's face in 457 mph winds? Well, you can watch a video of one of those wind tunnel tests here (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IU4SDDNXuUA). (That test was conducted at NASA Langley Research Center, where I worked before I started drawing internet comics for a living.) It doesn't look very comfortable—I didn't know cheeks could flap like that—but the pilot appears to stay alive. Luckily, he's strapped into that chair. He wouldn't be able to stand up in those winds! If he tried, he would go flying backward down the tunnel. High wind is really powerful. In a paper in the journal Weather, J. F. R. McIlveen showed how to calculate the force of wind on the human body.[1]McIlveen, J. F. R.. "The Everyday Effects Of Wind Drag On People. (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1256/wea.29.02/pdf)" Weather 57, no. 11 (2002): 410-413. The calculations on page 2 show how far you'd have to lean to stay upright in wind of various speeds. [Image: image] When wind speed rises above about 120 mph, it's no longer possible to stay upright no matter how far you lean; you'll start to slide backward across the ground,[2]When Hurricane Isabel hit Virginia in 2003, I had the bright idea of standing on a skateboard with a poncho held up like a sail, so the wind would blow me down the street. But the moment I got the sail up, the wind fell quiet. Later, I learned that people die from doing that (http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-1327705/Kite-surfer-28-dies-gale-drags-100mph-beach-drops-50ft.html). Oops. then quickly go head over heels and start to tumble. You wouldn't necessarily be thrown very high. If the wind were perfectly level, you'd tumble along the surface, bouncing against the ground. However, if there were any updrafts, you could easily be lifted up and carried away. The good news is that 500 mph winds are rare. The strongest hurricanes have wind speeds around 200 mph with gusts up to 250.[3]Courtney, J.; Buchan, S.; Cerveny, R.S.; Bessemoulin, P.; Peterson, T.C.; Rubiera Torres, J.M.; Beven, J.; King, J.; Trerwin, B.; Rancourt, K.. 2012 "Documentation and verification of the world extreme wind gust record: 113.3 m s–1 on Barrow Island, Australia, during passage of tropical cyclone Olivia. (http://www.bom.gov.au/amoj/docs/2012/courtney_hres.pdf)" Australian Meterological and Oceanographic Journal, 62 (1). 1-9. Tornadoes can reach 300 mph.[4]It's difficult to get accurate measurements of surface winds since those tornadoes destroy most measuring equipment (http://www.spc.noaa.gov/faq/tornado/#History)! 300 is a far cry from 500; the force from a 500 mph wind is several times stronger than the force from a 300 mph wind. There are a few ways you could experience wind speeds faster than 500 mph. One is to stand on top of a volcano when it erupts. When Mount St. Helens exploded in 1980, the column of ash was blasted outward at 700 mph, which is close to the speed of sound.[5]Kieffer, S. W., 1981, Fluid dynamics of the May 18 blast at Mount St. Helens, in Lipman, P.W., and Mullineux, D.R., eds., The 1980 Eruptions of Mount St. Helens, Washington: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 1250, p. 379-400. Another way to experience 500 mph winds is to trigger a hypercane.[6]Limits on Hurricane Intensity (http://wind.mit.edu/~emanuel/holem/holem.html) A hypercane is an exotic type of hurricane with 500 mph winds spinning in a very tight vortex just a few miles across. Hypercanes can't exist on Earth right now. To form, they require ocean temperatures of about 50°C. No matter how much we warm the planet, we're not going to get the temperature that high any time soon. However, there's one way these storms might happen. When an asteroid or comet—coincidentally, one about the size of the recently-named 4942 Munroe (http://blog.xkcd.com/2013/09/30/asteroid-4942-munroe/)—hit Mexico 65 million years ago, it punched a hole in the crust and left behind a sea of lava.[7]Christeson, Gail L., Gareth S. Collins, Joanna V. Morgan, Sean P.S. Gulick, Penny J. Barton, and Michael R. Warner. "Mantle Deformation Beneath The Chicxulub Impact Crater (https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/bitstream/10044/1/4214/1/icpub.pdf)." Earth and Planetary Science Letters 284, no. 1-2 (2009): 249-257. When water flowed back in to fill the hole, it would have been heated by contact with the molten rock. This might have created the conditions for hypercanes to form, and one paper suggests that these storms could have lifted a large amount of dust and debris into the upper atmosphere—thus contributing to a global winter and extinction of the dinosaurs.[8]Emanuel, Kerry A., Kevin Speer, Richard Rotunno, Ramesh Srivastava, and Mario Molina. "Hypercanes: A Possible Link In Global Extinction Scenarios (ftp://texmex.mit.edu/pub/emanuel/PAPERS/hypercane95.pdf)." Journal of Geophysical Research 100, no. D7 (1995): 13755-13765. [Image: image] In short, the answer to Grey's question is yes—500 mph winds would send you flying through the air. But don't worry about that. Instead, worry about is the thing that created the 500 mph winds. Odds are, that's what's going to kill you. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果风速达到 500 英里/小时，它会卷起人吗？
items.model_answer:
If wind speeds reached 500 miles per hour—nearly double the highest wind speed ever recorded on Earth—the resulting devastation would be apocalyptic, effectively scouring the affected surface clean. Because the aerodynamic drag force of wind scales with the square of its velocity, a 500 mph wind would not just be twice as destructive as a 250 mph EF5 tornado; it would be four times as powerful, and roughly 25 times more destructive than a 100 mph hurricane. 

At this velocity, human civilization above ground would be completely obliterated. Standard residential and commercial buildings would disintegrate instantly.
